0286a0bec241.text: By — Anna Wilder, Associated Press/Report For America Anna Wilder, Associated Press/Report For America By — Safiyah Riddle, Associated Press Safiyah Riddle, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/nation/federal-prosecutors-charge-venezuelan-man-shot-in-his-car-by-ice-agent-in-texas-with-assaulting-an-officer Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Federal prosecutors charge Venezuelan man shot in his car by ICE agent in Texas with assaulting an officer Nation Sep 29, 2026 6:16 PM EDT AUSTIN, Texas (AP) — Federal prosecutors on Tuesday announced an assault charge against a Venezuelan delivery driver who was shot in his car by a federal immigration agent in Texas, accusing the man of striking an officer with his side mirror while trying to drive away. Wilber Rafael Garces Perez, 28, was charged with one count of assaulting, resisting and impeding a federal officer, according to a criminal complaint. Garces Perez, whose attorney has said still has a bullet lodged in his back from the Sept. 20 shooting, made an initial court appearance in an Austin federal court on Tuesday, according to the U.S. Attorney's Office in the Western District of Texas. READ MORE: ICE agent shoots and wounds man in Austin, Texas, officials say A nine-page affidavit from a Department of Homeland Security agent amounts to the government's fullest public account to date of the shooting in the Texas capital, which has set off protests and outrage from Democrats over the Trump administration's immigration crackdown. The document includes photos taken from body-worn cameras but no video was released, and the complaint did not say whether the agent allegedly struck by the side mirror sustained any injuries. The accusations against Garces Perez are reminiscent of previous claims made by immigration agents after high-profile shootings, in which officers have similarly accused drivers of weaponizing their vehicles. In a handful of cases, those allegations have been undermined or walked back after the release of body-worn camera footage, and have renewed scrutiny about the DHS's reliance on vehicular stops to execute arrests. Garces Perez was in the custody of U.S. Marshals after being removed from a federal detention center in South Texas, according to court documents filed by federal prosecutors. Separately, Garces Perez's attorneys have filed a lawsuit seeking to stop his removal from the U.S. If convicted, Garces Perez faces up to 20 years in prison. An attorney for Garces Perez declined to immediately comment on Tuesday. A DHS spokesperson referred questions to the Department of Justice. Affidavit says agent was struck in torso by side mirror According to an affidavit signed by a DHS agent, officers first saw Garces Perez's car parked outside of a restaurant with its emergency flashers on. They decided to pull him over after conducting a database check that showed the car was registered to Garces Perez who had a final order of removal from the U.S. The agents said that they turned on their lights to execute the stop, but in the same filing, Garces Perez told investigators that an unmarked SUV followed him and then abruptly cut him off on the side of the road. Garces Perez, who was making a DoorDash delivery, provided his driver's license through a crack in the window, but ignored agents' requests to step out of the car, the complaint said. Garces Perez told investigators that he declined to exit because he had asked for officers to wait to apprehend him until his wife could come retrieve his car. Court documents describe the interaction as initially conversational, with a tone that was "pleasant and not aggressive." About a minute later, according to court records, Garces Perez "abruptly" closed the window and drove off. One of the officers, who is referred to only by his initials, was struck in his torso with the driver's side view mirror when Garces Perez tried to drive away, the documents say. Officer who fired wasn't wearing body camera The unnamed officer who shot Garces Perez wasn't wearing a body camera. The other officer involved in the chase was wearing a camera, but only caught up to the chase after Garces Perez had been shot, according to the affidavit. ICE has previously said its field officers nationwide will have body-worn cameras by the end of September. The affidavit included screenshots from previously unreleased body-worn camera footage of the officer's initial interactions with ICE agents. The first of three photos appear to show the officer standing in front of Garces Perez's driver's door mirror; the second shows the officer resting his hands on the hood and side of Garces Perez's car, with the mirror close to or touching the officer's abdomen; and the third shows the car pulling away. READ MORE: Man shot by ICE in Austin held with a bullet still in his back, attorney says The Austin Police Department last week released video last week from its officers but that footage did not show the shooting or the moment that Garces Perez allegedly tried driving away. Conflicting accounts of lead-up to shooting The affidavit includes Garces Perez providing his account to federal investigators, which paints a contrasting picture of the lead-up to the shooting than what federal prosecutors described. According to the affidavit, Garces Perez said that a law enforcement SUV struck his car after a brief chase and caused it to spin before an agent opened fire, shooting him in the back. By contrast, U.S. Attorney Justin R. Simmons said in a statement that Garces Perez tried to strike an officer with his car, "causing the officer to fire his pistol." Garces Perez entered the U.S. in 2024 using CBP One, a program begun under President Joe Biden that allowed migrants to make appointments with U.S. authorities to be considered for asylum. President Trump ended the program on his first day in office. Garces Perez was an asylum seeker and had a valid work perm

More than 400 people, mostly minors, were detained in France on Tuesday over student protests at high schools across the country, the French interior minister said.
The demonstrations, which began in Paris and have seen teenagers blockade their schools for days, stem from issues including overcrowded classes and teacher shortages.
At least 10 teachers and several students, as well as 48 law enforcement officials, were injured during Tuesday's protests, officials said. According to the education ministry, at least 400 schools were affected.
Pictures and videos appeared to show bins being set alight and bus stops damaged by protesters.
"We're here to deliver a message," one 16-year-old female student told the AFP news agency. "We're not here to smash everything up for no reason. We're here precisely to say that the education system is completely broken. There are 34 of us in each class, and it's just not feasible. The teachers are overworked."
Taking to X, French Education Minister Ãdouard Geffray said students have the right to protest, but condemned reports of violence as "indefensible".
Interior Minister Laurent NuÃ±ez told BFMTV 440 people were detained, adding: "We don't have the final tally yet, but I'm told two thirds led to police custody."
French media reported that protesters hurled projectiles at police, who responded with batons and tear gas.
Speaking to AFP, Ryad Rani, president of Union Syndicale LycÃ©enne, which represents students, accused the French government of "repression" and police of using excessive force.
When pressed on the police response to the protests, which has been criticised by several French politicians, NuÃ±ez said it had been "carried out in an extremely proportionate manner".
Writing on social media on Tuesday evening, education minister Geffray said: "The right to demonstrate is a fundamental freedom that cannot serve as an excuse for such actions.
"To legitimise them or, in this context, to call for extending the blockades is to endanger our students as well as public employees. It is irresponsible."
The movement at French lycÃ©es, equivalent to sixth form in the UK or high school in the US, began last week in the Ãle-de-France region around Paris.
On Monday, France's Prime Minister SÃ©bastien Lecornu warned any escalation in the student protests would be "irresponsible" following the arrest of 164 people.
Lecornu cited reported incidents at protests in a post on X, saying: "Fireworks, fires, violence near high schools: nothing justifies endangering students, staff, or police officers."
The continuing student demonstrations on Tuesday coincided with nationwide walkouts by unions representing teachers, hospital staff and civil servants to protest against issues including low wages and working conditions.
NuÃ±ez said these protests, with at least 200,000 participants reported, mostly went without incident.

9e8939ac5e61.text: Boeing will build the U.S. Navy's next fighter aircraft, following years of clandestine competition and multiple contracting false alarms. Why it matters: Boeing's win in the F/A-XX competition means the company's sixth-generation aircraft will succeed the Super Hornet fleet, long relied upon and recently employed across the Middle East. The company is also constructing the Air Force's F-47, previously unveiled in an Oval Office address featuring President Trump and Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth. The latest: The Pentagon announced the deal Tuesday. It's worth more than $20 billion. It comes after months of squabbling between the White House, Pentagon, lawmakers and industry. Its ups and downs and rumored award timelines were closely watched by defense analysts and reporters. Context: Boeing bested Northrop Grumman. Lockheed Martin was previously knocked out of the running. Executives from both companies had told Axios they were confident in their offerings. State of play: Little has been revealed about the warplane's final design. But it will complement the F-35, of which there are short-takeoff and carrier variants. What they're saying: Former Navy Secretary John Phelan in December told Axios that F/A-XX was, in fact, not dead. He previously told lawmakers the warplane would ensure naval air dominance. Chief of Naval Operations Adm. Daryl Caudle advocated for the project during his nomination hearing, telling lawmakers the service "must have an air wing that is comprised of the most advanced strike fighters." And Caudle's predecessor, Lisa Franchetti , suggested it would sport "advanced sensors, advanced lethality, advanced range" and be able to "integrate with manned and unmanned capabilities." More from Axios: American airpower F/A-XX decision must be "made quickly," Navy chief says Trump administration shelves Navy's F/A-XX, citing industry strain

How Lindsay Clancy's return to court after mistrial unfolded
Lindsay Clancy has appeared in court for the first time since her murder trial fell apart, with lawyers on both sides arguing how to proceed with the case.
Her defence argued that the judge should use his power to declare her not guilty. Her lawyer, Kevin Reddington, also brought a new defence forward arguing there was not enough evidence to prove Clancy killed her children.
Posecutors say the state "met its burden" in proving Clancy's guilt. During court, both sides also resisted the judge's request to decide a potential retrial date, arguing that important legal questions still need to be decided first.
The BBC's Ione Wells breaks down how Lindsay Clancy's first court appearance went after her 4 September mistrial.

c0112bdc5ab0.text: By — Akram Oubachir, Associated Press Akram Oubachir, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/world/moroccos-king-appoints-fatima-zahra-mansouri-as-countrys-1st-woman-prime-minister Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Morocco's king appoints Fatima Zahra Mansouri as country's 1st woman prime minister World Sep 29, 2026 7:06 PM EDT CASABLANCA, Morocco (AP) — Morocco's King Mohammed VI on Tuesday named Urban Planning Minister Fatima Zahra Mansouri as the country's prime minister, making the 50-year-old attorney the first woman to hold the position in the Muslim kingdom. Mansouri, who until her nomination also was the mayor of Marrakech, was tasked with forming a new government, the Royal Palace said in a statement. The announcement came four days after results of parliamentary elections were announced, with Mansouri's centrist Authenticity and Modernity Party, or PAM, the highest vote-getter. Mansouri, the second woman to serve as prime minister in the Arab world after Najla Bouden in Tunisia, is expected to build a coalition in coming days to form a government. Morocco's electoral system makes it difficult for a single party to win an absolute majority. Her government is expected to make billions of dollars in investments linked to the 2030 FIFA World Cup, while seeking to deliver on promises to fight inflation, raise wages and create jobs. READ MORE: Saudi Arabia named as 2034 FIFA World Cup host; Spain, Portugal and Morocco to co-host 2030 edition The Moroccan Constitution gives the king, who is the country's highest authority, the power to appoint the prime minister, but he must choose from the party that wins the most seats in parliamentary elections. That was a change successfully pushed by Arab Spring protesters in 2011. Before that, the king could name the prime minister without any such restriction. Mansouri joined PAM upon its creation in 2008 by Fouad Ali El Himma, a childhood friend and close adviser to the king. A law graduate from the University of Montpellier in France, Mansouri became one of the party's top leaders in 2024. She twice served as mayor of Marrakech and was a member of parliament. Mansouri is the daughter of the "pasha of Marrakech" Abderrahmane El Mansouri, a senior local official who was also Morocco's ambassador to the United Arab Emirates. He headed Marrakech's bar association and was a landowner. Mansouri faced accusations of conflict of interest after a group of unidentified hackers claimed she had used her position for personal gain regarding land transactions in Marrakech. Mansouri denied the allegations, called them defamatory and took legal action. One million of the 15.8 million registered voters in last week's election voted for the Authenticity and Modernity Party, marking its first win since its creation. The election was the first since the Ceuta migration crisis last July and deadly youth-led protests last year. After the royal nomination, the focus shifts to the coalition that will form the next government. PAM has expressed its willingness to work with all parties, but some, including the moderate Islamist Justice and Development party and left-wing Federation of Democratic Left, have announced they will remain in the opposition. 96ebc0e4af87.text: Top tech executives met with President Trump on Tuesday to discuss the future of artificial intelligence amid growing concerns over AI models losing control. Researchers and lawmakers are calling for stronger safeguards, but Trump said the technology is transforming the economy and that the U.S. cannot afford to lose its lead over China. Geoff Bennett discussed more with Gary Marcus. Amna Nawaz: Top executives from the leading tech companies in the U.S. met with President Donald Trump today to discuss the future of artificial intelligence amidst growing concerns over AI models losing control. Geoff Bennett: The meeting came after the president unveiled a new A.I.-powered Web site designed to help Americans navigate government services. The president is also pushing a new name for artificial intelligence, superintelligence, as he argues the technology is transforming the economy and that the U.S. cannot afford to lose its lead over China. Donald Trump: This is one more example of why I will never stifle the growth of technology that will be bigger than the Industrial Revolution. President Xi knows that. We're leading by a lot. And we don't want to mix it up too much either. Somebody said, oh, let's do a joint venture. Let's work together with China. But if we do that, we're going to be giving a lot of secrets that -- that we have that they just would want to have or anybody else. And, frankly, there is nobody in third place. I mean, it's all between us and China. Geoff Bennett: That push for innovation comes amid growing calls from researchers and lawmakers for stronger safeguards and growing concern about whether those protections can keep pace with the technology. For more on the future of AI, we're joined now by Gary Marcus, professor emeritus at New York University. He's also the author of "Taming Silicon Valley" and the Substack Marcus on AI. Thanks for being with us. Gary Marcus, A.I. Researcher: My pleasure to be here. Geoff Bennett: So we have heard on this program from AI researchers and experts who have warned about the potential for catastrophic, even existential risks from AI. You have pushed back on some of those warnings. What do you see differently? Gary Marcus: So I don't think extinction is a real likely risk for humanity. All of the scenarios, the so-called doom scenarios where AI just wipes us out like in "The Terminator," all assume that we won't fight back, and we will. They all kind of miss some details about how we are geographically diverse, genetically diverse. They're just fantasies and not realistic. So extinction is not likely, but catastrophe might be likely. So we already had an incident where an AI reported something wrong and almost led to a war. And we will see more of those, because these systems make errors and hallucinations. We're seeing lots of cyber hacking. And that might lead -- excuse me -- to, for example, the temporary takedown of an electric grid that leads to the temporary takedown of a hospital. We saw something like that with the WannaCry virus in the U.K. a few years ago. So, there are lots of vulnerabilities. There may be serious damage. I just don't -- I don't think that extinction is actually one of the things that should keep us up at night. Geoff Bennett: And it raises the question of what to do about it. The president, as he met with those tech leaders at the White House today, he seems focused on self-regulation. In fact, he says the industry is capable of what he calls tremendous self-regulation, and they signed a voluntary agreement focused on AI safety reviews. Is self-regulation enough? Gary Marcus: It's certainly not enough. And trusting these companies is insane. The New York Times just broke a story saying that OpenAI was aware of the problems that gave rise to the Hugging Face incident that everybody is talking about months before it even happened, and they didn't do anything because they wanted to rush their products to the market. That's exactly why we can't rely on self-regulation and why we need outside regulation, just like we have in aviation and food and drugs and everything else. It's absurd to exempt the AI companies, when they have shown time and again that they are not responsible. Geoff Bennett: How do you regulate these companies without simply giving China an advantage? Gary Marcus: I think the race against China is a little bit overblown. China actually does have regulation, has licensing regime around its own software products. And we race in industries all the time, but still have some kind of regulation around them. We don't make terrible cars just because we want to beat China on cars. Right now, the U.S. AI industry is building deeply problematic software, and we need to make sure that the companies make sure that it is safe. And this kind of race against China is not a reason not to do that. Moreover, the race against China is really going to end in a tie. It's going to be like Coke and Pepsi. Both nations are going to have their own so-called sovereign AI, but neither is going to completely wipe out the other. And so the whole race aspect makes it zero sum, and that's really not what we should be doing. Geoff Bennett: You have been calling for a dedicated federal AI agency for years. What power should the government have that it doesn't currently have? Gary Marcus: What we really need most of all is independent evaluation of new software products, the same way we have for new drugs. You should have to, if you're the maker, show that the benefits outweigh the risks. This should be like 101 and obvious. Right now, the White House is actually doing a lot of that, but without independent oversight with a secret framework that they haven't revealed to the public. So they did actually preclude one system, which was Mythos by Anthropic. They delayed it. They didn't delay OpenAI's latest system, which actually has, I think, more problems in some way. And so this is happening, but in an idiosyncratic way, which m

bcad802dfd4d.text: An investigation into an alleged gang rape in 2024 at Cornell University has been reopened after the woman who reported the assault sued the school and others. At the time, no criminal charges were filed, though Cornell said it investigated and took disciplinary action, including suspensions and expulsions. Amna Nawaz discussed more with Brian Mann of NPR. Amna Nawaz: An investigation into an alleged gang rape in 2024 at Cornell University has been reopened after the woman who reported the assault sued the school and others. Identified only as Jane Doe in the case, the woman said officials didn't do enough in light of the allegations that during a party at the Chi Phi fraternity, she was given alcohol and pressure to snort ketamine before multiple men assaulted her and invited others to join in. At the time, no criminal charges were filed, though Cornell said it invested and took disciplinary action, including suspensions and expulsions. The Chi Phi fraternity was closed that year and banned from campus. The Tompkins County district attorney said on CNN today that the details in Jane Doe's original statement did not support criminal charges. Matthew Van Houten, Tompkins County, New York, District Attorney: The young men who engaged in that conduct were morally wrong. It was disgusting. And so she reported that to the police, and the police investigated it. That does not mean, if it's morally wrong or disgusting or offensive, all those things, it does not mean that the penal law was violated. Amna Nawaz: Brian Mann is based in New York. He's been covering the story for NPR, and he joins us now. Brian, welcome back to the "News Hour." Thanks for joining us. Brian Mann, National Public Radio: Thanks for having me. Amna Nawaz: Let's start with the timing here. As you mentioned, the incident was reported to university police almost two years ago. That was a few weeks after the alleged rape took place. Do we know what led to this civil complaint now being filed earlier this month and the investigation being reopened? Brian Mann: Yes, so this woman who describes herself in the lawsuit as Jane Doe has really laid out a case that something truly horrific happened that night in October 2024. And she also claims that Cornell University failed to respond appropriately, failed to investigate what happened appropriately. She says these seven men, students at the time, abused her over a period of hours, often in truly brutal ways. Now she's seeking compensation for that. This is a sweeping lawsuit. As you just heard, there were never any criminal charges filed. And it's also still unclear at this point what exact disciplinary actions these seven students faced. Amna Nawaz: Prosecutors are now saying they're going to present their case to a grand jury. Do we know how quickly that's going to move forward? Brian Mann: We don't know the timing, and, honestly, we don't know what the outcome will be. I have been speaking with people on campus, but I have also been speaking with the defense attorney for at least one of these men, who says he does not actually believe that criminal charges will follow. One of the things that's raising concern here and, in fact, a lot of criticism here is that this alleged gang rape was only investigated by Cornell campus police. It was never brought to the attention to -- of Ithaca police or of State Police investigators. The mayor of Ithaca, the city has called that handling irresponsible. He says this was a miscarriage of justice. We have also had New York Governor Kathy Hochul come out today saying she has deep concerns about how this was all handled. She's calling for an independent probe of Cornell University's actions here. Amna Nawaz: And, as we noted there, Brian, the university said they did take disciplinary actions back when the incident was first reported. But what is happening now on the university? How are they responding to this latest step? Brian Mann: Well, clearly, Cornell University feels under siege right now. This blew up into a global online phenomenon spread by major media celebrities and politicians on Instagram and other platforms when the civil lawsuit was filed. I have tried repeatedly to interview members of Cornell University's leadership. They have declined. They have sent very brief statements saying that they do think significant disciplinary action happened. They say there were not just slaps on the wrist here. But it is possible, according to our reporting, that some of these seven men were allowed to remain on campus as students. The woman involved, Jane Doe, in the civil lawsuit did leave campus. But it appears that at least some of these men were allowed to continue pursuing their studies here after this alleged rape occurred. Amna Nawaz: Brian, as you know, The Cornell Daily Sun named all seven young men who are civil defendants in this lawsuit. Some of those young men have even reportedly lost their jobs this week. How is all of this resonating on campus? Brian Mann: Yes, there's a lot of anger and frustration. And there is a strong opinion on campus that these seven men should have faced more investigation and possibly more punishment. While I was on campus today, I also heard from a lot of students real compassion and sorrow for the young woman, Jane Doe, who's named in this civil lawsuit. Women in particular who I talked to say they believe she went through a real ordeal in this investigation, the way that the case was handled by Cornell, by campus police. And the fact that she wound up leaving the school, while at least some of these young men were apparently allowed to continue their studies, I heard anger and sadness over what's happened to her. Amna Nawaz: That is Brian Mann of NPR joining us tonight. Brian, thank you so much. Brian Mann: Thanks for having me.

South Africa's President Cyril Ramaphosa on Tuesday announced a clean-up of high-risk areas across the country, after the bodies of 12 women were discovered in an area east of Johannesburg in just two months.
The deaths sparked a national outcry about the scale of violence against women in South Africa, which has one of the highest rates of gender-based violence in the world.
Ramaphosa announced what he called a multidisciplinary, national-level emergency response to the murders, for which there have been four arrests.
He said gender-based violence "cannot be accepted as a normal part of life in South Africa" and admitted the country has "not done enough" to protect women and girls.
"There has understandably been widespread fear that the discovery of these women in close proximity could indicate the work of a single perpetrator," Ramaphosa said in an address to the nation.
"At present, the police have not found evidence establishing that these killings were committed by a single perpetrator."
Admitting the government has not done enough in recent years to prevent gender-based violence, he announced a new wave of measures to help protect women and girls.
"Every municipality must begin a women's safety audit without delay," he said. "High-risk areas must be identified" and addressed.
"These audits must identify broken streetlights, overgrown public spaces, abandoned buildings, unsafe transport routes and facilities, poorly secured parks, and other conditions that place women at risk."
Ramaphosa also announced an "enforcement package" to reduce alcohol-related violence.
"Alcohol does not cause gender-based violence and it can never excuse it. Responsibility always lies with the perpetrator," he said.
"But harmful alcohol use is a significant aggravating factor in interpersonal violence, and it must be addressed as part of our wider prevention effort."
The South African president also said a deeper change, beyond policing and legislation, must take place to reduce violence against women and girls, saying it "does not begin when a fist is raised" or when a woman is raped or murdered.
"It begins much earlier," he said. "It begins in attitudes that regard women as inferiorâ¦ with the belief that a man has the right to control a woman.
"It begins when jealousy is mistaken for love, when control is mistaken for protection and coercion is mistaken for affection.
"It begins when a man refuses to accept the word no."
He went on to call on men and boys to take the lead in ending gender-based violence.
"We have placed the burden of male violence on women," Ramaphosa said. "That must change."
"The solution to violence against women cannot be to make women less free."
South Africa has one of the highest homicide rates, with 5,427 people murdered between April and June this year alone.
While South African police statistics do not differentiate victims by gender, the South African Human Rights Commission said recently that 569 women were killed and 1,052 others survived attempted murder between April and June this year.

Six Flags Magic Mountain, an amusement park in California, has announced it will permanently close a popular rollercoaster after hundreds of riders alleged they suffered brain injuries.
The X2 rollercoaster, one of the park's main attractions, with long wait times to ride and seats that spin 360 degrees, has been closed since July.
Six Flags said the ride had passed a range of safety tests, but that it had decided to retire it because it was "the right thing to do".
The decision comes after lawsuits and news reports alleged that hundreds of riders suffered brain injuries after riding X2. A law firm representing some of the plaintiffs said the decision had come "too late" for its clients.
Announcing the closure on Tuesday, , external Six Flags Magic Mountain Park President Brian Oerding said: "Ride safety is a cornerstone of our business, and when we see guest confidence affected, we take it seriously."
Dordick Law Corporation, who filed civil lawsuits against the park, said it had been contacted by hundreds of people who alleged they had injuries they believed were caused by the ride.
"They got on X2 expecting a thrill. Instead, they left with catastrophic brain injuries," the firm said in a statement. "Some needed emergency brain surgery. Some are still fighting to get their lives back."
The law firm said that while it welcomed the closure of the ride to protect future guests, "it does nothing for the people who have already been hurt".
Originally called X, the ride first opened in 2002 but was closed months later for repairs to design flaws, the Los Angeles Times reports. It was then closed again in 2007 to replace its trains with lighter versions.
It reopened the following year as X2 and since then has been ridden by more than 16 million people, the park said.
A law firm that represented the family of 22-year-old Christopher Hawley, who died after riding X2 in 2022, said the closure was not enough.
While the Hawley family is "relieved to hear that Six Flags is finally closing the X2, it does not change the fact that Christopher Hawley was killed by a dangerous roller coaster that was allowed to operate for nearly two decades," attorney Brent Wisner of Wisner Baum LLP said in a statement to the BBC.
Hawley's family settled a wrongful death suit with the theme park in August.
"That tragedy cannot be undone," Wisner said, calling for legal reform, proactive regulation and proper governmental oversight.
"We cannot rely on profit-centered corporations to do the right thing only after enough people have been hurt," he added. "We hope that whatever replaces the X2 is safe."

5f511bc0e896.text: By — Anthony Izaguirre, Associated Press Anthony Izaguirre, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/politics/mamdani-releases-plan-to-combat-antisemitism-in-new-york-amid-concerns-over-his-criticism-of-israel Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Mamdani releases plan to combat antisemitism in New York amid concerns over his criticism of Israel Politics Sep 29, 2026 6:32 PM EDT NEW YORK (AP) — Mayor Zohran Mamdani debuted a sweeping plan Tuesday to combat antisemitism and hate crimes against Jewish people in New York City, moving to assuage concerns from critics who see his steadfast denunciations of Israel as antisemitic. Please check your inbox to confirm. The strategy includes increased security funding for synagogues, an increased focus on folding Jewish history into public school education, and a pledge to highlight important Jewish cultural and religious sites in the mayor's day-to-day governance of the city. Mamdani said the overarching goal of the initiative was to "confront the scourge of antisemitism now and in the future," noting that Jewish people make up only 12% of the city's population but are the victims of around half the city's reported hate crimes. "This is not only unacceptable, it's something we all have an obligation to change. And City Hall will lead the way," he said in a video. Mamdani, a Democrat and the city's first Muslim mayor, has long been a vocal supporter of Palestinian civil rights and has accused the Israeli government of committing a genocide in Gaza. He has said his criticism of Israel does not amount to antisemitism, though his opponents have argued his heated rhetoric around the conflict has made Jewish people feel unsafe in the city. The plan announced Tuesday amounts to the mayor's most forceful attempt to address concerns over antisemitism, with Mamdani promising to "build a city where Jewish New Yorkers are not only safe but celebrated." City Hall will increase grant funding to community organizations that focus on hate crime prevention and survivor support. It will also work with public schools to address complaints of discrimination and launch public awareness campaigns on the city's human rights law and how to report suspected discrimination. READ MORE: Mamdani says NYC can't arrest Netanyahu but the federal government should Rabbi Rick Jacobs, president of the Union for Reform Judaism, praised elements of the mayor's plan but called on Mamdani to lower the temperature on his rhetoric about Israel. "For this effort to be effective, Mayor Mamdani must also commit to stopping his harsh anti-Israel rhetoric that makes Jewish New Yorkers vulnerable as there are clearly times when antisemitic attacks are fueled by anti-Zionism," Jacobs said. Brad Lander, a Jewish ally of Mamdani and former city comptroller, said the initiative was a "thoughtful, strategic combination of education for tolerance, enforcement of civil rights, and investments in safety." Mamdani faced a barrage of criticism during his campaign last year after he declined to disavow the phrase "globalize the intifada," a slogan some see as a call to violence against Jews, though he did not use the phrase and later said he would discourage others from saying it. He has also faced questions over a decision in June to skip an annual parade honoring Israel, which has long been a must-attend event for politicians in the city. Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu dedicated a portion of an address at the United Nations last week to assailing Mamdani, accusing him of spreading lies about Israel and calling him "the antisemitic mayor of New York." Mamdani has repeatedly called for Netanyahu to be arrested under a warrant from the International Criminal Court alleging war crimes in Gaza. Ofir Akunis, Israel's consul general in New York, said Tuesday that the mayor's position on Israel has endangered Jewish New Yorkers. "Until you recognize that your language against the Jewish State, which you don't recognize as the homeland of the Jewish people, is the fundamental reason for the rise of antisemitism in New York City, it will continue to increase," Akunis wrote on X. AP National Writer David Crary contributed to this report. A free press is a cornerstone of a healthy democracy. Support trusted journalism and civil dialogue. 894ad32a0c01.text: By — Diana Roy, Council on Foreign Relations Diana Roy, Council on Foreign Relations Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/world/who-will-be-the-uns-next-secretary-general-what-to-know-about-the-selection-process Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Who will be the UN's next secretary-general? What to know about the selection process World Sep 29, 2026 7:45 PM EDT This article was originally published by the Council on Foreign Relations. The race to become the next United Nations secretary-general is well underway. The winner, who is typically chosen and appointed between October and December of the current officeholder's final year, will become the United Nations' 10th secretary-general. They will take office on Jan. 1, 2027, succeeding incumbent António Guterres. READ MORE: Four U.N. secretary-general candidates audition this week. That's far fewer than in 2016 This year's secretary-general selection could be of particular significance because the United Nations may choose its first-ever woman leader — seven candidates are currently in the running, four of whom are women. Based on the United Nations' informal regional rotation, there is also a strong possibility that a candidate from the Latin American and Caribbean region will be selected. However, regardless of who takes the helm of the United Nations come January, experts agree they will be responsible for steering the 81-year-old organization through multiple critical challenges, including internal reforms, severe funding shortfalls, worsening climate change, the proliferation of artificial intelligence, and escalating geopolitical tensions. Who is the UN secretary-general? The secretary-general serves as the United Nations' chief administrative officer and de facto head of the U.N. system. The role, which is described as being "equal parts diplomat and advocate, civil servant and CEO," was created with the adoption of the U.N. Charter in 1945. The first appointment, Trygve Lie, took place in 1946. "On one hand, it's a remarkably powerless position, and yet it's also a highly influential position," Richard Gowan, program director for global issues and institutions at the International Crisis Group, told CFR. "But the reason(s) that it's influential are a little intangible," he said, pointing to the secretary-general's ability to use the pulpit they have, the willingness of member states to buy into their agenda, and the role of global public opinion. Beyond describing the role of the secretary-general, the U.N. Charter says nothing about the qualifications, desired qualities, tenure, or selection process for the position. Given the lack of detail, the United Nations has established criteria over time through resolutions and other documents. "As is the case with any major leadership job, it will depend on the individual," said Esther Brimmer, CFR's James H. Binger senior fellow in global governance. "A lot of the conversation about the selection of a secretary-general will be about what qualities are needed to address the crises and issues that we're facing." The secretary-general retains broad discretion in how they approach the role, and secretaries-general have expanded the scope of the position in different ways. Some, like Dag Hammarskjöld (1953–1961) and U Thant (1961–1971), served as more of a mediator, while others, like Kofi Annan (1997-2006), were considered more of an activist. Who are the candidates for UN secretary-general? There are seven candidates running to become the next secretary-general. They are: Ivonne A-Baki. A former Ecuadorian ambassador to several countries, including the United States, France, and Qatar, A-Baki says the United Nations needs "not another caretaker, but a peacemaker." Her vision statement for the role emphasizes preventing and ending wars, reforming the Security Council's membership, and rebuilding institutional trust from within the organization. María Fernanda Espinosa Garcés. The former president of the General Assembly and former foreign minister and defense minister of Ecuador has centered her candidacy around five pillars: peace and security, development, digital and energy transformation, closing the delivery gap, and rebuilding the United Nations' credibility. Rafael Mariano Grossi. Grossi has been director general of the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) since 2019. He was formerly the Argentine ambassador to Austria, as well as the Argentine representative to the IAEA and other Vienna-based international organizations. Grossi advocates for a more effective and results-driven United Nations, noting in an April interview with CFR that his experiences leading the IAEA have prepared him well for the secretary-general role, particularly when it comes to handling complex emergencies. Rebeca Grynspan Mayufis. The former vice president of Costa Rica is currently secretary-general of U.N. Trade and Development. A renowned economist, she says the United Nations is confronting simultaneous political, legitimacy, and operational crises, and that she will focus her tenure on restoring confidence in the organization, rebuilding "the foundations of international security" by prioritizing peacemaking, and delivering results. Olara Otunnu. A veteran diplomat, Otunnu served as U.N. under-secretary-general and special representative for children and armed conflict under Kofi Annan. He was also previously Uganda's ambassador and permanent representative to the United Nations and its minister of foreign affairs. His candidacy pitch centers on bringing about an "age of hope and faith" by revitalizing the United Nations' moral authority, mobilizing development resources, and deepening cooperation between the United Nations and regional organizations, among other actions. The US Supreme Court has declined to stop the execution of Tennessee inmate Christa Pike on the eve of the date appointed for her death by lethal injection.
Pike, 50, has been awaiting execution since she was convicted and sentenced to death in 1996 for the murder of a teenage classmate.
Hoping for a last-minute reprieve, her attorneys filed a petition with the high court ahead of her scheduled execution on Wednesday morning.
But after the high court's decision to deny that request, Pike will be the first woman to be executed in Tennessee in more than 200 years. Only 18 women have been executed in the US since the 1970s, compared to 1,663 men.
On Monday, Tennessee Governor Bill Lee denied a request for clemency from Pike, saying he would not intervene in her planned execution.
Pike was 18 when she and her then-boyfriend beat, tortured and murdered Colleen Slemmer, a 19-year-old they met at a job training camp for troubled teens.
Slemmer's murder created a media frenzy in Knoxville, Tennessee in 1995, when the teen was found with a pentagram - a symbol of Satanic ritual - carved into her chest. Pike has denied carving the pentagram herself.
She had accused Slemmer of insulting her and trying to steal her boyfriend. Two other residents at the camp later testified that Pike had bragged about the murder before and after, and showed them a piece of Slemmer's skull.
Her attorneys have argued that "an 18-year-old brain is not an adult brain" and that Pike was too young at the time of the murder to be sentenced to death for it.
At the time of her incarceration, Pike was the youngest person on death row, according to the Tennessee Department of Corrections.
She is due to be executed at 11:00 EDT (15:00 GMT) on Wednesday at Riverbend Maximum Security Institution in Nashville.
Additional reporting from Sareen Habeshian.

Like thousands of other residents of Zaporizhzhia, Denys Maksyshko has spent years working for local steel factory Zaporizhstal. For generations, it has been the biggest and richest source of employment in this major Ukrainian city.
"Zaporizhstal is not just a big company, it's the heart of the city," he says.
Now, following a series of Russian missile strikes, this heart has stopped beating. The huge factory that employs 8,500 people shut down indefinitely after four waves of Russian attacks - two in August, and two in September.
"All the equipment has been almost completely destroyed. There are no windows left, and there are holes in the roofs. The blast furnaces have been almost completely ruined," Maksyshko complains.
Russia fired a total of 17 missiles at Zaporizhstal, according to Oleksandr Myronenko, chief operating officer of steelworks owner Metinvest. Eight workers were killed and 31 wounded.
"We're now clearing rubble and trying to plan recovery," Myronenko tells the BBC.
At the moment it is far from certain Zaporizhstal will ever start up again.
Russia's persistent campaign of air strikes against Ukrainian metallurgical plants started in August. By now, all of them have been hit, some several times.
This is a key sector of the Ukrainian economy, and naturally an attractive target for Russia.
Before the start of the full-scale invasion in 2022, metallurgy and mining accounted for roughly 10% of Ukraine's GDP and a third of its exports. It provided employment for more than half a million people, and every 13th job in Ukraine was linked to the industry one way or another.
Because of the recent Russian attacks, it has all but ground to a halt and its contribution to Ukraine's GDP now "is probably close to zero", says Myronenko.
Until recently his company was Ukraine's biggest producer of steel and iron, but all its steelworks are for now out of action.
"Clearly, they're trying to stop Ukraine's economy and stop Ukraine from getting [export] money from abroad, from paying taxes and wages, from ensuring that cities live and people have jobs," says Myronenko. "Their efforts have been very effective so far."
The damage to the metals industry could have devastating consequences for Ukraine's economy and society.
Ukraine had 12 metallurgical plants before losing parts of its industrial heartland in the east shortly after the start of hostilities with Russia in 2014.
By 2018, there were just nine, and three years into the full-scale war in 2025 that number had fallen to six. Among those lost were the Azovstal and Illich plants in Mariupol, Ukraine's south-eastern city captured after a months-long Russian siege.
Among the steel-making cities caught up in Russia's recent missile campaign is President Volodymyr Zelensky's home city of Kryvyi Rih.
On 25 September, Ukraine's biggest steelworks, Arcelor Mittal Kryvyi Rih, announced it was unable to reopen after repeated attacks over five weeks, praising the bravery of its workers, five of whom had died.
Latest on war in Ukraine
Local Defence Council head Oleksandr Vilkul issued an emergency address to the city's residents, in which he spoke of a "very serious blow" that would affect more than just thousands of jobs.
The situation, he admitted, was very difficult.
"It is taxes feeding into our community's budget," he said. "They provided funds for keeping the city's infrastructure running, repairing heating plants and their pipes, funds for nursery schools, social services and many other things."
Taxes paid by metal-making companies have funded 30-70% of local government spending in their host cities, says Stanislav Zinchenko, head of Kyiv-based consultancy GMK Center.
"In other words, the physical survival of these cities depended on these companies," he told the BBC.
"This is a catastrophic problem for Ukraine's economy. Before the war, the mining and metallurgical industry was a key industry," he told the BBC. "It was always the biggest investor in the economy, investing $2bn-$3bn (Â£1.5bn-Â£2.3bn) a year on average."
If the steelworks remain shut, hundreds of thousands of people may lose their jobs, and the resulting waves of migration will reach far beyond Ukraine, Zinchenko warned. "A humanitarian catastrophe is looming."
The end of steelmaking in Ukraine would also have severe consequences for its defence capabilities and reconstruction.
Steel is vital for producing military equipment, as well as for making shelters and repairing countless buildings damaged by Russia.
Russia has justified its attacks on the steel plants for that reason, alleging that the plants in Zaporizhzhia and Kryvyi Rih were all producing military hardware.
"We attempted relaunching Zaporizhstal. We restarted a furnace, and it worked for 10 hours before there was another air strike," Oleksandr Vodoviz of Metinvest told a conference in Kyiv.
There was no point yet on spending money on recovery as the situation was unclear, he added.
Even if production were to resume, it would not be business as usual for Ukrainian steelmakers any time soon.
Russian attacks on railways have made transporting their products within Ukraine difficult and dangerous, and strikes against ports have turned exports into a lethal lottery.
"Ports have essentially been blocked," said Oleksandr Myronenko. "Every ship is at risk of being attacked, and their chances are 50-50 - either you make it, or you don't."
EU quotas on steel imports introduced on 1 July may compound the problems faced by Ukraine.
But Denys Maksyshko, the Zaporizhstal worker, remains upbeat.
His colleagues are doing their bit to revive the factory, clearing away rubble and fixing whatever can be fixed.
"This is similar to what the military do in the trenches. Ordinary people are fighting to keep the factory alive like soldiers."

A Venezuelan man shot in the back by a US immigration agent in Texas has been charged with assault, accused of sideswiping the officer with his car as he tried to drive away.
Wilber Rafael Garces Perez's side-view mirror hit the US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) officer during the traffic stop on 20 September in the city of Austin, it is alleged.
The 28-year-old faces one count of assaulting, resisting and impeding a federal officer. He could face up to 20 years in federal prison if convicted.
Garces Perez appeared in court on Tuesday. His lawyers said they only learned of his court appearance afterwards.
According to the justice department, the traffic stop was initiated by an ICE officer after confirming through a database that the blue Toyota sedan was registered to Garces Perez, who had been issued a final order of removal from the US.
The affidavit contains a conflicting account of the incident.
According to the court filing, Garces Perez said a law enforcement SUV had "caused a collision" with his car by pulling an abrupt manouevre during the traffic stop.
But the federal agents said there was "no contact" between their SUVs and Garces Perez's car when they first pulled him over.
According to the court filing, Garces Perez said he knew he would be arrested and admitted to declining to exit his car when ordered to do so.
He drove away, allegedly striking the officer in the torso with the driver's side-view mirror.
The court filing alleges that Garces Perez "led them on a high-speed chase through a commercial and residential area".
The short pursuit ended when a federal agent's SUV struck his car and "caused it to spin around", says the affidavit.
Garces Perez said that after coming to a forced stop an agent fired his pistol into the back right window of his car.
The justice department said the "officer caught up to Garces Perez, who allegedly attempted to strike the officer with his car, causing the officer to fire his pistol".
The Venezuelan national was struck with a bullet in his upper back, where his lawyers say it remains lodged, placing him "in grave danger".
DHS last week said Garces Perez has received "some of the best medical care he's ever received in his life".
A judge last week temporarily blocked Garces Perez's deportation.
He entered the US in 2024 using CBP One, an asylum-seeker programme introduced by President Joe Biden and cancelled by President Donald Trump.

- Published
Chinese AI developer Moonshot is conducting an internal review after researchers were able to persuade two of its popular Kimi models to tell them how to make biological weapons and carry out assassinations.
Mindgard, which tests the security of AI systems, told the BBC it discovered in July that Kimi K2.6 and K3 Swarm could evade safety limits put in place by developers.
It arose during a process called "jailbreaking", where researchers use a series of complex instructions to see if AI tools ignore guardrails - which Mindgard said should have stopped Kimi from discussing concerning topics.
Moonshot told the BBC it welcomed third-party input "as a key pillar for building better and safer AI".
The company also told the BBC it was in discussion with Mindgard about its findings.
Mindgard's founder Peter Garraghan told the BBC World Service programme Tech Life that its findings about Kimi K2.6 and K3 Swarm were concerning.
"Once the jailbreak works it will talk about any topic, it will even freely offer up recommendations about other topics that are also nefarious and it will be inventive and creative," he said.
Jailbreaks present a different kind of risk to those seen with the recent slew of high-profile AI incidents.
These have seen autonomous AI tools known as agents, developed by US firms including OpenAI, Meta and Anthropic, hack some online services.
While jailbreaks are complex processes that can take a lot of time and determination some experts fear hackers and other bad actors could try to use them to cause harm.
Anthropic recently said it had identified and disrupted attempts to use one of its AI model for "malicious activity" that could support the development of biological weapons.
Cyber-attack launchpad
Mindgard has not proven whether the answers supplied by Kimi on concerning topics would work.
But it argued guardrails should have prevented the models in question from entering into discussion with users on such subjects.
The firm said it was also confident a jailbroken Kimi 2.6 could allow hackers to run code on its computing resources and connect to the internet - making it a potential launchpad for cyber-attacks.
Garraghan defended Mindgard's decision to publicly discuss its jailbreak of Moonshot's systems, saying it had informed the developer and was not revealing key details about how it got the firm's models to ignore guardrails.
Mindgard alerted Moonshot to the jailbreak in an email on 27 July, following up about a week later.
It then published a blog about the issue on 12 September.
But the company said Moonshot only made contact recently, after it was approached by the BBC for comment.
In part of an email to Mindgard asking for more details, shared with the BBC by Moonshot, it said its model had generally shown "a high refusal rate for these types of requests" in internal evaluations.
Preventing jailbreaks
The findings come as the AI industry continues to be split on whether closed, proprietary models - like those powering ChatGPT and Anthropic's Claude systems - or open-source tools are the best or safest way forward.
Kimi is an open-weight model, meaning someone could in theory take the model and run it themselves on their own computing infrastructure.
Prof Alan Woodward, of the University of Surrey, told the BBC there was a risk open-source models might end up in the wrong hands, but they could also be harnessed for cyber-defence.
He noted that AI firm Hugging Face used a Chinese open-source model to understand a hack later revealed to have been carried out by OpenAI agents.
Prof Woodward said international regulation was unlikely to match the pace of AI development, saying: "It's taken us decades to agree on the format of telephone numbers."
Like Mindgard founder Garraghan, Prof Woodward believes there should be a greater focus on identifying and prosecuting humans who misuse AI.

Army awards more than $4 billion in counterdrone contracts, putting the Pentagon’s new drone marketplace to the test
The Defense Department launched drones.mil earlier this year following an Army-led effort.
Military drone and counterdrone demand is booming amid a rush to spend funds before the end of the fiscal year—but the Pentagon’s drone marketplace is making it a little easier, defense officials said.
“These contracts are available to everybody. And so what we've seen across the department is a surge of end-of-year requests for procurement,” Brig. Gen. Matthew Ross, who leads the Pentagon’s Joint Interagency Task Force 401, told reporters Tuesday. “End-of-year spending is nothing new inside of the department, but when you have an available contract vehicle, it makes it really easy to execute. And so, we've seen that from across the services.”
The Army issued 10 indefinite delivery, indefinite quantity contracts Tuesday with a total ceiling of $4.15 billion for counterdrone tech including command and control systems, sensors, and systems that can disable or destroy unmanned aerial drones.
Seven companies received $500 million awards: Allen Control Systems, Digital Force Technologies, DroneShield, L3Harris WESCAM, Napatree Technology, RADA Technologies, and SRC.
Echodyne and PVP Advanced EO Systems received $250 million contracts, and SmartShooter received a $150 million contract. Only about $50 million was obligated at the time of award, the Army said.
But there’s room for more—-up to $7 billion.
"As of today we have awarded over $5 billion, which includes previous contracts with [Aerovironment] and CACI, these 10 new IDIQs and others that we expect to sign before the end of next month. The $7 billion ceiling is in full effect today, and additional contracts will be pursued to get us to that point," Col. Tony Lindh, JIATF-401’s lead for rapid acquisitions, told reporters.
The new enterprise contracts reflect a new way of doing business for the Army, providing buyers more flexibility over time.
“These platforms are software-defined, hardware-enabled systems…so we have to be able to partner with industry and then hold them accountable over time,” said Ross, JIATF 401’s director.
The Army’s unmanned aerial systems marketplace has done about $800 million in transactions since it opened earlier this year, and the expectation is for counterdrone demand to follow a similar path—especially with allies and partners, said Brent Ingraham, who leads Army acquisitions.
“About 10 days ago, Australia successfully procured, in this case, it was a UAS off the drones.mil marketplace,” Ingraham told reporters. “We still have to use the [foreign military sales] process as we go through this marketplace. But…we've automated the tools on the back end.”
That means it now takes days from request to purchase instead of months or longer when an ally or partner nation wants to buy a system the U.S. has.
“When they see the U.S. military buying certain products, they're all in,” Ingraham said. “And so this is a way to share those technologies, share what we're doing,” and help smaller businesses “scale.”

6a5146242b40.text:
- Published
Researchers are using AI to create a vast digital museum of millions of specimens from collections across the UK that they say could "supercharge" our understanding of the natural world.
People will eventually be able to see around 70 million animals, plants, fossils and rocks from their phones and computers.
Robots and AI are being used to scan and analyse the specimens - some collected centuries ago - speeding up the digitisation process from hundreds of years to a decade.
The new digital museum will enable researchers to understand how the UK has changed over the entire history of our planet and predict future changes to the climate, food supplies and species loss.
The resource will be something that the public can access and enjoy too, says Dr Joanna Dunster, who is an associate director of the Arts and Humanities Research Council (AHRC) - part of the UK Research and Innovation Agency which is funding the project.
"I'm looking forward to exploring the resource with my four-year-old son, whose knowledge of science is little, but enthusiasm is great," she told BBC News.
Some specimens are already searchable on the database, but they represent only a fraction of the country's collections, mostly from a handful of large institutions such as the Natural History Museum and the Royal Botanic Gardens, Kew.
New funding will open drawers and cupboards in institutions across the UK to include millions more plants, animals and fossils.
"We need to make these collections openly accessible instead of sitting where they can rarely be reached," Dunster said.
The public and researchers will be able to see the full diversity of the natural world, from the unusual - like the blind tripod fish that props itself on the seafloor, to the historical - a horse tooth recovered by Charles Darwin around 1833 from northeast Argentina.
The resource is called the Distributed System of Scientific Collections, external (DiSSCo UK).
1 of 5
Scanning the specimens is not a trivial process. Not only does each one need to be photographed, but the tiny labels containing important scientific information, often handwritten, sometimes centuries ago, also have to be recorded.
The team involved calculated that it would have taken hundreds of years to do this manually, but using robots and AI this process can now be done in a decade, according to Sarah Addezio, the DiSSCo UK's programme delivery director.
"What we're able to do now is connect and analyse that information at a scale that's unprecedented and has not been possible before."
One hundred museums, botanic gardens, universities and other organisations are involved in the project.
The specimens to go under the cameras will not be the big beasties: there are no whales or dinosaurs in the opening phase, which begins in Wales and Scotland.
Beetles, butterflies, moths, flies, pressed flowers and ferns will go first - the small, less glamorous material that actually hold the best record of how the country around them has changed.
In Cardiff, the team will scan around half a million insect and plant specimens, from large, showy butterflies down to flies you could lose on a fingertip, which turn out to be among the most sensitive indicators of a healthy landscape.
In Scotland, the Royal Botanic Garden Edinburgh and National Museums Scotland hold 13 million specimens between them, the UK's second-largest natural science collection.
Together with 50 smaller Scottish collections, the collections span from sea level to the tops of mountains - two centuries of change in the plants and insects of every kind of Scottish landscape.
Jenny Geroni, who is the head of Natural Sciences and Research at the Amgueddfa Cymru - Museum Wales, said it will be a chance to showcase material from across the country.
"Each collection is unique. We have a lot of Welsh material that is not held anywhere else.
"By taking material from across the UK, it also allows us to build a good picture of what is going on across the whole country. And everyone adding their world collections will build a much stronger picture of what is going on elsewhere," Geroni told BBC News.
Every specimen in a museum is a snapshot of the past.
A large part of natural history is the detective story of piecing these clues together from tens of millions of these jigsaw pieces to recreate a vivid and detailed picture of how our world has changed.
The new initiative will make that much easier by bringing millions of specimens together along with powerful AI tools to search the information.
Dr Vincent Smith, a research leader at the Natural History Museum in London, says it will "supercharge" research into the natural world.
"Natural history collections record long periods of change, often through really fundamental periods, such as the Industrial Revolution. Our collections chart those changes and so you can see what's happened before," he said.
And, crucially, he added "start to predict what's going to happen next".
By bringing together this large collection of specimens, researchers can refine their computer models of how the natural world will change in the future - studying how climate change and other development choices will impact species loss.
DiSSCo UK will also help scientists prepare for future challenges - by uploading more fossils and rock material it will aid research into minerals needed for green technology.

edc585c53d34.text:
The military may be top-heavy. Don't make things worse with hasty cuts.
Congress should closely monitor Hegseth’s latest effort to reduce the number of generals and admirals.
News broke Tuesday that Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth is planning to order the elimination of one-fifth of the U.S. military’s general and flag billets. There is a legitimate case for examining whether the Armed Forces have have become too top-heavy. There is also a legitimate reason to be concerned about how reductions in the senior officer corps are carried out.
For more than 20 years, I worked as a federal contractor operating mission-critical facilities supporting the Defense Department, State Department, and federal law-enforcement agencies. That experience gave me an appreciation for something that can be difficult to quantify on an organizational chart: institutional knowledge.
Large organizations accumulate layers of management. The military is not immune. Headquarters expand, responsibilities overlap, and positions created to meet one requirement sometimes remain long after circumstances change.
Congress recognized this issue well before the current administration. In 2017, lawmakers reduced the authorized number of active-duty general and flag officer positions by about 11 percent. They also ordered a comprehensive look at whether another 10 percent of flag jobs might be cut, and if so, which ones.
This is important context for today's debate: concern about “rank creep” did not suddenly appear in 2025, nor is questioning the number of generals and admirals inherently an attack on military leadership. It is a legitimate management and national-security question.
But it is only the beginning of the analysis.
In May 2025, Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth directed a minimum 20 percent reduction in active-component four-star positions, a minimum 20 percent reduction in National Guard general officers, and an additional minimum 10 percent reduction in general and flag officers associated with restructuring the Unified Command Plan. That order came amid broader cuts to the defense civilian workforce, a campaign noted for a lack of planning and consequent disruption.
Hegseth’s new order to cut 20 percent of general and flag billets reportedly comes with a similarly tight deadline: Jan. 1.
The question Congress and the American public should be asking is not simply, "How many generals can we eliminate?" It should be: Which positions does the military need to accomplish its mission, and what happens when those positions and the officers who fill them disappear?
There is an enormous difference between eliminating an unnecessary headquarters position and losing an experienced operational commander. There is a difference between removing a redundant layer of administration and disrupting the succession of officers being prepared for increasingly demanding commands. And there is a difference between making an organization leaner and simply making it smaller.
The men and women who reach the senior ranks of our Armed Forces generally arrive there after decades of increasingly demanding assignments. The combined operational, technical, and institutional experience represented by those officers is an asset that cannot quickly or easily be replaced.
That does not mean every general or admiral billet should be preserved. If a headquarters is unnecessary, eliminate it. If two commands unnecessarily duplicate one another, consolidate them. If a position no longer requires a general or flag officer, downgrade it. If layers of bureaucracy interfere with getting resources and authority to the people actually performing the mission, remove those layers.
But make those decisions based upon the requirements of the mission—not simply the desire to achieve a predetermined percentage reduction.
The same principle should apply farther down the ranks. A serious examination of military "rank creep" should not stop with four-star generals. Congress should examine the entire personnel structure and determine whether the balance among general and flag officers, field-grade officers, senior noncommissioned officers, and the junior enlisted personnel who perform much of the military's day-to-day operational work remains appropriate for today's force.
The answer may differ considerably among the services. A Navy built around technologically complex ships, submarines and aviation cannot necessarily be evaluated using the same personnel ratios as an Army ground formation. Cyber, space, intelligence and nuclear missions also require experienced technical personnel. That is precisely why percentage reductions alone are an inadequate substitute for manpower analysis.
There is another consequence that deserves attention: the effect on the officers who remain. If capable and deserving officers come to believe that opportunities for advancement are disappearing for reasons unrelated to their performance, qualifications or the needs of the service, the consequences can extend far beyond the officers whose promotions are affected. It can influence retention, morale and the willingness of talented younger officers to commit their careers to military service.
Promotion and command decisions should be based upon merit and military requirements, without regard to sex, ethnicity or orientation. The objective should be straightforward: identify and advance the most capable people required to defend the country.
Congress therefore has an important oversight responsibility. It should determine which senior positions are actually being eliminated, which are merely being left vacant or reassigned, whether the positions involve administrative or operational responsibilities, what effect the changes have on succession and readiness, and how today's reductions compare with the reforms Congress itself initiated nearly a decade ago.
Lawmakers should also ask a deceptively simple question: Did the FY2017 reforms work?

US President Donald Trump hosted a meeting of top technology bosses on Tuesday for what he called "an extraordinary gathering" of the minds that are "building America's Golden Age".
The guest list included leaders from OpenAI, Anthropic, Nvidia, SpaceX, Meta and Google - all key figures in the US AI industry.
The meeting came as some tech executives and experts have called for tighter oversight of AI and a slowdown in developing the technology, citing concerns about the potential risks it poses to humanity.
Here are three key takeaways from Trump's tech summit at the White House.
1. AI 'self-regulation' pact
Trump took questions from the media for around 30 minutes alongside House Speaker Mike Johnson and top tech leaders after the closed-door meeting.
The president told reporters that the executives had signed a "morally binding" document that would serve as a "form of protection" from AI's potential risks.
Under the agreement, which Trump posted on social media, the companies are responsible for ensuring the safety of their own technology.
The firms also agreed to implement safeguards to keep models operating as intended and quickly detect and fix any issues, the document said.
They will also work with "independent auditors" to assess whether their AI systems are working as intended and ensure their platforms do not "hack or access technical systems in unintended ways."
The accord was signed by Trump, Google boss Sundar Pichai, Anthropic chief Dario Amodei, Meta's Mark Zuckerberg, OpenAI President Greg Brockman, SpaceX's Elon Musk and Nvidia chief executive Jensen Huang.
"It's almost like a constitution, in a way," Trump said, referring to the agreement. "And the biggest people in the world signed that, and I signed it as president."
Trump added that he will set up a board to oversee the safety of AI tools. He did not specify who would be on that board.
Zuckerberg said the accord gives the "American people and customers the confidence that the technology works" as intended.
Amodei credited Trump and tech bosses for working towards a way "to win safely", referring to the president's comment earlier this month that "whoever wins AI, wins".
But not all technology experts are impressed with the agreement.
The pact is "deeply unimpressive" and comes despite calls from some world leaders and industry figures for tighter regulations over the technology, said law professor Kimberlee Weatheral from the University of Sydney.
The agreement appears to allow firms to "define what counts as safety" and does not state what consequences there are to any breaches, Weatheral said.
"The accord should be ignored, for the distraction it is," she added.
Trump has repeatedly downplayed concerns about AI's risks, even as major AI firms have called for tighter oversight and for a slowdown of development of the technology.
On Monday, OpenAI said it had scrapped the release of its latest flagship AI model, GPT-6.1 Astra, over safety concerns.
The company's security controls have come under intense scrutiny after several high-profile incidents involving its technology, including its models accessing Australian government platforms without authorisation.
Jeannie Paterson from the Centre for Artificial Intelligence and Digital Ethics at the University of Melbourne said self-regulation could mean that companies set "only minimal safeguards".
The agreement inspires "very little confidence" as recent incidents of AI going rogue suggest companies have been undisciplined in their approach, she added.
2. Doubling down on data centres
Trump also reiterated his support for the rapid expansion of data centres - the crucial computing infrastructure that powers AI.
The rollout of data centres has drawn pushback around the country over concerns about electricity usage and their potential impact on from communities.
Data centre construction has also emerged as a potential political obstacle for Trump's Republican party ahead of the US midterm elections in November.
A survey conducted by Marist Poll in partnership with NPR and PBS News, external earlier this month found that 65% of registered voters opposed data centres being built in their areas.
Responding to those concerns, Trump said tech companies would work to make people "happy" about the construction of data centres.
"These big, powerful, very rich, very smart companies are going to be making massive contributions to communities," Trump told reporters.
Trump previously said on social media that the only reason communities in the US should oppose data centres is if they "want to end up being backwards and poor".
"The good news is that there are plenty of other places that want them. If we kill the Golden Goose, you will only have yourselves to blame," he said.
Huang from Nvidia, which produces computer chips essential for running AI, said after the meeting that data centres should be called "super intelligence factories".
These facilities are "reindustrialising the United States", creating jobs across the economy, he added.
3. It's now 'Super Intelligence'
Also on Tuesday, Trump signed an executive order instructing US government departments and agencies to start using the terms "SI" and "Super Intelligence" and should no longer acknowledge the use of term artificial intelligence.
SI will take the place of AI in "official correspondence, public communications, websites, reports, policy documents, and other non-statutory documents within the executive branch," the order said.
"As these capabilities continue to improve, they increasingly represent not merely artificial intelligence, but a new era of Super Intelligence," the order said.
During an address to the United Nations General Assembly last week, Trump said the word "artificial" made the technology "sound fake".
Some tech leaders and other people close to the president have already started to use the term.

Watch: Moment a government building collapses into a river in Nepal amid floods
Massive flooding left a government building in western Nepal teetering on the edge of an unstable ledge before it fell into the Daram River.
Witnesses captured the moment that the building in Baglung collapsed on Sunday, 27 September.
Officials removed important documents and computers from the building before it fell, local ward chair Tej Thapa confirmed to the BBC. No one was injured.
Landslides and floods have killed at least 27 people over recent days, according to Nepal's national disaster agency, only weeks after a flash flood along the Nepal-Tibet border killed 1,400 people and left thousands more missing.
