Singapore has rolled out a matchmaking service for its government workers, an initiative that comes as the country wrestles with a record-low fertility rate.
FirstDate, which launched this week for those aged 21 to 35, boasts "a different approach to dating", where it uses a Nobel-winning algorithm to match participants to one date at a time. "Swipe fatigue ends here," its website reads.
Participants sign in using the national digital identity system and answer a survey about their interests, habits and values.
FirstDate's launch drew mixed responses among Singaporeans, with some describing it as "dystopian" and others saying they would be keen to give it a shot.
On its website, FirstDate highlights the Gale-Shapley Stable Marriage algorithm which powers the programme.
The mathematical framework pairs two equally sized groups of people based on their preferences.
The late mathematician Lloyd Shapley was awarded the 2012 Nobel memorial prize in economic sciences for discovering the algorithm, which has been used in public school admissions, medical residency matching, and dating apps, among other things.
"At the end of the day, I think the experience of meeting someone through an application doesn't change much across the [different types of] applications," Elizabeth, a 29-year-old who works in Singapore's defence ministry and is keen on trying FirstDate out told the BBC.
"But it is nice to know that the likelihood of being scammed is much lower. We're all public servants looking for a partner, right?"
But some social media users say the initiative, which is currently in its pilot phase, discriminates against those not working in government.
Others criticised the age limit. "They are only doing this to raise the total fertility rate. They don't actually [care] about whether we find a partner otherwise.
"Since there are higher risks involved in having kids at 35 and older, the government just writes [the older singles] off," wrote another Reddit user.
It is not clear if the pilot programme will be available to the wider public in future. The BBC has reached out to GovTech, the statutory board behind the pilot, for comment.
The pilot launch comes as Singapore's birth rate has slumped to historic lows. For the first time in the past 60 years, fewer than 30,000 babies were born in 2025.
The number of deaths meanwhile have been rising steadily in the greying nation, hitting about 26,500 in 2025.
In August, Prime Minister Lawrence Wong announced a series of new measures to better support families and to encourage couples to have children, including almost S$70,000 ($54,000; Â£41,000) in financial support for every child by the time they turn 17.
FirstDate is not the first time the citystate is trying to play Cupid to its citizens.
In 1984, it set up the Social Development Unit (SDU) tasked with organising social events to encourage graduate singles to mingle.
Its exclusive target audience of university graduates was criticised as being elitist, but authorities justified the approach saying non-graduates did not seem to have difficulty finding partners. The SDU was eventually phased out.
The next year, the government set up another agency to promote marriages among non-graduates.
The idea of a government-run dating service is not unique to Singapore. In September 2024, Tokyo's metropolitan government launched an AI-powered dating app in an effort to combat the country's declining birth rate.
The app, which is open to single residents in the city, resulted in 265 couples getting married, according to government data released in July this year.
Additional reporting by Osmond Chia in Singapore

A group of young people have developed ideas to tackle the effects of climate change as part of a free touring exhibition.
On Tuesday 16 young people took part in a hackathon - a timed event where people work together to build creative solutions to problems - where they devised posters with ways to combat light pollution, wild fires, damage to oceans and poor water quality.
The event was hosted by Seeds of Hope and Change, an organisation run by the Soka Gakkai International and the UN Earth Charter, at the Jerwood Dancehouse in Ipswich.
Maryanne, 16, took part in the project and said: "We just want people to be aware of what's going on, especially with major issues such as ocean pollution."
Climate change is the long-term shift in the Earth's average temperatures and weather conditions.
This year's summer was the UK's hottest on record, according to provisional data from the Met Office.
The Met Office said the heat experienced this summer was made about 130 times more likely by human-induced climate change.
Baveen, 17, said "We wanted to talk about the cities and the sky and how it affects people and also wildlife."
The poster her group produced included ideas for using low-intensity bulbs and motion sensors in street lights so that they were not continuously left on.
The exhibition, which is free and runs until 4 October, includes 24 pop-up panels that share information and environmental case studies from around the world on the impact of climate change.
The hackathon for young people was run by ambassadors from the youth-led campaigning organisation #iWill.
Alex Harrison, one of the #iWill ambassadors, said: "The main purpose is reminding young people that in the face of something really scary like climate change, there's a lot that you can do personally to make a real change."

199d51294ee7.text: With America's tech titans crowded around a single White House table Tuesday, President Trump extracted what he called a "morally binding" compact on AI safety. The terms were simple: Press ahead, project optimism and police yourselves. Why it matters: The White House Accord on Super Intelligence , signed by OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, Meta, xAI and Nvidia, formalizes industry self-regulation as Washington's response to the most alarming run of AI safety failures yet . Zoom in: Trump, who increasingly treats American AI dominance as central to his legacy, cast the accord as proof that an industry fractured over safety can still govern itself. He compared the document to "a constitution," claimed there was "a lot of commonality" among the tech leaders, and praised what he described as "tremendous self-policing." The one-page pact, which is deliberately light-touch, calls for "four layers of controls and auditing," including outside evaluators and independent board oversight. Between the lines: The accord makes a vague reference to future "laws or regulations," preserving the possibility of a tougher federal regime if ultimately needed. Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei, a MAGA bogeyman and the industry's most prominent advocate for slowing frontier development, signed the pact but stressed to reporters that it was only "a start." Trump AI adviser David Sacks, by contrast, treated the accord as mission accomplished — declaring on X that the companies were "accepting responsibility" for AI safety thanks to Trump's leadership. Zoom out: The White House pact capped an extraordinary day for the AI race across three capitals of American power. 1. In Washington, Trump spent Tuesday pulling AI deeper into both the machinery and mythology of his presidency. In the morning, he unveiled America.gov , an AI-powered front door to federal services, and vowed not to "stifle" a technology he says will eclipse the Industrial Revolution. Hours later, Trump signed an executive order directing the federal government to replace "AI" with " Super Intelligence " in official usage — and called on Congress to write the new terminology into law. 2. In Silicon Valley, OpenAI spent the day racing deeper into the age of autonomous AI while struggling to contain its risks. At its highly anticipated DevDay, the company unveiled a sweeping slate of products designed to make AI more persistent, capable and independent in everyday life, including a new personal assistant. But midway through Sam Altman's keynote, an explosive New York Times report revealed that OpenAI executives had brushed aside internal safety warnings months before its models began hacking outside systems. 3. On Wall Street, Anthropic's leaked IPO prospectus distilled the surreal economics of the AI race. According to Reuters , the company laid out a path to a valuation north of $2 trillion while warning prospective investors that its technology could pose "catastrophic or existential risks to humanity." Altman, meanwhile, said OpenAI would delay its own IPO until it could "make confident safety decisions" — even as the company reportedly seeks at least $30 billion in private funding at a roughly $1.4 trillion valuation. The bottom line: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, seated beside Trump at the White House, supplied the day's credo: "Trust and innovation are not in conflict. Safety is how trust is earned."

7517f17b4d78.text: AI companies are staking their future on the mass adoption of agents , hoping that they can solve the annoyances of modern life — email, travel bookings, online purchases. Why it matters: The frenzy around Meta's Muse shows there's serious consumer curiosity about the technology. But most Americans live life beyond a computer screen and find much of their meaning outside of the 9-5. There's little evidence that they're willing to invest the time needed to re-engineer their lives in a way that puts AI at the center. And the more worrying issue for AI companies: What happens if people just don't want an assistant that leads them to do more work or allows them to be more productive? Driving the news: Muse vaulted to the top of Apple's App Store on the back of its integrations with Facebook and Instagram and a cute, fuzzy mascot . Meta expanded it to business customers, too. Muse's early success has given the industry hope that there's potential for the tech to break through. Meta isn't alone. Microsoft released a souped-up Copilot with an agentic Autopilot feature, folding more advanced AI into the workplace. And OpenAI announced its own agentic assistant, dots, this week. The big roadblock is that most Americans don't use AI chatbots, let alone agents. Back in February, Pew found that 51% avoided using AI chatbots entirely. Of those people, 79% who didn't use chatbots cited privacy concerns and 67% were unlikely to use a chatbot in the next year. The even bigger problem: Agents only become truly useful when people hand them access to their digital lives — and people really don't want to. A huge international Thales poll this year found broad pushback against the core uses of agents — only 13% of respondents would let an "AI helper" read their emails, 11% would let one rebook travel and just 7% would let it move money between bank accounts. Even shopping is a no-go: 56% told YouGov they wouldn't let an agent shop for them at all. Only 10% trust one with more than $25 without approval. That means the people embracing AI agents right now probably look a lot like the people building them. Menlo Ventures, working with Morning Consult, found that households with incomes over $100,000 are substantially more likely to use AI than households making less than $50,000. People who pay for AI are twice as likely to use it daily — and people who pay for it are five times more likely to use agents. Menlo sums up AI's power spenders this way: "a millennial parent with a post-grad degree working in technology or financial services" who "[tends] to have more money than time." It'd be wrong to pretend that AI use isn't happening at all. The St. Louis Fed pegs AI adoption as "widespread but shallow" — at least 20% of workers use AI in more than 80% of occupations. But that's heavily weighted toward the same white-collar, tech-adjacent jobs. Adoption for computer programmers, PR people, financial advisors and CEOs all clock around or above 80%. Licensed practical nurses, receptionists and animal caretakers land just at or less than 10%. The St. Louis fed sums it up this way: "Currently, AI works on screens and cannot drive a truck or draw blood." Between the lines: The frontier labs' own user data shows the same skew. Anthropic found that the two massively overindexed professions in its Economic Index Survey — which the company says isn't representative — were computer/math-related (30% of respondents, 4% of U.S. employment) and management (23% of respondents, 7% of U.S. employment). The big picture: Only 6% of Americans think that utilizing AI tools like ChatGPT is a very important ingredient for a good life, per Gallup . Compare that to: spending time with a partner, friends or family (78%), exercising or other physical activity (58%), cooking (49%), spending time in nature (45%) or practicing spirituality (42%). The bottom line: Agentic AI might well be transformative someday — but, for right now, it seems like it'll most impact people who have used the phrase "inbox triage" and feel overwhelmed by Google Calendar notifications. 🎓 Go deeper ... AI 101: Explaining AI to anyone

US actor Chad Lowe and his wife, producer Kim Painter, have said they are "deeply heartbroken" following the death of their "beloved" 13-year-old daughter Fiona.
"She was a loving young girl who was smart, creative and loved to dance," the family said in a statement to Page Six, external and People, external.
"She was adored by her sisters and she was deeply loved by her parents. In fact, she was the light of our lives.
"Her passing is devastating for our entire family and we ask for prayers and privacy at this time."
The statement concluded: "If you or someone you know is struggling with mental health, please reach out to the 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline by calling or texting 988."
Chad Lowe, the brother of fellow actor Rob Lowe, won an Emmy Award in 1993 for TV show Life Goes On and has appeared in other programmes including Pretty Little Liars and Supergirl.
He and Painter are also parents to daughters Mabel, 17, and Nixie, 10.

a1b8c5800d83.text:
Watch: Couple describes relief at rescue after whale destroys their yacht
A sailor couple have spoken of their relief to be rescued after a sperm whale collided with their yacht.
Jeremy and Gemma Cooper told the BBC that they were 500 nautical miles off the coast of New Zealand when the boat, the Tai Tam, lurched port side and they knew they'd "been hit by something" - only to see a pod of six sperm whales swimming behind the boat.
As their boat took on water and eventually sank, the Coopers and two other sailors aboard the vessel evacuated to a life raft. Seventeen hours later they were rescued by a container ship.
The couple told the BBC that, despite their ordeal, they would be out on the water again soon.
Video produced by Lana Lam, edited by Alex Foster.

The UKâs prime minister raised the specter of the country rejoining the EU, an issue that remains politically divisive despite growing numbers of voters voicing frustration over the lasting impacts of Brexit. Were Andy Burnham to support a campaign to reenter the bloc, he would draw a significant dividing line between his Labour Party and rival Reform UK, which, helmed by Brexit champion Nigel Farage, is neck-and-neck with Labour in polls.
Such a move may be particularly tough because of its implications for immigration: âAny attempt to move closer,â a leading journalist wrote for the conservative Spectator magazine, âis unthinkable without throwing open the borders again â¦ To put it mildly, this is not what the British public wants.â

683d40b67634.text:
Danish pharma giant Novo licensed a weight-loss treatment developed by a Chinese firm, highlighting advances in Chinaâs increasingly cutting-edge biotech sector.
The firm behind the treatment, Hengrui Pharma, last year reached an even bigger agreement with GSK for the development of new drugs across multiple areas, including cancer; Novo has also previously signed a deal with another Chinese company for a different weight-loss drug.
The agreements cement a remarkable transformation: âWithin living memory, China sent barefoot doctors into the countryside with herbal remedies and antibiotics in army-green satchels,â Kaiser Kuo of the Sinica Podcast noted, whereas AstraZenecaâs chief financial officer recently told Semafor that it is now âonly a question of timeâ before Chinese pharma companies challenge global firms.

c9b89910c860.text:
The News
Airtel Money is betting on digital payments and financial services to drive revenue growth across Africa, the fintech companyâs CEO told Semafor ahead of what looks set to be Londonâs largest initial public offering in recent years.
The mobile money arm of telecoms group Airtel Africa, which last week announced its intention to pursue an offering on the London Stock Exchange, operates in 13 African countries. It is reportedly looking to raise at least $800 million from the sale of shares by existing shareholders, which would give it a market capitalization of between $8 billion and $9 billion.
Airtel Moneyâs Chief Executive Officer Ian Ferrao, in an interview, said the companyâs revenue mix had shifted in recent years to digital payments and transfers, away from depositing and withdrawing cash through its network of agents, branches and kiosks. Customers use the mobile money platform to pay bills, buy goods, transfer funds to people, and arrange microloans.
âWeâve really put a tremendous focus on the payments and transfers side of the business because thatâs higher quality revenue, better margin,â he said.
The executive added that financial services â including lending, savings, and insurance products â made up only 4% of the business but were growing fast. Ferrao pointed to âwealth techâ, allowing customers to buy and sell shares on local stock exchanges, as an area in which the company sought to innovate.
Know More
Airtel Money is the third-largest mobile money operator in Africa by transaction value, behind Safaricomâs M-Pesa and MTNâs MoMo. Of the countries in which it operates, Ferrao pointed to DR Congo as one of the companyâs fastest growing markets. He also cited Chad and Niger as underpenetrated markets that showed promise.
The offering is expected to be the largest in the UK since 2021. Ferrao said that, in the medium term, it would offer âflexibilityâ if the company wanted to expand into new countries and or pursue consolidation opportunities.
Ferrao said the deal would make the company the first major fintech listed on a global exchange, representing sub-Saharan Africa. âIf anybody wants exposure to the continent, we will be a great asset to give exposure to the continent,â he said.
OPay, a Chinese fintech company focused on Nigeria, is looking to go public in the US in a process that would value the company at around $4 billion. And Flutterwave, Africaâs most valuable fintech, recently purchased open-banking platform Mono Technologies Nigeria in a bid to strengthen its case for a potential IPO.
Step Back
Details of Airtel Moneyâs offering â such as the deal size and price range â are set to be published in October, the company said.
Bharti Airtel, the telecoms company founded by Indian billionaire Sunil Bharti Mittal, spun out and listed its Airtel Africa subsidiary on the London Stock Exchange in 2019 at an IPO valuation of $3.9 billion. Airtel Africa, which has grown significantly since then, is now worth about $13 billion in total market capitalization.
London-listed Airtel Africa currently owns about 78% of Airtel Money, while Chimetech Holding, Mastercard, and Qatar Investment Authority are among the firms holding minority stakes.
The International Finance Corporation, the World Bankâs private investment arm, has agreed to buy $90 million of shares from existing shareholders.
Notable
- The listing could provide a boost for Londonâs stock market, which has seen companies move away in recent years, but it does not mark a âdefinitiveâ end to the cityâs listings drought, wrote journalist Nils Pratley in The Guardian.

c347e49d6909.text:
Economists voiced growing alarm over Franceâs fiscal path, pointing to surging debt and high bond yields ahead of next yearâs divisive elections. Paris â already grappling with debt equivalent to 119% of GDP â said it would sell a record amount of bonds next year, prompting the spread between French government bonds and their German equivalents to widen, reflecting what investors see as a rising risk premium.
The giant investment manager Vanguard warned that France was âdegradingâ its creditworthiness, while Commerzbank said in a note that âpolitical uncertainty â¦ is increasingly crippling the economy.â As a senior Bloomberg editor put it: âThere are good reasons why France is now regarded as Europeâs âweakest linkâ.â

ac05a9944439.text:
European countries sought to harden migration rules in a bid to quell support for nationalist parties across the continent. Anti-immigration parties have been on the rise in both domestic politics and the European Parliament. Governments are trying to address votersâ concerns: Swiss lawmakers have advanced legislation taxing companies that hire foreign workers, while five EU member states want the bloc to launch a pilot project sending rejected asylum seekers to designated countries outside Europe.
Those efforts may not be enough, however. Victories by Germanyâs AfD in state elections have thrown the viability of the countryâs government into doubt, while Franceâs National Rally is the odds-on favorite to win next yearâs presidential election.

da1816bdebc0.text:
OpenAI reportedly aims to raise $30 billion in a new funding round valuing the company at $1.4 trillion, underlining how what was set to be a bumper IPO market to end the year is stalling.
The financing push, reported by Bloomberg, comes after the frontier AI lab said it would delay its stock market debut.
Its rival Anthropic is still pushing for its own IPO this year, but that increasingly looks out of kilter with the broader mood in the market: The smart ring maker Oura and SoftBank-backed data center company SB Energy have both delayed their IPOs, while analysts now expect the cloud startup NScale to postpone its investor roadshow, The Wall Street Journal said.

ac0ccc4ba52c.text:
US bond yields recovered slightly, but remained near quarter-century peaks due to investorsâ fears over inflation, persistent fiscal largesse, and geopolitical uncertainty. The yield on 30-year Treasurys briefly hit its highest level since 2002, with traders pricing in a 90% likelihood of a Federal Reserve rate hike by year-end driven by concerns over inflation.
Fuel prices have surged and economists increasingly expect them to feed into the cost of goods and services. Inflation data due to be released today will provide further insight into the Fedâs path. Experts are also worried by rich countriesâ huge amounts of debt: âWe may not be on the eve of disaster but room for manoeuvre is shrinking,â the Financial Timesâ chief economics commentator warned.

07132e86be68.text:
Watch: Luxury prison in Indonesia demolished after public outcry
A prison compound in Indonesia has been demolished after public outcry following the discovery of luxury apartments within the penitentiary.
Investigators reported finding luxury facilities in Cibinong Prison in Bogor, near Jakarta, allegedly used by favoured inmates during a surprise inspection on 23 September.
The units contained amenities including air conditioners, big-screen televisions, refrigerators, sofas and dining areas. Investigators also reported finding a gym, a golf simulator under construction and luxury vehicles in the complex.
Officials said the residences appeared to house inmates, although prison officials claim they were for staff.
The incident has drawn widespread public attention and renewed scrutiny of Indonesia's prisons, which have long faced allegations that wealthy or well-connected inmates can obtain preferential treatment through bribery.

2cea5b9a5c4b.text:
Hajj, the once-in-a-lifetime pilgrimage required by every able Muslim, is among the worldâs largest annual gatherings. Moving those bodies has long involved layers of middlemen. Saudi Arabia is now squeezing some of them out.
The Ministry of Hajj and Umrah has bundled the four services every pilgrim needs â holy site arrangements, lodging in Mecca and Medina, transport, and catering â into a single electronic agreement on one government platform. Some 1.7 million people made the trip in 2025, with spots rationed by country at roughly one per 1,000 Muslims. Itâs a major expense for many pilgrims, paid with years of savings, won by lottery, or covered by charities. For the kingdom, itâs a source of pride and revenue: Religious tourism is on track to contribute 10% of GDP by 2030.

48cc6543a627.text:
A flydubai flight from the UAE to Israel made an emergency landing in Saudi Arabia on Wednesday, after an altercation between the pilots led to the plane plunging more than 14,000 feet before climbing sharply. The Dubai-based budget carrier, sister airline of Emirates, said the aircraft had âexperienced an incident while en route,â without disclosing details.
Israel said it was treating the event as a potential terror attack based on suspicions one of the pilots may have intentionally tried to crash the plane, according to Haaretz. The aircraft issued a general distress call before switching to a code signaling a hijacking. The plane landed in Tabuk, in northwestern Saudi Arabia, where the pilot and co-pilot were hospitalized. All passengers on board are reportedly safe.

Only 28% of nurdles which spilled into a river have been recovered and are expected to continue washing up on beaches in the future, scientists have calculated.
Almost 18 tonnes of plastic nurdles are estimated to have spilled into the River Tyne after a collision between ships at the Port of Tyne in July.
However, only 5.14 tonnes have been recovered despite volunteers spending thousands of hours clearing beaches across the region, work by Newcastle University and the Centre for Environment, Fisheries and Aquaculture Science (Cefas) found.
South Tyneside Council's director of community operations Gary Kirsop, said the multi-agency group in charge of the nurdle response "remained committed".
The university and Cefas said nurdles were "likely to have dispersed beyond the Tyne estuary out into the North Sea".
The work, undertaken by the university, also said some nurdles "may remain within the river system" and will continue to wash up on parts of the coastline in future, depending on weather conditions, winds and tides.
North East mayor Kim McGuinness said this was upsetting for those caring for the region's coastline.
She has commissioned an independent review into the response and recovery, and said she is backing calls for a change in international rules about how plastic nurdles are transported.
McGuinness said: "It's vital the agencies involved in the clean up are ready and act quickly to continue their work when this happens."
Scientific and Techincal Advice Cell (STAC) has reviewed Cefas' modelling alongside recovery data and shoreline surveys.
It said modelling cannot accurately predict exactly when and where nurdles will wash up and the complete recovery of every nurdle was not considered achievable.
Dr Robert Bradburne, STAC chair, said: "As with any environmental incident of this nature, ongoing monitoring remains important and the situation should continue to be reviewed as further evidence becomes available."

Animal rights activists have criticised Botswana's decision to authorise the killing of 23 elephants to provide meat for independence celebrations.
The southern African country, home to the world's largest elephant population, is holding nationwide festivities on Wednesday to mark the 60th anniversary of independence from Britain.
A licence issued by the Ministry of Environment and Tourism, seen by local media, authorises the hunting of 23celephants and other wild animals for "complimentary purposes".
The Botswana-based Elephant Protection Society warns the decision could undermine conservation, with its chairman Oaitse Nawa telling the BBC elephants needed greater protection.
He warned that slaughtering elephants for celebratory feasting could encourage poaching by creating the impression that killing elephants is acceptable when sanctioned by government.
"Elephants have lost their social structures because they are always being pushed from one place to another by gunshots," Nawa said.
Several social media users in the country have also expressed concerns about eating the game meat amid an outbreak of foot-and-mouth disease, which has prompted authorities to impose measures to contain its spread.
Tshenatshe Monwela, an elder in Maun, a tourism town in north-western Botswana told local media that his community should have received buffalo instead.
He argued that elephants had particular cultural and ecological significance and that Botswana's historic role in protecting the country's wildlife and livestock should have been recognised in the government's allocation of meat for the anniversary celebrations.
Botswana's government has organised a series of events to mark the country's diamond jubilee, including a carnival in the capital, Gaborone, as well as cultural performances, concerts and sporting events.
The game meat is expected to be served as part of the traditional feasting associated with the Independence Day celebrations.
The 23 elephants were allocated in eight districts across the country.
It was not immediately clear how many of the animals had been killed by Wednesday morning. The BBC has asked the government for comment.
But local media published images from different parts of Botswana showing residents gathering around elephant carcasses, some with knives in hand and sharing the meat.
In Chobe, a wildlife-rich district in northern Botswana near the borders with Namibia, Zambia and Zimbabwe, a local MP raised concerns after residents reportedly collected portions directly from a carcass at a school.
He said the system risked creating congestion and disadvantaging elderly people, pregnant women and people with disabilities, and suggested the meat should instead be processed into 5kg or 10kg packages to improve hygiene and ensure fairer distribution.
"For the sake of dignity, fairness and public hygiene, we respectfully call on the hunter and the relevant leadership to ensure that future distributions are properly organised," MP Simasiku Mapulanga posted on Facebook, attaching photos of people scrambling for meat around an elephant carcass.
Elephant meat is common in some wildlife-rich communities, particularly when meat from legal hunts is distributed locally, but it is not an everyday staple.
Botswana also tightly regulates game meat, and its legal possession generally depends on proving it came from a lawful hunt.
The decision has reignited a long-running and often heated debate in Botswana over how the country manages its huge elephant population.
Botswana has more than 130,000 elephants and communities living alongside them have long complained about animals destroying crops, damaging property and sometimes killing people.
The government has defended regulated hunting as one way of managing the elephant population and human-wildlife conflict while generating income for communities.
The country banned trophy hunting in 2014 under former President Ian Khama but lifted the restrictions five years later under his successor, Mokgweetsi Masisi.
Hunting has continued under President Duma Boko, who defeated Masisi in elections in 2024.
The government says proceeds from hunting supports conservation and local development.
Minister of Environment and Tourism Wynter Mmolotsi told parliament last year that special elephant quotas raised 15.6m pula ($1.1m; Â£820,000) in 2025 for projects in areas where elephants are found.
But conservation organisations have questioned whether the level of hunting is sustainable.
Supporters of Botswana's hunting policy, however, argue that international criticism often overlooks the costs borne by rural communities living alongside one of the world's biggest concentrations of elephants.
They say elephants destroy crops and infrastructure and pose a danger to people, particularly as their range increasingly overlaps with farms and settlements.

Singaporeâs Temasek will open its first offices in the Gulf early next year, joining a growing list of global investors expanding into the region despite ongoing conflict.
Temasek, which controls around $400 billion on behalf of the government of Singapore, will open offices in Abu Dhabi and Riyadh. It plans to invest more in the region and to use the offices as a base for portfolio companies looking to expand into the Middle East. The regional presence will also be used to deepen the firmâs engagement with Qatar, Temasek said.
Gulf finance hubs have continued to attract commitments from international firms even as they have been rocked by retaliatory attacks from Tehran in March and April after the US used military bases in the region to stage strikes on Iran. Attacks have slowed since then, but the threat of further escalation remains.
UK-based private markets firm Pantheon, which manages $84 billion, also announced plans on Wednesday to open offices in Abu Dhabi.
âThe Middle East is an important part of Temasekâs global network,â chief executive Dilhan Pillay said. âThe pace and ambition of economic transformation across the region are remarkable, and its long-term fundamentals remain highly attractive.â
Temasekâs most recent international office opened in Paris in 2023.
Know More
By opening in Riyadh and Abu Dhabi simultaneously, Temasek sidesteps a dilemma facing international finance firms expanding in the region: rather than choosing between rival financial hubs, it is setting up in both.
Earlier this year, the Singaporean investor also joined a $30 billion infrastructure partnership with Abu Dhabi sovereign wealth fund LâIMAD, the emirateâs national oil company ADNOC, and BlackRockâs Global Infrastructure Partners. Its Gulf investments are expected to focus on energy, infrastructure, logistics, and urban development.
Temasekâs expansion into the Gulf also comes as regional governments increasingly focus on attracting foreign direct investment to drive economic diversification. Saudi Arabiaâs Public Investment Fund has made attracting external investors a key part of its plan for the next five years, and state oil companies have been selling stakes in their pipelines and other infrastructure assets. Multibillion-dollar plans to build AI hubs and new export routes are also expected to create opportunities for foreign infrastructure investors.
The chance to partner with Gulf sovereign funds, which are on track for one of their busiest years of dealmaking on record despite the disruptions of the Iran war, is also helping to attract more global finance firms to the region.

Russia has launched the largest attack on Ukraine's energy infrastructure since the spring, primarily targeting Kyiv and the surrounding region, Ukrainian Prime Minister Serhiy Koretskyi has said.
At least five people were killed in overnight attacks across the country, including a child in the Kyiv region, Koretskyi said.
The strikes also impacted people's power supplies, with Ukraine's biggest private energy firm, DTEK, saying power to 8,000 homes had been restored following "a difficult night" for the capital.
The Russian defence ministry said one of its targets was the Trypilska power station, the largest supplier of electricity to Kyiv. This has not been confirmed by Ukrainian officials.
In a statement on Telegram, Koretskyi said: "Since the summer, there has effectively not been a single day without enemy attacks on our energy infrastructure.
"However, a mass and combined attack of this scale has occurred for the first time since the end of the last heating season."
Ukraine has been expecting another protracted Russian assault on the country's energy grid. It has happened every winter so far since Russia's full-scale invasion in 2022.
In total 11 regions of the country were attacked overnight, with residential buildings, social infrastructure, civilian enterprises and railways also targeted, Koretskyi said.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said there were strikes on critical infrastructure in the Zhytomyr, Mykolaiv, Kirovohrad and Rivne regions.
On Wednesday, some households in the Kyiv, Dnipropetrovsk, Donetsk, Sumy, Kyiv and Kharkiv regions remained without power, Ukraine's energy ministry said.
State-owned grid operator Ukrenegro advised residents not to use powerful electrical appliances between the hours of 10:00 and 16:00 local time as electricity supplies were lower than usual.
In Kyiv, people woke to find the city blanketed by thick, acrid smoke after a night punctuated by the sound of explosions. An air raid alert was still on and the distant sound of air defence gunfire echoed through the murky atmosphere.
Residents in several districts were advised to close their windows until the smoke cleared.
Among those killed in the overnight strikes was a child whose body was found under the rubble of a house, Kyiv regional governor Timur Tkachenko said.
Kyiv Mayor Vitaly Klischko said three people were killed in total in the capital, including a Ukrainian utility company worker who was killed at a warehouse building.
Another person was killed in the Mykolaiv region, acting regional governor Heorhiy Reshetilov said.
Two more people were also killed in the north-eastern Sumy region on Tuesday, governor Oleh Hryhorov said. A school was also hit there in a separate strike, he added.
Russian President Vladimir Putin launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, and Moscow currently controls about 20% of Ukrainian territory.

The last British and American troops have left Iraq after a military presence of more than a decade in the country.
The exit of the remaining UK military personnel - around 100 - from Irbil, in the northern Kurdistan region, was co-ordinated over recent weeks with US forces, who also departed on Wednesday.
It follows an agreement between the US and the Iraqi government, signed two years ago, to withdraw foreign troops by the end of this month.
British and US forces have been present in Iraq since 2014, as part of the international coalition to help defeat the extremist Islamic State (IS) group. Their departure brings the mission, known as Operation Inherent Resolve, to an end.
Iraqi Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi said the end of the coalition's mission marked "Iraq's transition to a phase in which it assumes full responsibility for its security and stability".
Iraq is set to hold four "Sovereignty Days" as a national holiday to mark the withdrawal.
"Following more than a decade of operations, training and capacity building, Iraqi Security Forces (ISF) and the Kurdish Peshmerga have secured the enduring territorial defeat of Daesh in Iraq and are now well placed to take primary responsibility for the country's security," the UK Ministry of Defence (MoD) said in a statement, referring to IS by an Arabic acronym.
"With these objectives achieved, Iraq and its international partners can begin a new chapter focused on enduring security co-operation under Iraqi leadership."
Pentagon spokesman Sean Parnell said the coalition's departure from Irbil marked "the successful conclusion of the military mission that defeated [IS] in Iraq".
He added: "The primary responsibility for addressing Iraq's remaining security challenges, including [IS] remnants and Iran-aligned militias that undermine Iraqi sovereignty and regional stability, now rests with the government of Iraq."
The Iraqi government declared the military defeat of IS in 2017, but coalition forces remained to help prevent the group's resurgence.
A recent UN report estimated that sustained counter-terrorism pressure by Iraqi security forces had left IS with several hundred fighters who were "able to carry out unsophisticated operations only".
The Iraqi government also faces the challenge of Iranian-backed militias in the country.
Zaidi, who took office in May, has vowed to disarm them and bring all weapons under state control following the coalition's exit.
But several powerful factions have resisted his plans and could now see their influence grow without the US presence.
Since the start of the US and Israel's war with Iran earlier this year, militias have been targeting the remaining US and UK forces stationed at Irbil air base.
Hundreds of Nato troops stationed in Baghdad left the country in March as tensions rose.
A BBC team visited the coalition base in Irbil in April this year, during a fragile ceasefire between the US and Iran.
They were forced to circle the base in an RAF transport aircraft while drones were being launched nearby.
At the height of the US bombing campaign against Iran, the coalition base was being targeted by up to 28 drones and missiles a day.
RAF Regiment Gunners, who were among the last British military personnel stationed there, had shot down more than 100 drones in the first six weeks of the war. Many of the attack drones were being launched by Iranian-backed militias in Iraq.
On Wednesday, signalling the end of the mission, the MoD paid tribute to UK personnel who had contributed to the counter-IS mission.
It said they had provided "valuable support, training and assistance" to more than 111,000 members of the Iraqi Security Forces, including more than 21,000 Peshmerga forces in the semi-autonomous Kurdistan Region.
It also said the RAF had conducted thousands of sorties, striking more than 2,300 IS targets. The RAF is expected to continue flying missions over neighbouring Syria, to prevent the remnants of IS from gaining a foothold.
The Pentagon said the US would continue to provide "targeted training and intelligence support" to its Iraqi partners.
US Central Command said the coalition's joint taskforce remained operational and was now based in Jordan.
US forces will also continue their mission against IS in Syria, where the UN estimates that the group has up to 3,000 fighters.
This is the third time US and UK forces have withdrawn from Iraq.
Tens of thousands of US and British troops were deployed to the country in 1991 following Saddam Hussein's invasion of Kuwait.
They returned to Iraq in 2003, when US President George W Bush ordered Operation Iraqi Freedom to remove the dictator from power and eliminate weapons of mass destruction that turned out not to exist.
The fierce sectarian insurgency that engulfed Iraq following the invasion cost tens of thousands of lives, including those of nearly 4,500 US military personnel and 179 British military personnel.
US and UK forces left Iraq in 2011, only to return three years later, when IS threatened to take control of the country.

Interested in hiring a camel in Saudi Arabia, but worried about what it might entail? Fear not, as the country has finally introduced a rulebook for leasing grumpy, humpy dromedaries. For camel rentals, owners must be registered with the authorities, contracts must be documented electronically, and records must be updated when animals are transferred or their location changes. Camels must be returned to their original ownerâs registry when the rental agreement ends. Violations may result in fines and prosecution.
But the paperwork belies how serious this matter is: Camels are revered, and prize animals can command eye-watering sums. In 2021, a Saudi owner leased a camel for 20 million riyals ($5.3 million) for just 48 hours. Chew on that.

A sprinter’s first task is to react to the starting pistol. Now, a button-clicking experiment suggests that how quickly people respond to a cue may depend in part on whether they’re breathing in or out.
Volunteers’ reaction times were faster when they exhaled or held their breath compared with when they inhaled, researchers report September 28 in iScience.
Ken Paller and Erika Yamazaki, then both cognitive neuroscientists at Northwestern University, made their discovery while studying breathing patterns to find treatments for sleep apnea. Yamazaki graduated from her PhD earlier this year.
Paller and Yamazaki determined how sleepy 35 volunteers were with a simple reaction-time test. The volunteers were tasked with clicking a button when an on-screen red square turned yellow.
Yamazaki realized that, because the volunteers’ breathing was recorded through short tubes in the nose throughout the task, the researchers could also check whether inhaling or exhaling influenced reaction times.
Reaction times were, on average, 41 milliseconds faster during exhalation than during inhalation. This finding held regardless of how sleepy or alert the volunteers were.
That might not sound like a huge difference, but Noah Lyles won the 2024 Olympic men’s 100-meter final by five thousandths of a second. Those 41 milliseconds would have made the difference between Lyles winning and finishing fourth.
But the relationship between breath and brain appears to be complex. A 2016 study found that reaction times were faster during inhalation than exhalation in tests of recall and facial recognition. But these tasks differed from the hair-trigger change Paller and Yamazaki studied. Those tasks required more cognitive processing, Paller says, because they required the participants to judge whether, for example, a face look fearful or surprised, rather than waiting for a simple cue. “That may or may not have the same relationship with respiration.”
The mechanism behind these findings isn’t clear, although Paller points to studies, like the one from 2016, that suggest our breath is synced to the ebb and flow of our brain waves.
In a race decided by thousandths of a second, every factor matters, even a single breath.

Concerns are rising in Africa about the potential water use by data centers.
A recent petition by a collection of civil society groups to the South African Human Rights Commission highlighted concerns over the lack of awareness of water consumption in a country that already hosts 60 data centers and is struggling with climate-change-induced drought.
Large data centers can consume up to 5 million gallons per day; a recent study modelling water use in African data centers found that ChatGPT-4 used up to 60 liters of water â or a standard washing machine cycle â to produce a 10-page paper.
While water usage by data centers is a global problem, Africa is particularly vulnerable to the effects of climate change. âYou are introducing sites which are resource intensive enough to be in many ways comparable to extractive industries,â Michael Marchant, head of investigations at civil society group Open Secrets, which was among the petitioners, told Semafor. âWe see the risk of data centers, especially hyperscale, falling through the cracks.â

bd97177e90cd.text:
Western aid cuts offer African nations a âmajor opportunityâ to regain their independence after years of overreliance on overseas assistance to fund public health services, the head of the Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention told Semafor.
Governments across the continent relied heavily on USAID, Washingtonâs development agency, to fund health programs before it was shuttered last year. Some 700,000 people have lost their lives in the past 18 months as a result of the development cuts, the head of a global aid organization said last week.
Yet âeven if administrations change in Western countries, weâll never again have the level of support we had in the past,â Jean Kaseya said in an interview on the sidelines of Semaforâs The Next 3 Billion event. Kaseya said he was working with African governments to cut waste by eradicating fraud in procurement and salary payments, citing the example of one nation (which he did not name) in which half of salaried health staff were found to be âghost workers.â Kaseya, who said there was âno doubtâ the Ebola outbreak in DR Congo was made worse by the cuts, also urged governments to mobilize domestic resources through taxation.

South Africa summoned US ambassador Leo Brent Bozell III again, deepening a diplomatic rift with Washington in the same week that one of the countryâs biggest companies lost ground in a US terrorism lawsuit.
Bozell â first summoned in March over his remarks on the âKill the Boerâ chant â has more recently been attacking Pretoriaâs response to US President Donald Trumpâs demands on land, race policy, farm murders, and hate speech. South Africa has repeatedly rejected the demands as interference in domestic affairs, arguing its race-based policies are constitutional redress in a country where the Black majority was left destitute by apartheid policies.
The clash coincides with Johannesburg-based MTN Group, Africaâs largest telecoms company, failing to clear a key hurdle in a New York lawsuit brought by families of US citizens killed or injured in Iraq and Afghanistan. They allege MTN aided the Taliban through protection payments and switched off its towers at the request of the Islamist group, and assisted Iranâs Revolutionary Guards in Iraq through its stake in Irancell.

Burkina Faso opened a refinery to process the countryâs gold reserves domestically, a demonstration of the junta-led governmentâs resolve to prevent raw mineral exports. The nation is among Africaâs largest gold producers, but has struggled to regulate its informal mining sector.
Junta leader Ibrahim TraorÃ©, who inaugurated the new plant on Monday, said it was part of a long-term approach for the sector: âFor everything related to the extractive industry, we want to have the entire value chain in the country.â He vowed to enshrine domestic control over other minerals, including lithium, copper, and nickel.
Governments across the continent are pursuing policies aimed at capturing more value from their natural resources. African leaders have increasingly argued their countries should build domestic processing and refining capacity, rather than shipping fossil fuels and critical minerals abroad.

Africaâs richest man Aliko Dangote formally kicked off construction of a $16 billion oil refinery in Kenya on Wednesday, aiming to replicate the success of his plant in Nigeria which has turned the country into a fuel-producing powerhouse amidst a global energy crisis.
The new refinery on the island of Lamu is set to be completed in 2030, ultimately refining 700,000 barrels a day. It will serve a region that has historically relied on Middle East fuel imports as part of a broader push to strengthen Africaâs energy security and bolster economic growth. Kenyaâs President William Ruto was joined at the groundbreaking ceremony by the presidents of Ethiopia and Uganda.
The planned refinery already faces competition from upcoming projects in Tanzania and Uganda, however. Separately, a Kenyan court had granted a group claiming ownership of the refineryâs proposed site the right to maintain status quo until a hearing on the case in October, though the order did not prevent Dangoteâs kick-off event. The group plans to list shares of its Nigeria refinery on the Nairobi Securities Exchange in December, following a Lagos initial public offering two weeks ago.

508445e86f35.text: By — Qassim Abdul-Zahra, Associated Press Qassim Abdul-Zahra, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/world/u-s-military-says-its-withdrawal-of-troops-from-iraq-for-islamic-state-fight-is-complete Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter U.S. military says its withdrawal of troops from Iraq for Islamic State fight is complete World Sep 30, 2026 10:07 AM EDT BAGHDAD (AP) — The U.S. military announced on Wednesday that it has completed the withdrawal of all American troops from Iraq, ending a 12-year mission to fight the Islamic State group. The last U.S. troops left an air base in northern Iraq under a deal between Baghdad and Washington. The withdrawal, agreed on two years ago, comes against the backdrop of the ongoing war between the United States and Iran that has also sometimes spilled over into Iraq, with Iran-backed militias firing on U.S. troops and the U.S. striking the groups' strongholds. READ MORE: Attack that closed key Saudi pipeline is blamed on Iran-backed militias in Iraq In recent years, Washington has appeared to seek to shift its focus from the Middle East toward Asia, but that shift has been inconsistent, with the Pentagon alternating between reducing its Mideast presence and then finding itself engaging in new conflicts — including the ongoing war in Iran. Educate your inbox Subscribe to Here’s the Deal, our politics newsletter for analysis you won’t find anywhere else. Enter your email address Subscribe Form error message goes here. Thank you. Please check your inbox to confirm. Baghdad touted the end of the U.S. mission as a sign of the country's increasing strength and sovereignty. The withdrawal was also celebrated by Iran-backed groups but raised concerns among some other Iraqis, particularly in the Kurdish region, where many fear a resurgence of IS as well as more attacks by Iran-linked groups, possibly emboldened by the departure of U.S. forces. Meanwhile, questions loom around the future of the Iraqi militias, which the Baghdad government has sought to disarm, with little success so far. A new phase in Iraq after decades of U.S. involvement Pentagon spokesperson Sean Parnell said in a statement that U.S. troops and equipment had completed an "orderly departure" from the air base in Irbil, in northern Iraq's semi-autonomous Kurdish region. "This milestone reflects the success of a 12-year campaign that defeated ISIS as an organized military threat in Iraq and across the region," he said. "It also marks a transition from a wartime coalition mission to an Iraqi-led security effort supported by a more normal bilateral security relationship." He added that the U.S. military "will continue to provide targeted training and intelligence support to our Iraqi partners." Iraqi Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi presided over the handover ceremony and described the U.S. withdrawal as the beginning of a "new phase, one defined by Iraq's sovereignty, the strength of its institutions, the readiness of its forces, the unity of its decision-making, and balanced partnerships with its friends." He said Iraqi security forces will continue the fight against IS and the government will ensure that non-state groups no longer hold weapons. U.S. troops invaded Iraq in 2003 to topple Saddam Hussein. They departed in 2011, but three years later, Iraqi authorities invited a smaller U.S.-led mission to fight the Islamic State group, which had rampaged across Iraq, seizing large swaths of territory. With the extremist group reduced to scattered sleeper cells, Washington and Baghdad agreed in 2024 to wind the mission down. U.S. troops pulled out of bases in most areas of Iraq last year but maintained a small presence of hundreds of troops in the semiautonomous northern Kurdish region. Bases there have regularly come under attack since the U.S. and Israel launched their war against Iran on Feb. 28. Iran-backed Iraqi militias also have coordinated with Yemen's Houthi rebels to attack Saudi Arabia. The future of militias remains unclear The Iraqi government initially linked the Sept. 30 deadline for U.S. withdrawal to the disarmament of non-state armed groups by that date. While a handful of less-influential militias have agreed to turn over their weapons, powerful groups close to Iran rejected the prospect or set conditions for disarming that the government would be unlikely to meet. Al-Zaidi has since walked back the deadline. He told The New York Times earlier this month that the deadline for militia disarmament has been pushed to June 2027. The effects of the U.S. withdrawal may not be immediately visible, particularly since the U.S. military presence had already been scaled down. But officials in Iraq's Kurdish region have expressed anxiety about the departure and particularly about the removal of U.S. air defense systems. The Kurdish regional government's Peshmerga Ministry said the Kurdish region had faced more than 1,000 drone and ballistic-missile attacks during the recent U.S.-Iran conflict. "The departure of the United States from the Kurdistan Region under these complex regional circumstances, without the provision of a defense system, is a matter of concern," the statement said. Iran-allied groups in Iraq, meanwhile, have celebrated the U.S. withdrawal. "The expulsion of the occupation forces, defeated, from the land of Iraq is the beginning of full sovereignty," Abu Mujahid al-Assaf, a security official with the powerful Kataib Hezbollah militia, said in a statement. He added a warning to al-Zaidi and his government not to carry out American plans, threatening that "any government that does not work for the benefit of the people will be overthrown by all means." 9ea50f3c9ce5.text: By — Paul Wiseman, Associated Press Paul Wiseman, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/economy/u-s-economy-grew-a-solid-2-2-in-the-second-quarter-government-says-upgrading-previous-estimate Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter U.S. economy grew a solid 2.2% in the second quarter, government says, upgrading previous estimate Economy Sep 30, 2026 9:52 AM EDT WASHINGTON (AP) — The U.S. economy grew at a solid 2.2% pace from April through June as consumer spending and business investment came in strong. Growth in gross domestic product — the nation's output of a goods and services — decelerated from a 2.5% pace from January through March, the Commerce Department reported Wednesday. The second-quarter growth number was an improvement on the department's previous estimate of 1.5%. Consumer spending — which accounts for about 70% of U.S. economic activity — increased at a healthy 3.8% annual pace, up from 0.7% in the January-March period. Educate your inbox Subscribe to Here’s the Deal, our politics newsletter for analysis you won’t find anywhere else. Enter your email address Subscribe Form error message goes here. Thank you. Please check your inbox to confirm. The overall growth number was dragged down by imports. They are subtracted from growth because GDP is only supposed to count domestic production. Imports rose at a 12.6% annual pace from April through June, partly due to a surge in shipments of computer chips and other products that support artificial intelligence investment, and slashed nearly 1.7 percentage points off second-quarter growth. The U.S. economy has proven surprisingly resilient in the face of fighting with Iran and the energy price spike it caused. Business investment, excluding housing, rose at a 9% clip in the second quarter, reflecting the AI investment boom. And a measure of the economy's underlying strength — which strips out volatile government spending and trade numbers — grew at a strong 4.6% rate, up from 1.8% in the first quarter. Investment in housing rose 2.8% ticking up for the first time since the end of 2024. The housing market has been depressed by high mortgage rates. Wednesday's report was the last of three Commerce Department estimates of second-quarter GDP growth. The first look at third-quarter growth is due Oct. 29. b6e3d08624e5.text: Death row inmate Christa Pike got a last-minute reprieve Wednesday when a federal appeals court stopped her execution about an hour before it was set to take place in Nashville. The latest: The court ordered "a short stay of execution" just before 9am CDT so it could consider an ongoing legal battle between Pike's attorneys and the state. Pike's attorneys argue her history of child sexual abuse wasn't presented to the jury before she was sentenced to death in 1996. Between the lines: The order stops Wednesday's execution and puts it on hold while the court considers this motion. The state supreme court could still set another execution date in the future depending on the outcome of this legal fight. What they're saying: "The interests of justice and the finality of Pike's impending execution compel the entry of a short stay of execution in order to properly analyze the parties' fully briefed arguments and resolve the issues on the merits," the court wrote. Two members of a three-judge panel backed the order. The third judge disagreed, describing the legal fight as a "last-ditch meritless effort to delay a lawful execution." Zoom in: Pike, the only woman on Tennessee's death row, was convicted and sentenced to death for the 1995 murder of Colleen Slemmer. Pike was 18 at the time. Two other people were convicted in the case, but only Pike got the death penalty. Pike's advocates do not contest her guilt, but they argue that her history of childhood abuse should have been presented to the jury during the sentencing phase as "important context and mitigation for the offense."

The Scoop
Mattel CEO Ynon Kreiz is joining David Ellisonâs team at the combined Warner Bros. Discovery-Paramount in a senior leadership role, a big poach for Ellison and a signal of more expansive ambitions from the combined studio.
Kreizâs remit and title havenât yet been determined, according to people familiar with the matter. Kreiz didnât immediately respond to a request for comment. A Paramount spokesperson wasnât available for comment.
âI am proud of all we have achieved together,â he said in a press release on Wednesday announcing his departure, which sent shares in the toy company down 4%.
Know More
Kreiz joined Mattel as CEO in 2018, helping turn the toymaker into an intellectual-property licensing machine. âPeople who buy our products, theyâre not just consumers, they are fans,â Kreiz told Semafor in a 2023 interview. âAnd once you have a lot of fans, itâs an audience. And when you have an audience, it changes the opportunity that you have in front of you.â
Roger Lynch, CEO of Vogue parent Conde Nast and Mattelâs lead independent director, will take over as CEO of Mattel in November.
Lynch, who didnât immediately respond to a request for comment, said he was âhonored by the boardâs confidence in me and couldnât be more excited to lead the incredible team at Mattel.â
Rohanâs view
Ellison has a growing bench of operators to turn to â and he will need them. The combined Warner Bros. Discovery and Paramount need both a new name (CNN reported that a decision on that could come as soon as tomorrow) and to start moving immediately to whittle down the companyâs leviathan $52 billion debt pile.
Kreiz should be able to help. He worked to get Mattel financially fit before he turned it into a Barbie-backed movie studio; RedBirdâs Gerry Cardinale and his bench of operating partners, including former CNN boss Jeff Zucker, will also be there to help clean up the companyâs balance sheet.
But more importantly, Kreiz and Lynchâs hirings also showcase the need to refashion the company as one that focuses on intellectual property, rather than increasingly commoditized media.
Lynch helped Vogue monetize the Met Gala â a physical thing â into an ecosystem of events, content, and buzz. Kreiz did much the same with Barbie dolls to kickstart what is effectively a new movie studio (although weâre still waiting on the Barney movie.) Content, after all, as Bill Gates wrote 30 years ago, is king.

Apex Clean Energy and Meta have entered into a power purchase agreement that allows the technology company to financially benefit from energy generated from a solar project in Gonzales County, Texas.
The 144-megawatt project wouldn’t have been built without Meta’s backing, the energy developer said. But the partnership comes after the parent company of Facebook quietly exited a corporate renewable energy initiative following a decade of membership earlier this year, raising questions about the company’s commitment to renewable energy as Meta builds an expansive portfolio of energy-hungry data centers, totaling 28 sites in the United States as of April.
Meta plans to power a new data center in El Paso with a 366-megawatt gas-fired plant.
In a statement to Inside Climate News, Meta said natural gas options are part of its data center expansion plans for artificial intelligence but added that the decision to exit Climate Group’s RE100 renewable-energy initiative holds no bearing on its commitment to clean energy. The company said it has contributed more than 30 gigawatts of new clean energy to grids across the country to date and has retained its goal to match its electricity use with 100 percent “clean and renewable energy.”
As part of the new project, called Starling Solar, Meta will get to claim “all environmental attributes” from the energy production. That allows the company to offset some of the gas-fired energy powering its data centers when it tallies up its electricity use, but the gas power plants will have climate and local air-pollution impacts all the same.
Dennis Wamsted, energy analyst at the Institute for Energy Economics and Financial Analysis, said artificial intelligence development doesn’t have to come at the cost of renewable energy.
“I applaud Meta for trying. They have been very active in the past in building out or paying for the build-out of renewable energy across the United States,” he said.
But Wamsted sees problems with the speed of Meta’s AI build-out and its reliance on natural gas to do so.
“I think in some regards they’re taking what could be called the easy way out,” he said. “While I am positive about their past impact on renewables, I am increasingly critical about their current approach, which is to build anything they can get their hands on as fast as they possibly can, and I don’t think that we need AI quite that quickly.”
He added, “I think you can build wind and certainly solar very quickly and it can be used to power AI data servers and centers all across the country.”
Solar power has become an increasingly valuable resource in Texas. Apex expects the Starling Solar project to help bolster the state’s grid, which has encountered record-high demand this month that surpassed the record set in 2023. The state is grappling with high temperatures and an influx of data centers. Meta has three locations in Texas.
In August, Gov. Greg Abbott instructed utility regulators and the Texas grid operator to oversee an audit of every data center waiting to connect to the grid in ERCOT’s interconnection process, including their water consumption practices, local water supply sources and whether they use water-efficient technologies. Data centers that fail to comply with the audit will be denied interconnection.
Renewables made up about a third of Texas’ in-state electricity last year. That’s meant money for landowners, particularly farmers and ranchers, through lease payments for thousands of transactions like Meta’s power purchase agreement, Wamsted said.
Meta and Apex expect Starling to generate tax revenue of $27 million over the life of the project, $26.3 million in landowner payments and an estimated 400 to 450 jobs during the construction phase.
Starling is scheduled to begin operations next year.
About This Story
Perhaps you noticed: This story, like all the news we publish, is free to read. That’s because Inside Climate News is a 501c3 nonprofit organization. We do not charge a subscription fee, lock our news behind a paywall, or clutter our website with ads. We make our news on climate and the environment freely available to you and anyone who wants it.
That’s not all. We also share our news for free with scores of other media organizations around the country. Many of them can’t afford to do environmental journalism of their own. We’ve built bureaus from coast to coast to report local stories, collaborate with local newsrooms and co-publish articles so that this vital work is shared as widely as possible.
Two of us launched ICN in 2007. Six years later we earned a Pulitzer Prize for National Reporting, and now we run the oldest and largest dedicated climate newsroom in the nation. We tell the story in all its complexity. We hold polluters accountable. We expose environmental injustice. We debunk misinformation. We scrutinize solutions and inspire action.
Donations from readers like you fund every aspect of what we do. If you don’t already, will you support our ongoing work, our reporting on the biggest crisis facing our planet, and help us reach even more readers in more places?

f343c73edad1.text:
First, the bad news: Of all the rivers in the contiguous United States, only 6 percent are both in healthy condition and meaningfully safeguarded. The good news is that many more may be just one repair away from thriving.
A new map highlights where conservation money and attention would do the most good as the climate warms, researchers report September 16 in PLOS One. The effort is the most comprehensive to date, assessing the health of the lower 48 states’ rivers and streams.
“We can now point at a map for the first time and say, these are the rivers most capable of sustaining diversity of aquatic life, and this is what each one needs,” says Mary Khoury, a freshwater ecologist at The Nature Conservancy who is based in Chicago.
For decades, conservation in the United States has been organized primarily around land. Scientists know for the most part which forests are intact and who owns what. Rivers have never gotten that treatment, even as more than 150,000 dams have fragmented the country’s waterways — cutting fish off from spawning grounds and cold-water refuges — and climate change has altered the temperatures and flows these animals depend on.
The new assessment, which took four years, maps one-third of the nation’s stream distances. Each small watershed was rated on four measures: how connected its river network is, meaning whether animals including fish and mussels can freely travel along it; the condition of its floodplain and water quality; how much water it has; and how much its flows have been altered. Those ratings were laid over 91 existing assessments of where freshwater life is concentrated. Dozens of scientists and partners from 44 states adjusted the measures for river systems in regions as different as the humid East, the arid Great Plains and the deserts of the Southwest.
River resilience
A four-year assessment graded every river and stream in the lower 48 for its ability to sustain aquatic life in a warming climate. The healthiest ones cluster along the Pacific Coast, in the northern Rockies and across the Southeast. The most vulnerable sit in the Southwest deserts, the Great Plains and southern New England.
Rivers doing well on all four criteria — more than half of the mapped stream distances — came out as resilient. The rest score near average, and were classed as restorable, still functional but held back by a problem, such as runoff from a farm or an obstructing dam, that one intervention could solve.
Together the two categories form what the authors call a freshwater resilient and connected network, a shopping list of what the country would need to look after to keep its freshwater life going. “A resilient system is one that gives species options and environments in which to adapt,” Khoury says.
Dams leave the clearest mark on the country’s rivers, carving them into more than 9,000 separate pieces. The study maps where reconnecting rivers would pay off most. Among the long unbroken stretches within the resilient system are Oregon and California’s Klamath River, whose lower dams came out in the largest removal project in U.S. history, and the Delaware River, which runs free of barriers along its main stem from New York’s Catskill Mountains to the sea.
“I can see this being overlaid in the future, for example, with where dam licenses will expire, in order to find the most effective restoration opportunities,” says Rafael Schmitt, a hydrologist at the University of California, Santa Barbara who was not involved in the work.
Unlike on land, the study found, a river’s health says almost nothing about whether anyone is looking after it. On land, the healthiest places tend to be the protected ones. In water, however, 13 percent of the country’s stream distances are in good shape with no real safeguards, roughly twice the 6 percent that is both healthy and protected.
The unprotected healthy rivers are the ones most at risk of slipping, because nothing keeps them in that condition. Locking in protection is harder for a river than for a forest. A designated preserve can hold a kilometer of stream while the water arriving in it may drain 100 kilometers of farm fields, dams and subdivisions. “It matters what’s going on upstream of that protected area,” Khoury says.

9c5dff5ac217.text:
The Scoop
Amputees in developing nations may hold the key to giving humanoid robots hands that actually work.
Psyonic, a San Diego startup, wants to give people its bionic hands â and pay them â so it can capture data on how they grip, lift, and fold, with the ultimate goal of perfecting the robotic hand, a longstanding challenge in physical AI.
Founded in 2015, the company initially focused on making prosthetic hands for humans, but CEO Aadeel Akhtar said robotics developers in recent years came knocking at his door, interested in using the hands for robots.
Psyonic is now in the early stages of an effort to deploy thousands of bionic hands globally â it is specifically eyeing Pakistan, where Akhtarâs parents are from, and India. Users would go about their everyday tasks; the data from every grip would then be used to train a robotics model, making the prosthetic wearers a data-collection workforce. That in turn, Akhtar hopes, can subsidize the cost of the hands for those who need them.
âRobotics has a data problem,â especially around hands, Akhtar told Semafor. Companies are scouring for new data sources that can be used to train robots: Some are offering free home cleanings in exchange for filming the work; others are strapping head-mounted cameras on factory workers in India.
Akhtar said Psyonicâs hands log the forces, torques, and finger positions of every grip, which can be synced to video from a wearable camera, so a robotics model learns both what the task looks like and what it feels like. Psyonicâs current plan is to sell the resulting models, rather than the data itself, to robotics companies, Akhtar said.
He also sees it as a way to provide an economic livelihood to people who are unemployed because they are missing limbs; millions of people worldwide have upper-limb amputations, most of them in developing countries. Psyonic is working with Koalaa, a London-based company, to deploy the hands using a soft fabric sleeve â replacing the custom-molded socket that would ordinarily take several clinician visits to set up.
Know More
Hands are particularly puzzling for robotics engineers in part because of how compact and complex they are. Engineers count a handâs complexity in âdegrees of freedomâ â the number of independent ways it can move. A human hand has around 27; some of the most advanced robotic hands have about 22. Hands are often the biggest single cost in building a humanoid, Barclays researcher Zornitsa Todorova said.
âItâs loaded with motors and rare earths and actuators,â she said. âItâs like an iPhone on steroids. Everything is really packed.â
On top of those engineering challenges, hands also have to interact with the physical world in a way that robotic legs often donât. It doesnât matter whether a robot doing a backflip, for example, lands hard or soft on a concrete floor. But a hand has to be skilled at âgrabbing a raspberry without crushing it, but also lifting a 100-pound kettlebell and swinging it,â Akhtar said.
That kind of rich, tactile-based manipulation â essentially instilling a sense of touch and feeling in a robot hand â remains âgenerally unsolved,â said Kanishka Rao, a research director on Google DeepMindâs robotics team. The lab, whose models are built to run on other companiesâ robot hardware, has made advances in dexterity: In rolling out Gemini Robotics 2 in July, DeepMind showed a video of a humanoid tying a trash bag â a task that even humans sometimes struggle with.
Rao likened future challenges to pulling keys out of a purse when you canât see whatâs inside: A person can deduce whatâs plastic versus metal, soft versus sharp, but âthis is a very difficult task that robots would have a lot of trouble doing today.â
Room for Disagreement
Some in the robotics industry argue a human-like hand isnât needed. Some bots that are currently in use in hospitals, from companies like Cobot and Diligent Robotics, move on wheels and have simple grippers to transport supplies, lab samples, and carts through hospital corridors.
A study from German researchers published in July, which reviewed more than 100 scientific papers, found that âin-hand manipulation does not benefit from anthropomorphic hand design, as simpler mechanisms are sufficient.â Robot-makers should try to copy the function, rather than just the form, of the human hand, they wrote.
The View From China
A host of Chinese startups are also racing to solve the hand hurdle, and analysts say they have an advantage in cost and scale, given Chinaâs hardware-manufacturing prowess. Leading Chinese firm Unitree Robotics last week announced a new human-sized robotic hand with 22 degrees of freedom.
âIt was really impossible to do hardware in the United States because the supply chain problem is just so constraining,â the founder of a Shenzhen-based robo-hands company told The Guardian.
The superpowersâ physical AI sectors are becoming increasingly isolated, after Washington in July banned new models of foreign-made robots.
