- Published
Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth is expected to announce the firings of 20% of admirals and generals across the US Armed Forces, according to US media.
The announcement is anticipated Wednesday at Marine Corps Base Quantico in Virginia, adding to an earlier round of personnel cuts in 2025.
There are over 800 active-duty generals and admirals across the Army, Navy, Marine Corps, Air Force and Space Force, according to the latest defence department tally.
The last time Hegseth assembled military leaders at Quantico, in September 2025, he criticised the department as being too "woke" and slammed its leaders for being out of shape, saying "fat generals and admirals" is "a bad look".
Hegseth's anticipated firings are the latest in a broader overhaul of the US military under his leadership, seeking to insert what he calls a "war fighter ethos" into the defence department, including a rebrand, calling it the Department of War.
According to the BBC's news partner, CBS News, at least 20 generals, admirals and civilian military leaders have been terminated or quit their jobs since Hegseth became defence secretary.
This includes the firing of the chairman of the joint chiefs of staff and top uniformed officials in the Army, Navy and Air Force.
Federal law sets a limit to the number of general and flag officers. There is no requirement that unfilled positions be replaced.
Amid the shakeup, Hegseth also has been accused by various civil rights groups, including the NAACP and the National Women's Law Center, of blocking the military promotions of black people and women.
Senator Mark Kelly, a Democrat from Arizona, told reporters on Tuesday that Hegseth was "in the process of purging the upper echelon of the military from its best leaders".
"We need strong leaders. These folks have decades of experience, some of the best leadership our military has ever had. He's getting rid of them," Kelly said.
A report from the Congressional Research Service in May noted that there were some disadvantages of having too many senior leaders at the top.
These include the higher cost of employing top-ranked servicemembers compared to lower-ranking officers, and the potential to "slow down decisionmaking processes".
Hegseth's trimming of the US military's top brass also comes as the US-Israel war with Iran stretches into its seventh month, depleting ammunitions stockpiles.

7002aa9bac30.text:
- Published
At least 52 civilians have been killed during three days of heavy fighting around Alamata in Ethiopia's northern Tigray region, hospital sources have told the BBC.
It appears government troops have taken control of the town from regional fighters and intend to push north towards Mekelle, the region's main city. Social media clips show army tanks on Alamata's streets.
Clashes broke out last week after months of tension between the government and the party that controls Tigray, with both accusing each other of violating a 2022 deal that ended a two-year civil war.
Fighting has also affected neighbouring regions with 33 tourists stranded for the last week in Lalibela, a Unesco world heritage site.
"We have heard fighting, gunfire and artillery cannons firing throughout the week," a British tourist, who asked not to be named, told the BBC's Newsday programme about clashes near Lalibela in the Amhara region.
He said there was a large military presence in Lalibela, famous for being home to 13th Century churches hewn from rock and a holy site for millions of Orthodox Christians.
Most visitors to the tourist hub had been unable to leave since the airport closed to commercial flights last Wednesday, though he said 14 Israeli tourists had been evacuated by military helicopter on Monday.
The fighting around Lalibela has involved the army and an Amhara militia that has allied with Tigrayan fighters.
Earlier in September, they joined forces with other Ethiopian armed movements to form a seven-member alliance with the stated intention of removing the government in the capital, Addis Ababa.
There is also a fear that neighbouring Eritrea could be drawn into the conflict - as the government accuses Asmara of supporting the armed groups, something it denies.
The BBC is unable to report from Tigray and surrounding areas and it is difficult to find out what is happening because communications to the region have been cut.
The two sides disagree over who started the latest fighting.
The Tigray People's Liberation Front (TPLF), the party that runs Tigray, says it was responding to a federal offensive, including drone strikes, while the government says Tigrayan forces attacked first after seizing control of airports in the region.
TPLF fighters are also fighting in the Afar region, in a strategic area which connects landlocked Ethiopia to Djibouti and its ports.
Over the last few days, medical charity MÃ©decins Sans FrontiÃ¨res (MSF) said more than 700 wounded people had been admitted to hospitals it supports in Tigray.
The doctor at Alamata General Hospital, who requested anonymity, told the BBC the fighting in and around the town had taken place between Saturday and Monday, and involved heavy explosives and artillery, some of which landed in residential homes.
Those killed in the crossfire included children as young as three days old, mothers and cattle herders.
Twelve people had died in a single strike on the town's marketplace, the medic said.
Since the fighting erupted, banking services in Tigray have been suspended by the government. Access to the internet has also been cut - though it is not clear who ordered the closure.
A separate source in Alamata told the BBC there was a worsening humanitarian crisis in the area, as the town swelled with people fleeing fighting.
"All the residents of the surrounding areas entered the town of Alamata by walking on foot for as long as an hour, hoping the town would be safe.
"Unfortunately, everything is blocked - no banking service, no money transfer, no power, no internet, no phone. Hence people are in crisis, simply suffering, everyone is desperate and frustrated."
The British tourist in Lalibela said online banking was working in Lalibela but there was a shortage of physical cash.
He said the situation around the town had calmed down in the last two days and there were indications the airport, which was still being used by the military, might reopen on Thursday.
"The local people, they are still scared of what might happen. The military presence here in the town has remained and a larger military force has been seen leaving the town heading north," he said.
When the airport was first closed, 53 tourists had been in the town, he explained.
But some had since been evacuated, including the 14 Israelis airlifted out on Monday while another five had left the day before via an NGO convoy, despite advice not to travel by road.
Of the remaining tourists in Lalibela, the largest group were Americans, with Israelis, Britons, South Korean, South Africans, an Ethiopian-New Zealander and a Mexican also stranded, he said.
Meanwhile, for those cut off in Tigray because of the telecoms shutdown, the Tigray Broadcasting Service (TBS), based in Addis Ababa, has started an initiative to help reconnect families.
The broadcaster has said it will collect video messages via its Telegram channel from people outside the region and air them via satellite TV.
While limited to greetings and updates, this will provide a rare lifeline for families separated by the blackout.
The clampdown on Tigray's banking services is also affecting Tigrayans who are not physically in the region.
Customers have told the BBC that bank accounts opened in Tigray have been frozen or restricted.
"I boarded public transport from Addis Ababa to Adama and tried to pay using a mobile transfer, but it didn't work," said a former Mekelle resident who moved to the capital two months ago because of growing tensions in Tigray.
"It has created havoc for many people like me who escaped the situation in Tigray," he told the BBC's Tigrinya service.
"Many Tigrayans are now in trouble."
Additional reporting by Yemane Nagish

574e6a4a637b.text:
California’s next governor will face tough decisions on a highly controversial piece of healthcare policy: what to do about health coverage for the more than 1.4 million low-income residents without legal status. Democrat Xavier Becerra and Republican Steve Hilton present starkly different choices as public opinion wavers.
US Poised To Boot Legal Immigrants From Medicaid, Including Refugees and Sex-Trafficking Victims
Hundreds of thousands of immigrants with legal status are at risk of losing government health coverage starting Oct. 1, state data shows, signaling that the impact of Medicaid changes in President Donald Trump’s signature legislation from 2025 may be greater than anticipated.
Many lawfully present immigrants will be among the first people to lose Medicaid coverage under congressional Republicans’ One Big Beautiful Bill Act, which is expected to cut spending by more than $900 billion through 2034 for the state-federal health program for people with low incomes or disabilities. The law will strip many more immigrants of their Affordable Care Act plan subsidies and Medicare coverage next year.
Those losing their health benefits who were previously eligible include refugees of war, asylees who fled persecution, victims of sex trafficking, and interpreters who risked their lives assisting U.S. service members in Afghanistan — all of whom are in the country with the federal government’s permission. The law does not affect coverage for a few groups, including those who hold green cards.
The Congressional Budget Office, the nonpartisan budget scorekeeper, estimated the law’s changes eliminating Medicaid eligibility for many noncitizen adults with legal status would lead to about 100,000 more immigrants being uninsured by 2034.
KFF Health News asked several states how many Medicaid enrollees they had identified as being at risk of losing coverage under the provision. More than 281,000 immigrants from nine states and the District of Columbia are expected to lose Medicaid in October.
While some may be able to obtain coverage elsewhere, the state numbers suggest hundreds of thousands of immigrants nationally are at imminent risk of becoming uninsured.
The CBO declined to comment.
Florida alone identified nearly 177,000 immigrants who would no longer qualify for the state’s Medicaid program starting in October, said Anna Holaday, a spokesperson for the Florida Department of Children and Families. The agency verified the enrollees’ immigration status through government databases and sent notices to people to give them an opportunity to provide more information proving they remain eligible, Holaday said.
Arizona predicts nearly 28,000 could lose eligibility. New Jersey expects 15,000 to 25,000 of its noncitizen residents to lose their Medicaid coverage. In North Carolina, it’s about 29,000, and in Washington state it’s 11,000. Final numbers from states on how many Medicaid enrollees have been terminated from the program won’t be available until later this fall.
Lawmakers rely on the CBO to understand the budgetary and economic impacts of proposed legislation. Yet the federal agency did not publish estimates on the One Big Beautiful Bill Act’s impact on noncitizens enrolled in Medicaid until a month after Congress passed the bill and Trump signed it into law.
Much of the attention around Medicaid changes in the law has centered on implementation of work requirements as a new condition of eligibility for many enrollees starting in January. The CBO estimates the requirements will increase the number of uninsured Americans by about 5 million by 2034.
Without health coverage, immigrants are likely to lose access to doctors, prescription drugs, and most other medical services. They still could qualify for coverage of emergency care under a separate program known as Emergency Medicaid.
“I came here to live a better life,” said Ahin, a refugee who left war-torn Syria for Turkey in 2011 and came to the U.S. in October 2024. She spoke with KFF Health News on the condition that she be identified by only her first name, out of concern for her privacy and security.
Soon after arriving in the U.S., she developed severe abdominal pain that required intestinal surgery. Those costs, along with ongoing visits to specialists, were covered by Medicaid.
“I’m really worried about this,” she said. “It’s truly a terrible situation.”
Ahin, 25, said she doesn’t know what she will do if she needs to go to the hospital — she wouldn’t be able to pay the bill. She lives in a small apartment in New Jersey with her mother. Medicaid has also been vital to her mother, who has asthma.
Health Benefits Wane for Immigrants
The federal government required states to notify immigrants who will soon lose coverage, but immigrant rights advocates say some states did not begin sending letters until September. That’s given enrollees little time to react, including to respond if the state was mistakenly ending their coverage.
Cutting off Medicaid coverage is just the first move to drop government health benefits provided to many lawfully present immigrants. Under a change starting in January, the CBO estimates, about 1 million will lose eligibility for government subsidies to buy individual health coverage on Affordable Care Act marketplaces by 2034. And they will also lose access to Medicare, a change expected to affect about 100,000 immigrants, the agency forecasts.
Trump has argued that taxpayer-funded programs should be reserved for American citizens. As Congress debated the legislation in May 2025, the White House put out a news release with the misleading claim that the One Big Beautiful Bill Act would remove Medicaid coverage for people who are in the country without authorization.
Under long-standing law, people who are in the country without authorization do not qualify for the general Medicaid program that is funded by state and federal dollars.
The health coverage cuts are part of a broader Trump strategy to send a message

981a701313e9.text: By — Jesse Bedayn, Associated Press Jesse Bedayn, Associated Press By — Bill Barrow, Associated Press Bill Barrow, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/politics/watch-live-vance-addresses-gop-midterm-election-rally-in-texas Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter WATCH LIVE: Vance addresses GOP midterm election rally in Texas Politics Sep 30, 2026 1:23 PM EDT HARLINGEN, Texas (AP) — Eric Flores, a former federal prosecutor and Army National Guard infantry captain, was one of the Republican Party's prized recruits in this year's midterm elections. With help from a redrawn congressional map in Texas, he seemed primed to dislodge longtime Democratic Rep. Vicente Gonzalez in a region that swung toward Donald Trump in the last presidential election. Vice President JD Vance is expected to speak at a rally Wednesday. Watch live in our video player above. Now he's one of several candidates locked in a tougher race than originally envisioned as Republican-run states heeded Trump's call to begin an unusual round of redistricting to help retain control of the U.S. House. WATCH: Affordability and accountability top priorities if Democrats take House, Jeffries says Republicans hoped to pick up as many as nine seats between Texas and Florida. However, even though the districts were redrawn to make them easier to win, the party remains weighed down by dissatisfaction with Trump, the economy, the war with Iran and the president's deportation agenda. Educate your inbox Subscribe to Here’s the Deal, our politics newsletter for analysis you won’t find anywhere else. Enter your email address Subscribe Form error message goes here. Thank you. Please check your inbox to confirm. The political landscape remains competitive enough that Vice President JD Vance is traveling to Texas on Wednesday, where he'll appear with Flores, and then visit Florida on Thursday. House Democrats' national campaign chair, Rep. Suzan DelBene, recently circulated through Florida districts that Republicans were hoping to claim for themselves. Vance joined Texas Gov. Abbott at a manufacturing facility groundbreaking ceremony earlier Wednesday. "Republicans arrogantly thought they were going to redistrict seats to pick up more," DelBene said in an interview during her trip. "Instead, what they have is people across the state souring on the Republican agenda." Mike Marinella, House Republicans' campaign spokesman, said the party can still capitalize this year "with a more favorable map, historic fundraising and spending advantages, stronger candidates and a common-sense agenda." House seats are up for grabs in Texas Republicans won 25 of Texas' 38 seats in the U.S. House as Trump returned to power two years ago. Partially using that election as a baseline, the redrawn map was intended to help Republicans win up to 30 seats. Key to this plan was the Rio Grande Valley, a heavily Latino region on the southern tip of Texas, which had shifted toward Trump. Texas' 34th Congressional District, where Flores is running, includes some of the valley, and it opted for Trump by 10 points over Democrat Kamala Harris. But Flores said he expected his race to be close, which he credits to his opponent's five terms in office. Flores received Trump's endorsement, still pinned to his X account, and spoke at his unusual midterm convention in Dallas. But he also removed from his website a promise to "SUPPORT PRESIDENT TRUMP'S AGENDA" as he looked toward general election voters and widening his base of support. "If I tell them the red meat issues or I tell them, you know, oh, Republican, Democrat, or anything like that, you lose them," he told The Associated Press. "I just sell them myself, sell them what I stand for." Republicans in Washington acknowledge that inflation, Trump's tariffs and the war in Iran have made their path harder. Latino voters' discontent with Trump's immigration agenda further scrambles their efforts. Republicans are also facing the potential loss of an incumbent who represents a redrawn district. Rep. Monica De La Cruz, who is running for a third term, faces a strong challenge from musician Bobby Pulido. A Latin Grammy winner whose top song on Spotify has 619 million streams, Pulido doesn't face the usual first-time candidates' challenge of establishing name ID. "I want a picture!" Eloise Ibarra, 42, exclaimed as Pulido walked through the crowd at a high school football game. Ibarra later said she'd "probably" vote for Pulido after sitting out the last presidential race. "I don't really like his policies," she said about Trump. "It's very expensive, I go to the grocery store and buy $50 worth of stuff and it's like five items." Democrats argue that Republicans miscalculated this year. "I think Republicans counted on Hispanics, and they counted on rural Texas, to deliver votes for them, and these are the two places that are hurting the most," said Terri Burke of the Texas Democratic Party. Speaking of redistricting, she said, "this is really no longer such a slam dunk for the Republicans anywhere." Democrats see opportunity in Florida Republicans already had 20 out of 28 seats in Florida, and they wanted to boost that to 24 with their new congressional map. But much like in Texas, their plan was based on 2024 results, when voters, including many Latinos, were dissatisfied with Democratic President Joe Biden on the economy and immigration. Republicans targeted Rep. Kathy Castor in metro Tampa and Rep. Darren Soto in the Orlando area, while putting south Florida Reps. Jared Moskowitz and Debbie Wasserman Schultz into the same district. Moskowitz shifted to a nearby Republican-leaning district, and Wasserman Schultz ran for another term in a separate, heavily Democratic district. Castor and Soto face longer odds in their redrawn districts, though DelBene believes they have a shot in the current environment. READ MORE: GOP hopes fade in Georgia and North Carolina as party

Six people traffickers have been found guilty in France of causing the deaths of 31 migrants in the worst ever small-boat accident in the Channel.
At the end of a four-week trial in Paris, the six were convicted of "involuntary homicide" and given prison terms of between six and 10 years.
Seven others were given lesser sentences of up to four years, and one person was found not guilty.
The boat went down early in the morning on 24 November 2021 after sending distress calls to French and British coastguards. The dead, including a child of seven, were mainly Iraqi Kurds but also included Afghans, Egyptians and Iranian Kurds. Only two men survived.
The charge sheet said the migrants had been put to sea from the French coast in a boat "that was of poor quality, uncertified, unsuitable for navigation at sea, overloaded, and without correct life jackets".
The trial established that the guilty men were members of two separate networks â one of which was Iraqi Kurd, the other Afghan â that co-operated to organise the cross-channel journey and bring migrants to the meeting point.
Unusually the court was attended at the start by several family members, who came to France from Iraqi Kurdistan and gave moving testimony about how the victims came to be on board the boat.
Speaking after the verdict, their lawyer Matthieu Chirez said the decision "comes as a relief for all the civil plaintiffs because it confirms the penal responsibility of the traffickers". He said the trial had "humanised the families of victims".
One family member, Zana Marmand Muhammed, told the court how his younger brother Twana had "wanted to go to England to find a job and because the geopolitical situation with us is dangerous. No-one in the family wanted him to leave, but we could not dissuade him."
Nabi Mustafa Mina, the father of Zanyar who was 19 when he died, told of how he tried to dissuade his son from leaving.
"I said I would help him to get married, I would give him my house, I would divide my salary in two. But no, he said he wanted a better life, that he would get by somehow. I ran out of arguments," he said.
The family-members explained how they had paid a deposit at a bank in Iraqi Kurdistan and then followed their loved ones' progress through Turkey, Italy and then France. In one of the last messages from Twana, he posted a picture of himself at the Eiffel Tower.
The court also heard a statement from one of the two survivors, Issa Omar, read out by his lawyer. Omar said that he "would have liked to appear before the judge but I do not have the strength. Since the wreck I have the impression that part of me disappeared beneath the waves."
His lawyer Matthieu Chirez said that Omar had "clung to floating bodies, to a life-jacket. He survived by keeping his eyes open so as not to go to sleep, and swimming to keep his heart beating".
Police investigating the disaster used phone tracking to identify members of the two networks.
The lesser figures were accused of sheltering migrants, transporting them across France to the so-called "jungle" camp outside Calais, and helping on the night of the departure.
The alleged leader of the Iraqi Kurd network â named as Bashdar â was not a defendant in the trial. He is in custody in Iraq. His close aide â Harem Ahmed Abawaker â was given eight years in prison.
The biggest sentence, of 10 years, went to Obaidullah Maroofkhel, who ran the Afghan network. He was tried in his absence along with one other defendant.
Most of the 14 were Afghans or Iraqi Kurds. All but one of the defendants appeared in the trial as free men, so following the verdict the court issued six arrest warrants.
A separate police investigation is under way into seven members of the French armed forces for allegedly failing to come to the help of the migrants on the night of the disaster.
The seven were at the regional sea rescue centre or on board a navy ship, and are alleged to have ignored distress calls from the boat. A decision on whether to recommend them for trial will be taken in the coming months.
The trial ended as France and the UK announced it was ending the so-called one-in one-out scheme under which the British government sent back irregular cross-Channel migrants to France, and in return accepted individuals with a likely prospect of being granted asylum.
France had already signalled that the year-long programme, which has seen a little more than 1,000 migrants switch country, was not producing expected results in breaking the traffickers' business model.

Users have already found hidden features in the White Houseâs new America.gov AI chatbot.
The bot, which was launched Tuesday with the goal of helping citizens navigate the governmentâs online bureaucracy, seems to come to life when users ask it to âplay Minecraft,â the 3D sandbox video game. The bot starts to answer users with language that mimics messages Minecraft players see on their screens when they beat the game: âIt thinks we are a chatbot.â And, âIt is reading our thoughts as though they were words on a .gov.â
The question, now, is whether the answer is an intentional Easter egg for video game players, and if so, whether it belongs on the same interface guiding Americans through Medicare enrollment.

99195489cb0b.text:
Davidâs view
As they prepared for Republicans to drop another billion dollars of ads on their heads this summer, Democrats passed around fresh advice on gender politics.
A memo from the Transgender Freedom Alliance, based on focus groups and polling in battleground states, warned that Democrats lost ground if they ignored anti-trans attacks â ubiquitous GOP ads about âboys in girlsâ sportsâ and âchild sex changes.â The group advised Democrats to respond, then accuse Republicans of being âfocused on transgender people instead of helping you.â
Right now, as they compete for states that Trump won by double digits, Democrats are feeling great about that guidance. Former Ohio Sen. Sherrod Brown used it nearly word-for-word for one of his ads: âââWith everything going on, thatâs what theyâre talking about?â New ads from a Democratic super PAC chide Republicans for running hundreds of millions of dollars in ads âjust about trans people.â
The theory is simple. In 2024, when the Trump campaign warned that Kamala Harris was for âthey/them,â the subtext was that Democrats were focused on identity politics instead of economic needs. In 2026, voters canât blame the out-of-power party for the cost of groceries; itâs MAGA Republicans who are obsessed with âthey/them,â not âyou.â
Iâve seen some analysis of the Democratsâ enough-already messaging that calls it a ânewâ strategy. Itâs not totally new; Brown lost his 2024 race after running ads about how he opposed letting âtransgender biological menâ play womenâs sports, which was already âbanned in Ohio.â
Whatâs new is that conservatives won, and their opponents retreated. The Trump administration has rolled back every significant executive-branch advance for transgender Americans â in healthcare, in schools, even at historic sites. In red states, the limits that Republicans passed during Bidenâs presidency are in no danger of being overturned.
Pro-LGBTQ rights groups, now aware of how much they lose when Democrats donât run things, arenât saying much about the new Democratic approach.
Iowaâs Rob Sand, who became the partyâs nominee for governor with no primary challenge, wrote the first page of that new book. Last summer, he told a conservative radio host that state policy on womenâs sports was âsettled law.â In Ohio, Democratic gubernatorial nominee Amy Acton went the same way.
Neither candidate rolled out their position with a PR campaign. They were asked, they answered, and they weathered criticism from LGBT groups. The impact was less than Republicans had hoped. Equality Ohio, the stateâs flagship LGBT rights group, announced that Acton had lost her âAâ rating and it would have to revisit its candidate report card.
With less fanfare, after Action held closed-press meetings with frustrated activists, it published the new report card. Acton had been downgraded to a âB,â while GOP nominee Vivek Ramaswamyâs âFâ rating stood. The nominee isnât going to be flying that B up a flagpole, but itâs a minor hit to take in order to neutralize one of the GOPâs most frequent attacks.
Those attacks are missing something else: Fresh outrage to draw on. In his 2024 campaign, the most frequently named target of Trumpâs riffs on the issue was Lia Thomas, the transgender University of Pennsylvania swimmer who won a 2022 womenâs freestyle event.
Thomas wouldnât be allowed to compete in that race if it happened this year, because the NCAA responded to the Trump administrationâs gender orders by barring anyone âassigned male at birthâ from womenâs sports.
Thatâs not what Democrats wanted in 2024. But itâs what they have now, and thereâs been a lot of thinking about how to stem their losses. Mara Keisling, the transgender rights activist whose interview with Harris was churned into the âthey/themâ ad, wrote in March that the movement âshould concentrate on issues we can win and temporarily defocus on issues we cannot.â Namely, sports.
In The Hard Path to Unity, Barney Frankâs posthumous book about resuscitating the left, he had the same parting advice. âAdvocates of allowing people who transitioned from male to female to compete in womenâs sports should continue to argue their case, but refrain from making it a litmus test,â he wrote.
Room for Disagreement
Republicans arenât cutting back any of their transgender-focused ads, despite the conventional wisdom that theyâre not working as well this year. In a memo last week, the conservative American Principles Project warned that the ads âmay not be sufficientâ if not hitched to a credible economic message.
âIf the candidate has a record thatâs problematic on trans, itâs still a good hit,â APP president Terry Schilling told Semafor. âIf Iâm a Republican running for office right now, Iâm saying: âHey, I had Trumpâs back. We kept our promises on protecting your kids and protecting rights as parents when it comes to the trans industry.â Look at all that weâve done!â
And the attack ads arenât stopping; Brownâs Ohio ads got a response from Republicans, returning to their 2024 theme that by voting against GOP gender legislation, he offered his real position.
Notable
- In The Washington Sun, Alex Roarty and Oriana Gonzales talked to strategists in both parties about why the ad barrage was not getting the same results now that it got in 2024.
- In The Nation, Gillian Branstetter wondered whether the 2024 results were a âfluke,â noting that ads on the same themes flopped in Virginia last year, as now-Gov. Abigail Spanberger said that the state should not be writing rules for something parents and athletic organizations could handle.
- On the Human Rights Campaignâs Substack, Kelly Robinson assessed Brown and other Democrats trying to defuse the GOP attacks with concessions. âWhen thereâs a misstep, our first step is a call. We provide information and advice. More often than not, campaigns express remorse and solidarity and work to clean it up.â

21ea63359157.text:
Reedâs view
While OpenAIâs new tool, dots, stole much of the spotlight at its annual developer day Tuesday, it was the change to its pricing tiers that says more about the company and the AI industry. OpenAIâs $200-per-month plan now comes with half the tokens. And thereâs now an eye-popping $500-per-month plan that makes the price of diesel these days seem like nothing.
The cost creep is another indication there is a severe compute bottleneck in AI. Offering always-on, agentic assistant tools will cost OpenAI and Meta â which recently launched its cutesy agent Muse â a ton of money, and itâs not clear yet that these agents will work well. AI products often overpromise because there just arenât enough tokens to go around (and it would be too expensive) to make them capable at their maximum potential.
I havenât yet worked with dots, but people are so far finding Metaâs Muse runs into paywalls and CAPTCHA hurdles they have to troubleshoot. Meanwhile, my Codex is humming away doing cool and useful things for me, and itâs not clear that my dot will be able to replace some of the projects Iâve already put time into building. Dots will likely wind up like a lot of new AI tools and features: completely amazing and, simultaneously, not quite there yet.
It costs OpenAI fortunes to do its more ambitious tasks, too. It recently spent about $10 million over roughly a weekend to solve part of the Navier-Stokes math equations. If AI was getting to the point where itâs so efficient it can take out humanity by Christmas, as so many fear, the price of tokens would be going down, not up, and it would cost a lot less to solve math problems.

c97bcb60bb54.text: A criminal investigation into allegations that a Cornell University student was gang raped by seven fraternity members in 2024 is fueling a new push by House Democratic women to strengthen federal protections against sexual violence on college campuses. Why it matters: The Democratic Women's Caucus is calling on congressional Republicans and the Trump administration to strengthen Title IX protections, arguing that the administration's changes to the civil rights law could leave students more vulnerable. The push comes just two days after the Trump administration rescinded Biden-era sex discrimination Title IX regulations and reinstated rules adopted during President Trump's first term. The Democratic Women's Caucus argues those changes have "eroded the processes in place for sexual misconduct investigations." Driving the news: "Her story should be a wake-up call Republicans cannot ignore: we need stronger protections and systems for survivors, and we need to act now," Democratic Women's Caucus Chair Teresa Leger Fernández (D-N.M.) and Vice Chairs Emilia Sykes (D-Ohio) and Hillary Scholten (D-Mich.) said in a statement first shared with Axios. The lawmakers argue the Cornell case underscores the need for stronger federal protections and more aggressive enforcement of Title IX, the landmark law barring sex discrimination at federally funded schools that also governs how schools respond to sexual harassment and assault allegations. They called on the administration and Republicans to "condemn what took place at Cornell, stand in solidarity with Jane Doe, and work with us to better protect survivors and ensure they can seek justice." Catch up quick: A former Cornell University student, referred to as "Jane Doe" in legal documents, is suing the school, seven Chi Phi fraternity members and others over allegations that she was drugged and raped at a fraternity house in October of 2024. Cornell conducted a Title IX investigation after "Jane Doe" reported the incident in 2024 that resulted in two of the students being expelled and lesser disciplinary action for the other students. The DA has said criminal charges were not pursued because Jane Doe's initial police statement did not allege that she was gang-raped or drugged against her will. A criminal investigation was reopened after the lawsuit was filed earlier this month, and the New York attorney general has launched a separate review of the university's handling of the allegations. No criminal charges have been filed. The lack of criminal charges and the university's handling of the alleged incident have has sparked intense scrutiny over how colleges respond to sexual assault. Cornell said in a statement last week that the university "investigated and adjudicated the allegations consistent with university policies," and said in a statement this week that the university supports the DA's decision to reopen the criminal case. Cornell did not respond to a request for comment from Axios. Zoom out: The latest Title IX fight in Washington has largely centered on sexual orientation and gender identity , but also impacts how colleges handle sexual misconduct allegations. The Biden administration broadened the definition of sex-based harassment covered by Title IX and gave colleges more flexibility in investigating sexual misconduct. Trump returned to his first-term rules, which narrow the definition of sexual harassment, require more formal proceedings for handling misconduct allegations, and give schools more flexibility in deciding how much evidence is needed to discipline a student. Democrats argue those requirements create additional hurdles for survivors seeking protection under Title IX. What we're watching: Whether the Cornell allegations generate bipartisan interest in strengthening federal campus sexual assault protections.

94a1f5362921.text: By — Christopher Rugaber, Associated Press Christopher Rugaber, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/politics/no-criminal-wrongdoing-in-federal-reserve-building-renovation-watchdog-says-but-it-was-mismanaged Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter No criminal wrongdoing in Federal Reserve building renovation, watchdog says, but it was mismanaged Politics Sep 30, 2026 2:25 PM EDT WASHINGTON (AP) — The Federal Reserve's internal watchdog said Wednesday that the agency has broadly mismanaged an expansive building renovation project but did not find any criminal violations, as alleged by Trump administration prosecutors. The Fed's inspector general said that a variety of missteps by its Board of Governors inflated the cost of the $2.4 billion renovation. The board did not secure a comprehensive cost estimate at the beginning of the project, nor did it nail down a maximum overall cost, a step that could have forced the building contractor to absorb the impact of inflation, the IG said in a 120-page report. Prices spiked after construction began in 2022. READ MORE: Federal Reserve rate hike reflects new world of sticky inflation and faster growth "Our review found that the Board has not effectively managed and executed its ... contract and repeatedly deviated from its cost-management provisions," the report said. Former Chair Jerome Powell requested that the IG review the renovation project last year. Educate your inbox Subscribe to Here’s the Deal, our politics newsletter for analysis you won’t find anywhere else. Enter your email address Subscribe Form error message goes here. Thank you. Please check your inbox to confirm. The building renovation project became a high-profile flashpoint in the Trump administration's attempts to pressure the Fed into cutting its key interest rate. President Donald Trump even visited the construction site last July, when Powell corrected Trump's estimate of the project's expected costs as the two stood before TV cameras in hard hats. Trump's Justice Department then launched an investigation into whether Powell had committed perjury during brief testimony on the building renovation before a Senate committee. That investigation was dropped in April after a judge quashed subpoenas issued by Jeanine Pirro, the U.S. Attorney for the District of Columbia. Pirro said then she would await the outcome of the inspector general's investigation before deciding whether to take any further action. READ MORE: Trump appointees pushed more marble in Federal Reserve building renovation White House now attacks "At no point during our evaluation did we find reasonable grounds to believe that a violation of federal criminal law had occurred requiring a referral to the U.S. Attorney General," the IG's report said. The report said that the construction costs to renovate two Fed buildings more than doubled from an original estimate of $921 million in February 2020 to $2.018 billion by December 2024. Construction is expected to last until December 2027, long past its originally slated completion date of mid-2024. Some aspects of the project that were criticized by the Trump administration and Republican members of Congress for being luxurious — water fountains, private elevators and marble facades — were not significant drivers of the excessive costs of the project. Instead, the IG said that a design change by the Fed in 2023 from a mostly open workspace to one with mostly closed office space caused a significant delay in the project's design. It also delayed the Fed from seeking a maximum cost ceiling for the project at that time. A free press is a cornerstone of a healthy democracy. Support trusted journalism and civil dialogue. 0e71478fb831.text: A Federal Reserve watchdog found no criminal wrongdoing by former chair Jerome Powell in its investigation of the central bank's expensive headquarters renovation, according to a report released on Wednesday. Why it matters: The findings effectively clear Powell after the Justice Department opened an unprecedented criminal investigation into then-Fed chair, which became public in January. What they're saying: "At no point during our evaluation did we find reasonable grounds to believe that a violation of federal criminal law had occurred requiring a referral to the U.S. Attorney General," the Office of Inspector General wrote in the report. The watchdog added that it "did not identify administrative misconduct during our evaluation." Yes, but: While the report clears Powell, it faults Fed management and oversight of the project as construction costs more than doubled to $2.5 billion . The Fed "did not take numerous actions available to it that could have better controlled costs and mitigated some of the significant construction cost increases," the report says. Flashback : The renovation became a flashpoint in President Trump's broader campaign against Powell and the Fed. Trump toured the construction site with Powell in July 2025 and publicly challenged him over the project's soaring costs. Zoom out: The Justice Department's investigation centered on Powell's June 2025 testimony to Congress about the renovation and its rising costs. Powell denied wrongdoing and argued at the time that the investigation was part of a broader effort to pressure the Fed over interest rates. DOJ closed the investigation in April as the Fed's inspector general continued its review. Zoom in: The watchdog said that inflation alone could not explain the project's higher costs. For instance, the report shows that two major mechanical, electrical and plumbing contracts more than tripled to $539 million from an earlier $178 million estimate, far outpacing the broader rise in construction costs. Of note : The report says that the key design features that drew scrutiny from Congress and other critics — including marble, water features and a garden terrace — did not materially contribute to the project's cost increases. The Fed removed four planned new fountains in June 2025 because officials worried about "external stakeholders, such as Congress and the media, raising concerns about the design," according to the report. What to watch: Powell has remained on the Fed's board after his term as chair ended in May — an unusual move that he said was tied to seeing the investigation through to its conclusion. Editor's note: This story has been updated with additional details.

37b95b0f43bd.text: By — Kim Chandler, Associated Press Kim Chandler, Associated Press By — Kristin M. Hall, Associated Press Kristin M. Hall, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/nation/court-halts-execution-of-christa-gail-pike-for-a-tennessee-murder-she-committed-at-age-18 Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Court halts execution of Christa Gail Pike for a Tennessee murder she committed at age 18 Nation Sep 30, 2026 2:01 PM EDT NASHVILLE, Tenn. (AP) — Tennessee's execution of Christa Gail Pike for a murder she committed at age 18 was halted Wednesday about an hour before it was set to begin, as a federal appeals court sought to review whether her allegations of childhood sexual abuse and rape were fully considered at her sentencing. Pike, now 50, and her boyfriend were convicted of the 1995 stabbing and beating of 19-year-old Colleen Slemmer, their classmate at a job training facility in Knoxville. She would have been the first woman executed in Tennessee in at least 200 years. READ MORE: Florida to carry out 13th execution this year in nation's busiest death chamber The 6th Circuit U.S. Court of Appeals halted the execution on a 2-1 vote after execution witnesses and others gathered at the Riverbend Maximum Security Institution in Nashville. Tennessee's attorney general immediately appealed the stay to the U.S. Supreme Court. Witnesses and media remained at the prison in case the high court allows the execution to proceed. Media witnesses were brought into the prison about 10:15 a.m. to wait, but then were let back out into a parking lot after about 90 minutes. More than 30 people, some wearing shirts that said "Love Heals," gathered in a fenced-in area outside the prison while police on horses watched nearby. The case garnered widespread attention at the time of the killing in part because a pentagram that was carved on Slemmer's body and other elements of the crime stoked fears of Satan worship during the "satanic panic" of the 1980s and 1990s. Pike's case renewed debate on the death penalty for teens As the execution date drew near, it renewed debate over the death penalty for young offenders. Pike does not deny committing the killing, but her supporters argue the state should consider Pike's age at the time, mental illness and a history of severe sexual abuse that included being raped from the time she was a toddler. Assistant Federal Defender Stephen Ferrell said Pike's death sentence is an outlier because other 18-year-olds in Tennessee have had such sentences vacated. After the killing, Pike was diagnosed with bipolar disorder and post-traumatic stress disorder. In her clemency petition she said she only wanted to fight Slemmer but killed her in a frenzied attack when she couldn't "put the brakes on." "I was a mentally ill 18-year-old kid. It took me numerous years to even realize the gravity of what I'd done. Even more to accept how many lives I affected. I took the life of someone's child, sister, friend. It sickens me now to think I had the ability to commit such a crime," Pike said in a statement. Victim's mother says she is waiting for death sentence Slemmer's mother wants the lethal injection to go forward, saying she has waited decades to see Pike's sentence carried out. "Every time I think about it, I think about Colleen feeling that pain and trying to get up and run," May Martinez told The Associated Press in a telephone interview on Saturday. Martinez said a group helped raise money so she and her husband could travel from Florida to witness the execution. She didn't respond to a message Wednesday after the execution was halted. Martinez said her daughter's age should matter too in deciding Pike's fate. "Not a day goes by, or a minute goes by that I do not think about Colleen. Holidays are the worst," she said, noting that her daughter would have turned 51 earlier in September. The killing rocked the city of Knoxville. Prosecutors said Pike, fearing Slemmer was trying to steal her boyfriend, lured her to a wooded area on Jan. 12, 1995. Pike cut Slemmer with a box cutter and beat her with a large chunk of asphalt. Shipp, Pike's boyfriend, has admitted that he was the one who carved a pentagram, a star-shaped symbol associated with Satan, into her body. Shipp was 17 when the crime happened and received a sentence of life in prison with the possibility of parole. Pike was the only one sentenced to death. Executions of women are rare in the U.S. Tennessee has not executed a woman for at least 200 years, according to Robin M. Maher, executive director of the Death Penalty Information Center. Older records can be spotty, though, so it's difficult to know precise details about the last woman who was put to death there. It's a rarity across the U.S. Since 1976, 18 women have been put to death in the country, representing about 1% of all executions, according to the center. Most recently, Missouri in 2023 executed Amber McLaughlin for a 2003 killing, in what is believed to be the first execution of a transgender woman in the U.S. In 2021, the federal government executed Lisa Montgomery, marking the first time in nearly seven decades that the U.S. government put a female inmate to death. Pike would be the 30th person executed in the U.S. this year. Florida carried out its 16th execution of 2026 on Tuesday. Associated Press journalists Jeffrey Collins in Columbia, South Carolina, and Ed White in Detroit contributed to this report. A free press is a cornerstone of a healthy democracy. 61b47fb7fcf6.text: The Massachusetts attorney general released a report Wednesday documenting more than 270 Catholic clerics accused of sexually abusing 944 children across three dioceses — but the investigation will result in no new indictments. Why it matters: The dioceses created an illusion of safety while church leaders repeatedly exploited loopholes to protect the institution's reputation, systematically concealing staggering levels of abuse. What they're saying: "We deeply understand that behind every number is a child whose safety was violated, a family that was changed, and a survivor who has carried the trauma of that abuse for years, and in many cases, decades," Attorney General Andrea Joy Campbell (D) wrote in the report . Catch up quick: The Massachusetts AG's office began its investigation in 2019, examining church responses to abuse allegations over more than six decades. Boston Globe reporters exposed widespread abuse and institutional cover-ups in the Archdiocese of Boston in the early 2000s. Wednesday's report sought to provide the first comparable public accounting of what happened in the Roman Catholic dioceses of Fall River, Springfield and Worcester. Investigators reviewed more than 300,000 pages of documents and interviewed more than 100 people, including survivors, attorneys and clergy. Worth noting: After reporters uncovered the abuse, Massachusetts lawmakers criminalized the reckless endangerment of children and expanded mandated reporter requirements to include clergy. But those laws can't be applied retroactively to crimes that occurred before they took effect. Most of the abuse detailed in the report occurred before 2002, and the AG says newly found misconduct fell outside applicable statutes of limitations. Many accused clergy are also dead, leaving survivors with few options for legal recourse. Zoom in: The report concluded that diocesan leaders actively covered up abuse allegations before 2002 by transferring accused clergy to new congregations without warning parishioners. Leaders also sent accused priests to psychiatric treatment facilities before allowing some to return to ministry. Some of these priests were then accused of reoffending. Between the lines: Survivors described church processes that left some feeling pressured to testify to internal church investigators or stay silent and say the dioceses used NDAs to stop survivors from discussing abuse allegations. One survivor recalled a staff member saying, "[t]he best way for this to go away is not to talk about it." The survivor said the church's internal investigator "was as curious to get my story as she was to protect his." Another said an internal review board resembled "a tribunal," adding: "The Church is like your mother: when they call, you answer." Survivor Phil Saviano told the Globe that he had came forward and refused to sign an NDA because he was "dying of AIDS … at that point my career was over, I was on my way out physically, my reputation was shot in the eyes of many people, and I didn't have a lot to lose." Zoom out: The institutional secrecy that enabled decades of abuse has not been fully addressed: 12 dioceses across the United States still have not published lists of credibly accused clergy. That represents less than 5% of all dioceses and orders. In Massachusetts, Worcester is the only diocese that still has not published a list. The Vatican did not respond to Axios' request for comment. The report says the lists can encourage survivors to come forward, reveal the scope of the abuse and promote transparency and accountability. A spokesperson for the Worcester Diocese didn't address Axios' question on why they haven't published a list of accused clergy, but said that they "welcome the AG's report." "Our procedures over the past three decades, including the way we screen candidates for ordination, as well as the awareness and safety training which was implemented in all our parishes and ministries, have made an enormous difference," they said. "The diocese has passed each year's independent compliance audit" since a new Charter was adopted in 2002. The charter now "serve[s] as a model for other institutions, public or private, who care for children and minors." The bottom line: The investigation provides a historical reckoning for nearly 1,000 survivors, but decades of concealment left hundreds with validation and little legal recourse. Go deeper: Vatican criminalizes sexual abuse of adults by priests

c68ddf09b865.text: By — Jaimie Ding, Associated Press Jaimie Ding, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/nation/gentle-giant-backpack-declared-winner-of-alaskas-fat-bear-week Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Gentle giant Backpack declared winner of Alaska's Fat Bear Week Nation Sep 30, 2026 1:39 PM EDT After a week of fierce competition, Backpack emerged victorious as Fat Bear Week champion, the heftiest bear of Alaska's Katmai National Park and Preserve. The nonprofit running the longstanding contest announced that the bear, known for his pacifist nature, was the winner Tuesday with more than 100,000 votes, giving him a close win over Bear 910 with just over 50% of the poll. READ MORE: Bear 910 vs. Backpack: It's the final showdown for Alaska's Fat Bear Week The contest, which is in its 12th year, celebrates the resilience of the 2,200 brown bears that live in the preserve on the Alaska Peninsula, which extends from the state's southwest corner toward the Aleutian Islands. Fat Bear Week was started in 2014 as an interactive way to inform the public about brown bears, the coastal cousins of grizzlies. Educate your inbox Subscribe to Here’s the Deal, our politics newsletter for analysis you won’t find anywhere else. Enter your email address Subscribe Form error message goes here. Thank you. Please check your inbox to confirm. Last year's winner, Chunk — known officially as Bear 32 — clinched his victory at an estimated 1,200 pounds. He was handily defeated in the first round of competition this year by Bucky, who went on to lose a faceoff against Backpack, known officially as Bear 89. The event this year featured 16 bears vying for the heavyweight title in a single-elimination, bracket-style tournament. All voting is done online at www.fatbearweek.org, and the winner was declared Tuesday evening after the final poll closed. The public could watch the bears on explore.org's livestream cameras before deciding on their favorite. "Fat bears are successful bears," the nonprofit says on its website. This group gorges itself on the abundant salmon that return to the Brooks River starting in late June. It's there that they can stuff themselves to accumulate the fat reserves they will need to survive the winter. To be featured in the contest, the bears must frequent the area around the river. Backpack is the son of former Fat Bear Week champion Holly, who introduced him to the Brooks River when he was a first-year cub in 2006. His name was inspired by his habit of climbing onto his mother's back when they swam the river. This year's fans cheered on Backpack in the contest's Instagram comments, noting his lineage and reputation as a gentle giant. "Unlike many large adult male bears, Backpack hasn't shown much aggression toward his competitors," his contestant profile reads. Backpack uses his "quiet strength" rather than brawling and is often seen in wildlife cameras sitting on a rock downstream, appearing to take in the scenery around him. He defeated Bear 910, who is also the daughter of a former champion: 409 Beadnose. Adult male brown bears typically weigh 600 to 900 pounds (about 270 to 410 kilograms) in midsummer. By the time they are ready to hibernate after feasting on migrating and spawning salmon, large males can weigh well over 1,000 pounds (454 kilograms). Females are about one-third smaller. The bears may each eat as many as 30 fish a day this time of year, working hard to eat a year's worth of food in about six months. During winter hibernation, the bears do not eat or drink and can lose one-third of their body weight. Fat Bear Week's contestants also included five bear families, in recognition of the record high number of families and cubs at the river this summer. A mother must feed and protect her cubs while also eating enough calories to sustain herself through hibernation. Cubs often face the risk of attack by other bears due to territorialism or food scarcity. Bear 132 and her three spring cubs advanced to the semifinals, but lost out to Bear 910. Bear 132 has become one of the largest and most experienced mother bears at Brooks River, according to her contestant profile. In mid-July, one of her cubs became separated from the family for several days, wandering the river corridor alone. They were reunited a few days later. ___ Associated Press writer Jamie Stengle contributed from Dallas. A free press is a cornerstone of a healthy democracy. - Published
The UK government has announced the "one in, one out" agreement with France to send back some migrants who cross the Channel has been scrapped.
The pilot scheme allowed the UK to return some small boat arrivals while agreeing to take in the same number of people from France who were believed to have a legitimate claim to come to Britain.
Only around 1,500 people have been removed to France since the scheme began just over a year ago.
The BBC understands the government would have liked the scheme to continue, but felt it did not reach the desired scale.
A Home Office spokesperson said "lessons learned" would be used to "accelerate efforts" to return small boat migrants with no right to remain.
"The government's pilot with France to remove asylum seekers in exchange for an equal number of legal migrants is no longer processing new cases," the spokesperson said.
"However, flights will continue over the coming weeks to swiftly remove small boat migrants from the UK, and we will use lessons learned from the pilot to accelerate efforts to return small boat migrants with no right to remain in the UK."
The government would continue working with France to tackle small boat crossings, the spokesperson said, adding that "real progress" had been made with numbers "significantly down on last year".
The French Interior Ministry told the BBC: "We are discussing with the British the terms of exit from the agreement."
Earlier this month, Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood admitted the scheme had "not been without its challenges".
"The numbers are still relatively small," she told MPs.
"What has been more operationally difficult is to scale up very large numbers of removals every week into the French system."
However, she also said the UN and other agencies had reported that some migrants were not getting on small boats because they thought there was a chance they could be accepted under the "one in, one out" scheme.
So far this year, 19,135 people have made the Channel crossing, which is 42% lower than the same period in 2025 when 32,188 crossed in small boats.

Passengers describe stabbing on Israel-bound plane
A pilot on an Israel-bound Flydubai flight stabbed another pilot and "apparently tried to crash the plane", Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has said.
The plane was travelling from Dubai to Tel Aviv when it plummeted 17,000ft (5,200m) in less than two minutes, before being diverted to Saudi Arabia.
Eyewitnesses inside the plane described the moment the incident happened, with one man calling for help in a video shared on social media.

95d132579aee.text: By — Fatima Hussein, Associated Press Fatima Hussein, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/politics/watch-senate-health-committee-advances-dr-nicole-saphiers-nomination-for-surgeon-general Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter WATCH: Senate health committee advances Dr. Nicole Saphier's nomination for surgeon general Politics Sep 30, 2026 3:04 PM EDT WASHINGTON (AP) — Dr. Nicole Saphier, President Donald Trump's third nominee for surgeon general, moved a step closer to confirmation after a Senate committee voted to advance her nomination on Wednesday. Watch the committee meeting in the video player above. Saphier, a radiologist and former Fox News Channel contributor, was advanced out of the Senate Committee on Health, Education, Labor and Pensions on a 12 to 11 vote to serve as surgeon general after she was grilled at her confirmation hearing earlier this month about her stance on childhood vaccines. WATCH: Dr. Nicole Saphier testifies in confirmation hearing for U.S. surgeon general She expressed support for vaccines and told lawmakers she didn't believe they cause autism. The Trump administration has sought to revisit claims about a link between vaccines and autism, although widespread scientific consensus and decades of studies have firmly concluded there is none. Educate your inbox Subscribe to Here’s the Deal, our politics newsletter for analysis you won’t find anywhere else. Enter your email address Subscribe Form error message goes here. Thank you. Please check your inbox to confirm. Timothy Westlake, who was nominated to serve as assistant secretary for mental health and substance use at the Department of Health and Human Services was also advanced out of committee on the same en bloc vote. It was not immediately clear when the officials would face a full Senate vote for their confirmation but they are expected to be approved. During her confirmation hearing, Republican Sen. Bill Cassidy pressed Saphier to declare whether she believed there was a link between vaccines and autism. Saphier responded that she does "not believe childhood vaccines cause autism," adding that "the MMR vaccine is our greatest tool for combating measles," in response to a question by Cassidy over whether parents should give children that shot. MMR stands for measles, mumps and rubella, and the president recently called for the shots to be spaced out, against the guidance of medical groups. The surgeon general position carries limited policymaking power but serves as a loud megaphone as the nation's top communicator to Americans on public health issues. Cassidy, who led the inquiry into Saphier's views on vaccines, ultimately voted in support of her nomination. Sen. Bernie Sanders, the ranking member of the Senate HELP committee, said ahead of Saphier's vote that he would vote down her nomination because in part Saphier "has questioned the need for the hepatitis B vaccine at birth, when the data science has been clear." "We need a surgeon general who will tell the truth about vaccines, not someone who misleads the public," Sanders said. At her confirmation hearing, Saphier said the universal birth dose of hepatitis B was safe and effective. READ MORE: Trump pulls Casey Means' stalled surgeon general nomination, picks Nicole Saphier instead Chris Klomp, who was nominated to serve as deputy secretary of the Department of Health and Human Services, was advanced out of the Senate Finance Committee last week on a 15 to 12 vote. He was questioned during the same hearing as Saphier about his duties associated with the role as the current chief counselor of the Department of Health and Human Services under the leadership of Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. as well as about his vaccine stance. In protesting Klomp's nomination at the Senate Finance Committee, Sen. Ron Wyden said Klomp "tried to create the impression that he will be the adult in the room on vaccines. Yet, as we sit here today, the vaccine chaos that we've come to expect from Robert Kennedy's HHS continues." A free press is a cornerstone of a healthy democracy. 0b8073b82c5b.text: By — Konstantin Toropin, Associated Press Konstantin Toropin, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/world/watch-live-hegseth-delivers-state-of-the-force-address-expected-to-make-cuts-to-top-ranks Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter WATCH LIVE: Hegseth delivers State of the Force address, expected to make cuts to top ranks World Sep 30, 2026 2:53 PM EDT WASHINGTON (AP) — Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth is planning to announce further cuts to the number of generals and admirals serving in the military in an address set for Wednesday, the Pentagon confirmed. Hegseth is expected to deliver an address at 3 p.m. EDT. Watch live in our video player above. According to Pentagon officials, Hegseth will direct all the military services to double the 10% reduction that he ordered last spring to the roughly 800 flag and general officer positions, making it a 20% total decrease to be completed by Jan. 1, 2027. READ MORE: Bipartisan criticism from senators about Pentagon briefing on U.S. defense strategy President Donald Trump or Hegseth already have fired or pushed to retire more than two dozen military leaders since taking office, including the Army's top uniformed officer, Gen. Randy George, in April. They also have fired the only two women serving as four-star officers, as well as a disproportionate number of other senior female officers. Educate your inbox Subscribe to Here’s the Deal, our politics newsletter for analysis you won’t find anywhere else. Enter your email address Subscribe Form error message goes here. Thank you. Please check your inbox to confirm. Hegseth plans to make the announcement in a speech to troops at the Marine Corps Base Quantico in Virginia, the second year in a row he will deliver what the Pentagon is calling his "State of the Force" address. Fox News earlier reported the new reductions, which could include any one-star general or above or officer of equivalent Navy rank. As part of last year's cuts, Hegseth also ordered the active duty military to shed 20% of its four-star general officers — the highest-level leader — and the National Guard to shed 20% of its top positions, but it is unclear if all those cuts have been made. READ MORE: Speaker Johnson recesses House early, blocking Massie's push to impeach Hegseth Hegseth gathered all the military's generals and admirals at the same time last year for an address in which he declared an end to "woke" culture and announced new directives for troops that include "gender-neutral" or "male-level" standards for physical fitness. However, that speech was overshadowed by the attendance of President Donald Trump, who proposed using American cities as training grounds for the armed forces and spoke of needing U.S. military might to combat what he called the "invasion from within." When Hegseth first announced the effort to trim the highest levels of the military ranks, he argued it was intended to remove "redundant force structure to optimize and streamline leadership." In a memo released in May 2025, he said the aim was to free the military from "unnecessary bureaucratic layers." The number of general officer positions in the military is set by law, but it is possible to let positions remain unfilled by not submitting replacements to Congress. Hegseth's relationship with Congress is already strained, and he faces articles of impeachment from a Republican, Rep. Thomas Massie of Kentucky, over his leadership of the Pentagon and management of the Iran war. Sen. Jack Reed, a Rhode Island Democrat and ranking member of the Senate Armed Services Committee, said eliminating senior leadership positions must be done in consultation with Congress and warned that the planned cuts "should alarm every American." "Congress has been clear with the Secretary that he must consult this body and explain his reasoning for senior officer removals and promotion holds. To date, we have not received satisfactory answers," Reed said in a statement. "Our military is conducting major operations around the world, and the force is already under strain," he added. "Eliminating senior positions and leaders now will add to that strain and disrupt command when continuity matters most." A free press is a cornerstone of a healthy democracy. The News
The US Federal Trade Commission is investigating top American AI labs â and a prominent safety watchdog â over the potential dangers of their technology.
An FTC official confirmed the probe, first reported by the New York Post. The investigation was launched before an unreleased OpenAI model went rogue and hacked open-source AI hub Hugging Face earlier this year, an incident that triggered a fresh wave of concern over the possible harms of uninhibited AI development.
In addition to labs, including OpenAI and Anthropic, METR, a California-based nonprofit that evaluates frontier AI models for risks, is also a target. METR conducted an investigation into the OpenAI-Hugging Face hack and released a report on the incident.
The agency is set to send civil investigative demands, which are similar to subpoenas, to the companies in the next few weeks.
OpenAI, Anthropic, and METR didnât immediately respond to requests for comment.
Know More
The probe steps up US government scrutiny of top tech companies, even as executives from many of those companies gathered at the White House this week and signed a voluntary pledge to self-police their AI models. US President Donald Trump said the industry was showing âtremendous self-regulation.â
FTC Chairman Andrew Ferguson earlier this month signaled opposition to government regulation driven by AI safety fears, telling Fox News that OpenAI and Anthropic shouldnât be able to âwhip everyone into a panic and then say, âWe need a whole bunch of regulations that we can comply with.ââ
He added: âThat is how companies build a moat around their businesses to make sure that people canât compete against them.â

ca6a33812f10.text: Sen. Marsha Blackburn (R-Tenn.) sued former special counsel Jack Smith Wednesday, alleging he unlawfully obtained her cellphone toll records during his investigation of Trump and the 2020 election Why it matters: The lawsuit escalates Republicans' efforts to challenge Smith's investigation more than a year after his probe ended. What they're saying: "Through his Arctic Frost witch hunt that targeted conservatives across America and even the President of the United States, Jack Smith perpetrated one of the worst abuses of government power in our nation's history," Blackburn said. "This lawsuit is solely about holding Mr. Smith accountable and ensuring that our nation's justice system can never again be weaponized against the American people. I thank the New Civil Liberties Alliance for their partnership in filing this complaint and for fighting to uphold our cherished constitutional rights." Driving the news: The suit was filed in the U.S. District Court for the Middle District of Tennessee one day after Smith testified at a Senate Judiciary Committee hearing Tuesday. The suit alleges Smith obtained a nondisclosure order without telling the judge that the underlying subpoena sought the records of a sitting senator. Blackburn's cellphone provider was ordered to keep the subpoena secret. Blackburn is asking the court to award her $1 in nominal damages to emphasize that she isn't seeking money but instead wants to hold Smith accountable for his allegedly unlawful actions. Legal counsel for Smith did not immediately respond to Axios' request for comment. Flashback: The lawsuit comes one day after Sen. Eric Schmitt (R-Mo.), a potential running mate for JD Vance in 2028, accused Smith of perjury at Tuesday's hearing but got his facts wrong and was later corrected by Smith and Sen. Amy Klobuchar (D-Minn.). The mistake went viral and drew extensive criticism on social media. Catch up quick: In October 2025, the GOP-led House Judiciary Committee released highly redacted documents showing that the FBI had investigated approximately 160 Republican figures as part of its probe into Trump's false claims that the 2020 presidential election was stolen. The probe, known as Arctic Frost, sought to identify those who "conspired to corruptly obstruct the United States Congress' certification of the 2020 Presidential election results by submitting allegedly fraudulent elector certificates." By the numbers: The lawsuit claims the Arctic Frost probe subpoenaed records associated with at least 20 Republican members of Congress. The lawsuit claims about 400 Republican individuals and organizations were targeted. The lawsuit says records involving roughly 4,782 Trump donors, including 102 Tennesseans, contained home addresses, bank account numbers and signatures. The bottom line: Blackburn's lawsuit extends the legal and political fight over the Justice Department's investigations into Trump after he left office. Trump and his allies have vowed to continue probing those who investigated or crossed the president, including New York Attorney General Letitia James (D), former FBI chief James Comey and Sen. Adam Schiff (D-Calif.). Go deeper: Jan. 6 probe potentially investigated over 150 Republicans, documents show

94a832095aec.text: Google is unveiling its long-awaited next-generation AI model, Gemini 4 Argon, to a small group of cybersecurity partners, the company said Wednesday. Why it matters: Gemini 4 arrives after a long gap at the top of Google's model lineup, in which the company kept rolling out smaller, cheaper Flash models while rivals OpenAI and Anthropic sprinted forward. State of play: Google says Gemini 4 Argon is built to handle complex, long-running tasks in software engineering, finance, legal work and cybersecurity. Google said the new model is state of the art on certain coding and knowledge work benchmarks, outperforming competing OpenAI frontier model GPT-6 Astra on several. The company is rolling the model out only to a group of trusted cybersecurity defenders and is participating in the U.S. government's voluntary pre-release process. Google says it will expand access after additional testing, with paying subscribers first in line. What they're saying: "Argon is a well-rounded model that has frontier capabilities across several domains," Tulsee Doshi, head of Gemini products at Google DeepMind, told Axios. "We've seen strong performance up close as Googlers have put the model through its paces in recent weeks, with many relying on it for their hardest coding and research problems." Flashback: Gemini 4 comes out nearly a year after the previous flagship model generation, Gemini 3. In May, Google CEO Sundar Pichai said the company's next major model release would come in June. That model, widely expected to be Gemini 3.5 Pro, never came out. In July, Axios reported that poor morale among Google DeepMind employees was part of the reason for the delay. Zoom in: Google's additional time investment may not be viewed as negatively in the context of the AI safety debate that has embroiled companies and users. OpenAI has had issues with agents going rogue, and recently said it is scrapping GPT-6.1 Astra due to security issues . Top AI developers OpenAI and Anthropic are investigating tens of thousands of incidents involving their agents misbehaving, Axios previously reported. The bottom line: If the developer community finds Gemini 4 to be as competitive with OpenAI and Anthropic's frontier systems as the benchmarks indicate, it would result in a massive catch-up for an AI company some had started to doubt .

07ae79d44b17.text: The Justice Department filed a complaint against a group of federal judges from Minnesota for speaking to The New York Times about the impact of the immigration enforcement surge on their court. The big picture: The complaint opens a new front in the Trump administration's standoff with federal judges, bolstered by a loyal Justice Department. Driving the news: The complaint , which was brought against two jurists who spoke on the record with the paper and those who spoke anonymously, alleged the behavior was "improper and unethical" and called for the judges to be recused from any DHS-related matters. It further urged the Eighth Circuit to investigate. The chambers of the named senior district judges, Patrick J. Schiltz and John R. Tunheim, did not immediately respond to Axios' request for comment. This is a breaking news story and will be updated.

b8dc65d341da.text: Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth took aim at the U.S. media during a speech at a Marine Corps base in Virginia on Wednesday, saying: "Our so-called press makes Iranian state media look reasonable." Why it matters: Hegseth cast news outlets as a threat to U.S. troops, escalating his attacks on journalists over reporting based on classified information . What he's saying: In his second annual "State of the Force" address at Marine Corps Base Quantico in Virginia, Hegseth accused some members of the media of "treason." While a free press is important, he said "partisan activism that intentionally smears the troops and the historic mission that they're undertaking is fundamentally anti-American. It's sick. It's a national betrayal. It's treason, actually." "It's your movements and bases that they reveal to the enemy," he said. "Ultimately, it's your lives they put directly at risk when they lie about munition stockpiles." Between the lines: Media reports about dwindling supplies of key munitions amid the war with Iran have drawn the ire of President Trump and his team. Hegseth frequently attacks the press and has taken unprecedented steps to restrict the media's access to the Pentagon. Driving the news: Hegseth returned to many culture-war themes in the speech, highlighting his efforts to reverse DEI and gender equity efforts in the interest of "meritocracy." "We are no longer the woke department or the weak department. Simple translation of that — no fatties, no trannies, no beardos, no weirdos, no wimps, no radicals. Just warriors." Zoom out: Hegseth also made substantive news in the speech. He confirmed plans for a 20% reduction in generals and admirals across the force, while rejecting descriptions of the cuts as a purge. "As usual, what the media levels as an accusation, I wear as an accomplishment," he said. Hegseth also announced a new Autonomous Warfare Command, an initiative to study the future of war that will involve Elon Musk, and a nationwide competition to host the next U.S. military base. Go deeper: Hegseth directs Pentagon to combat foreign interference in U.S. elections
