When the first day of the apple harvest rolled around in Washington State last year, the fruit was ripe and the pickers were ready â but the weather had other ideas.
"It was like 38Câ¦ it's not safe for people to work in that heat," recalls Joel Carter at Okanagan Specialty Fruits. "We had to stop at 10 o'clock in the morning."
He says that artificial intelligence (AI) models that forecast ideal harvest dates, taking into account the weather, would be useful. "You need to know more than just when your fruit is going to be ripe. How long do you have to pick it?" he says. "That's where these models are really helpful."
Carter's company has more than 1,250 acres of apple orchards in Washington, and the fruit is grown for sliced apple portions â often sold to hotels and schools, for example. The firm is investing in technology with the hope of maximising productivity. Even the apples are genetically engineered so that they don't brown easily once cut.
But planning a harvest is tricky. New tools that count and analyse fruit on the tree or vine, and predict when crops will ripen, are emerging. It matters because prices for fruit, especially high-value berries such as strawberries or blueberries can fluctuate wildly. Getting the harvest date wrong means you book seasonal workers when you don't actually need them, and risk missing out on the biggest profits.
Okanagan Specialty Fruits is already experimenting with cameras from a Canadian firm called Vivid Machines. The cameras are mounted atop tractors and they scoop up imagery of the apple trees as the tractor trundles by. AI identifies buds, flowers or fruit in that footage.
"Right now, Vivid is telling us crop estimates and harvest dates," says Carter. He notes that the system is good at picking out very tiny flower buds, which are hard to see at a glance with the naked eye.
But the accuracy of forecasts is noticeably dependent on the quality of historical information fed in to the system, adds Carter. "This isn't something where an AI can scrape the internet and figure out what's the average [yield] for Granny Smith," he explains. "It's going to be bespoke to your farm."
Apples are at least somewhat forgiving â the harvest window for those Granny Smiths is three weeks long, says Carter. For other fruit, such as berries, you might only have a few days.
"If a strawberry crop is on, you have to harvest it â otherwise your entire crop gets diseased very, very quickly," says Raymond Martin, co-founder and chief operating officer of FruitCast, a UK company that offers harvest forecasts to fruit growers here.
His firm offers growers crop predictions for strawberries and also raspberries, blackberries, blueberries and tomatoes. "We're moving on to grapes next year," adds Martin.
Don't experienced farmers know when their fruit will be ripe, I ask? Martin says they generally do â but not necessarily across their entire farm, which might be many acres in size, or have both outdoor and indoor growing areas. "We do exactly what the farmers could do but we just do it on a scale that they can't."
The system analyses footage of ripening fruit that can be captured by drones, someone walking up and down a field with a smartphone, or a camera mounted on a farm vehicle.
This year has been challenging, notes Martin, with hot weather and severe drought hitting much of the UK. This has stressed many fruit plants, putting them into thermal dormancy and slowing down fruit production.
The FruitCast model accounts for weather and irrigation conditions in its forecasts. The company says, "our forecasts land within 10% of actual picked volume one week out (90% accurate) and within 17% three weeks out (83% accurate). We guarantee less than 20% errorâ¦"
Angus Soft Fruits is one company that has worked with FruitCast. AI tech for forecasting fruit ripeness is not yet "a finished solution" says operations director Neill Finlayson: "This journey is still ongoing and, whilst significant progress has been made, the industry remains some way from achieving a fully integrated forecasting ecosystem."
Driscoll's, a California headquartered fruit seller with a big operation in the UK, also confirmed to BBC News that some of its independent fruit growers in the UK have used FruitCast's technology.
Researchers are also exploring new ways of analysing fruit in intense detail. Many farmers already use handheld brix meters to gauge the sugar content of their crop. These devices work by measuring how much light has changed direction, or refracted, after passing through a liquid â indicating the volume of solids present.
Some such meters use infrared light, meaning there's no need to cut into the fruit to take measurements. But Yasaman Ghasempour at Princeton University says millimetre waves, high frequency radio waves, can penetrate deeper "They basically respond very well to humidity, water [and sugar]," she says.
She and her students have come up with a millimetre wave-based ripeness detector, external that could be used by farmers â or even customers searching for perfectly ripe fruit in shops. Her students tried it out at a local market in New Jersey. "[Staff] there got kind of scared that we were doing something shady," laughs Ghasempour.
Such fine-grained analysis of fruit, if currently unripe, could also help inform forecasts of when it will be ripe.
But while some growers, such as Carter, are interested in trying out new tech, many will wonder whether investing in it is really worthwhile. "Adoption is very complicated," says Jing Zhang at North Carolina State University. "The grower has to have confidence in the research and whether or not it works."
Zhang has been working on a system to automatically count the number of blueberries, external captured in smartphone images of blueberry bushes.
The simplest systems need not be expensive. Kevin Wang at the University of Florida has developed another crop-counting tool that can harvest imagery, external from $100 (Â£74) dr

Hegseth plans ‘Autonomous Warfare Command’
The military’s 12th combatant command was among a slew of announcements in a Quantico speech Wednesday.
The Pentagon will create a combatant command to lead its efforts to develop and deploy robotic weapons, Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth said Wednesday in a speech peppered with Bible verses and insults to the press.
The new Autonomous Warfare Command, or AUTOWARCOM, will be “a new four-star combatant command with service-like authorities built to scale autonomous and robotic capabilities across the joint force,” Hegseth said. It is to stand up by Oct. 1, 2027, according to a memo released after his speech.
The secretary seemed to say that planning for the new command would flow from the three-month-old direct reporting portfolio manager for unmanned offensive and defensive systems, whose “culminating mission” will “take place over the course of months, clearing the path for Autonomous Warfare Command.” In the meantime, the office is being given a new task: to “prototype a new construct called warfighting acquisition” that “fuses operators with entrepreneurs in rapid adaptation cycles while distributing decisions and dollars closer to frontline units, to combatant commands.” He said the office would henceforth be led by Owen West, who currently runs the Defense Innovation Unit, and a Navy senior chief petty officer who is both a SEAL and a test pilot. It will also be renamed “Project Agincourt,” the secretary said, miming a bow and arrow.
To further speed the adoption of unmanned technologies, Hegseth said, the Army, Navy, and Air Force Departments will create “new MOS frameworks”—a reference to the job classifications of the Army and Marine Corps—”to support our shift to autonomy. We need institutional knowledge and career paths for a new generation of autonomous warfighters.”
The secretary also announced a committee with a four-month deadline “to creatively look to the future and identify the domains that we must conquer and capabilities we must master.” The committee, dubbed Project Meridian, will be led by defense contractors Elon Musk and Palmer Luckey and Newt Gingrich, the 83-year-old former Speaker of the House whose mixed scientific legacy includes dissolving Congress’ non-partisan scientific advisory office.
‘FORTRESS America’
Hegseth said that the U.S. military has become “Dependent on foreign mines for rare earths, on overseas factories for microchips, on foreign supply chains for weapons, and on a civilian power grid to keep the lights on at our bases.” So, he said, he is launching an effort to ensure that every U.S. military base will eventually generate its own electrical power; he gave no timeline or cost estimate. He also said the military will increase its stockpiles of munitions and critical supply-chain materials. It will also stockpile medicine and blood, part of what Hegseth called “a national insurance policy for the American homeland.”
As part of this “FORTRESS America” effort, Hegseth said, the U.S. military will build a new base in the state that makes the best pitch for it. A DOD statement said the base will “serve as a foundational hub for integrated defense operations, distributed command-and-control, and resilient cyber and technological capabilities.” The secretary said the base will cover “hundreds of thousands of acres,” house 15,000 to 25,000 troops, and have structures of “timeless classical architecture” to comply with an August executive order.
Other new initiatives include a planned Office of Religious Affairs that will report to Hegseth personally. “ORA will ensure religious affairs are no longer dispersed across distant bureaucratic layers, giving senior leaders a dedicated capability to protect free exercise, remove policy barriers, identify unmet requirements, and secure the support needed for the Service chaplaincies to succeed,” a DOD statement said.
Hegseth continued a pattern of espousing conservative evangelical religious beliefs in official speeches. He quoted the Bible several times, called children “precious souls made in the image and likeness of God,” and said that “America's military must understand the difference” between God and evil.
The defense secretary also took pains, beginning with the second sentence of his speech and continuing at intervals until his closing thoughts, to lambaste what he called the “hyperventilating” and “delusional” media for, among other things, reporting on the swift depletion of key munitions in the war on Iran. He said “partisan activism that intentionally smears the troops” amounts to “treason, actually.” He cited no evidence of smears or activism, nor any basis for telling the assembled troops that “it's your movements and bases that they reveal to the enemy.”
Hegseth prompted and drew light applause on a few occasions, a noted change from the resolute silence at his high-profile speech a year ago; the video feed did not reveal whether the clapping came from the carefully selected uniformed senior enlisted leaders and junior officers or others in the audience. “This is decidedly not a trifling matter of decorum or politeness. The safety of the American republic and the constitutional order depend on elected political leaders trusting that the military they have inherited from previous administrations will serve in a nonpartisan fashion,” Peter Feaver, a noted expert on civil-military affairs, wrote before the speech.

Defense Business Brief: End-of-fiscal-year advice for founders; Navy drone boats; Powerus to go public
WASHINGTON—The Pentagon’s comptroller has a bit of advice for tech makers and founders who want to do business with the military: Make tech that troops like, find out who can buy it for them, and hire someone who knows how things work. .
“Having the users like your products is incredibly necessary. That's a given. But it's the program offices and the [portfolio acquisition executives, or] PAEs who really have the power to make you successful,” Jules Hurst, the Defense Department’s chief financial officer, said at Y Combinator’s Startup Industrial Base event Wednesday. “You have to provide the solution to them. Again, they’ve made their budget. They made it a year and a half ago. They've made a plan to execute that budget. So anything you're bringing in is, at times, disruptive to them if they have an established program. So you've got to figure out how you can fit in.”
Fitting in could mean being a subcontractor for an existing program or helping program managers “shape requirements for a future capability,” but it has to be more than just a good idea, he said.
“You've got to fit into the cycle—and I know that's not what a lot of you want to hear. And we're working on changing that by doing acquisition reform, but it's still the case in a lot of programs across the department,” Hurst said.
Hiring someone familiar with doing business with the government “will help you immensely,” he said, as will finding the right Defense Department program offices.
“Shop for the program offices and program managers that are really interested in change, and you align yourself with that person and you start to help try to solve their problems with your team. If you find the right program office or program manager, they can do immense good for you. They can open up lots of opportunities across the department. They can introduce you to people, even if you're not a good fit for their program. So part of it is also personality shopping and finding somebody who really wants to make change and isn’t fixated on just compliance.”
And once in the door, companies must be able to make the tech in large quantities.
“The best thing is to show that you can make stuff. A lot of startups right now, sometimes they're paper deep—and that's kind of a risky bet for the government. Not that we shouldn't take it, right? Because sometimes our alternative is a company that does manufacture things, but doesn't produce in the timetable we want, or the capabilities we need, or the cost schedule we want,” Hurst said.
“So again, my best advice to you is: show that you can manufacture things. And if you are not manufacturing things, hire people who have experience manufacturing things, so you can show the government that you're bringing on the talent necessary to scale your product and capability if they decide to buy it.”
Welcome
You’ve reached the Defense Business Brief, where we dig into what the Pentagon buys, who they’re buying from, and why. Send along your tips, feedback, and song recommendations to lwilliams@defenseone.com. Check out the Defense Business Brief archive here, and tell your friends to subscribe!
USVs wading in. The Navy will buy 30 medium-sized unmanned surface vessels at about $40 million each from three companies: Galliano Marine Services, HII, and Saronic. Each company will build 10, the first of which are expected to be delivered in the last quarter of 2027.
- A little more: Six out of seven companies successfully completed sea trials for phase one of the Navy’s MUSV program. The three that didn’t get production contracts but had successful trials—Leidos, PacMar Technologies, and Sea Machines—“will automatically transfer into the marketplace and be eligible as part of phase two,” which will have broader requirements, Christopher Miller, the Navy’s acting direct reporting portfolio manager for robotic and autonomous systems, told reporters. Birdon participated in the trials and did not meet the program requirements but has a “viable path” to joining the drone marketplace in the future, he said.
- Pulling up: The MUSV program has been through a lot of changes in the last year (including a lawsuit.) But the more interesting part for me is what could come out of phase two, where other services, like the Army, can share requirements they have. This could have big implications for the Indo-Pacom region, and is something USARPAC commander Gen. Ronald Clark highlighted earlier this year. 
	
  - “The Army has a mission, and they actually operate a number of ships. And I think there's a great opportunity here…and we're just trying to make sure everybody sees the state of the market in terms of the capability, what the performance is. And then we'll obviously work closely on the requirements,” Miller told reporters. “But I'm excited about that because I do think there's opportunity for a close collaboration and partnering with the other services as they think about their future programs.”
  - Phase 2 is expected to start testing evaluations as early as Nov. 16 and continue over the next five years.
- Related tangent: Defense tech darling Saronic broke ground on its much-anticipated Port Alpha facility in Brownsville, Texas, today. Vice President JD Vance attended the event. Also, earlier this month, Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth visited the company’s Austin facility, praising the company’s USVs for aiding in the rescue of downed Apache pilots.
Making moves + other news
- Michael Brasseur joined Booz Allen Hamilton as an executive vice president. Brasseur was previously Saab, Inc.’s chief strategy officer and led the Navy’s Task Force 59.
- Dronemaker Powerus is expected to go public Oct. 1 as it finalizes its merger with Aureus Greenway Holdings, a publicly traded company on NASDAQ. The new company name will be Powerus Corporation.
- The FBI shut down an investigation into defense contractors’ alleged bribes to lawmake

d65100d555cc.text: Secretary of State Marco Rubio demanded on Monday that the Iranian delegation to the United Nations General Assembly immediately leave the country after negotiations stalled, according to a U.S. official and a second source with knowledge of the matter. Why it matters: Though the Iranians were likely to depart soon anyway, Rubio's move was a highly unusual diplomatic rebuke and laid bare the deep distrust between the two countries amid fruitless efforts to broker an end to the war. Qatari mediators tried to secure a diplomatic breakthrough between the U.S. and Iran but made little progress, with neither side willing to budge. Among those ordered to leave New York was Rubio's Iranian counterpart, Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi. What they're saying: "Secretary Rubio kicked out the Iranian delegation who had overstayed their welcome. The UN General Assembly was over, so it was time for them to go," the U.S. official said. Behind the scenes: On Monday morning, the White House thought there might be progress in talks with Iran later in the day. But by late afternoon it became clear negotiations were at a stalemate. Then on Monday evening, at Rubio's orders, the U.S. mission to the UN told the Iranian mission to the UN that Araghchi's delegation had to leave New York immediately, according to the U.S. official. The Iranian delegation, including Araghchi, left for the airport several hours later and boarded a flight from New York to Doha at 1:20 a.m. Tuesday. A second source confirmed that the U.S. demanded that the Iranian delegation leave, but said Araghchi was scheduled to travel back to Tehran on Monday night anyway. What's next: Qatari mediators are continuing to talk to both sides about their compromise proposal, regional sources say. "Maybe I will blow 'em up," President Trump told reporters on Wednesday when asked how he can reach a deal with a regime he says is crazy. "Maybe I blow 'em up. We have to make that decision. We will blow 'em up or make a deal. But the time is coming. It's gonna end very soon one way or the other."

- Published
Swiss glaciers have suffered a near-record loss of ice in 2026, new data shows, as intense summer heatwaves take their toll on Alpine peaks.
More than 5% of the country's remaining glacier ice has disappeared in the last 12 months, which scientists say is "extraordinary".
They warn that such rapid melting is no longer a surprise given the pace of climate change, but it could threaten water supplies for farming, hydropower and transport in the decades ahead.
The loss of glacier ice can also destabilise mountain slopes and increase the risk of landslides in some places - which can lead to flash flooding in extreme cases, as seen in Nepal in August.
There were multiple factors involved in that event, which was triggered when a large area of bedrock and glacier ice collapsed.
But scientists say long-term glacier thinning and the thawing of frozen ground likely raised the risks.
The notable finding from this latest report is not so much that Swiss glaciers are shrinking - which is to be expected in our warming climate, driven primarily by fossil fuel emissions - but the sheer pace of melting.
Until recently, glaciologists in the Alps considered 2% of ice lost in a single year to be "extreme". This year has seen an estimated 5.5% disappear.
"It's really just disastrous," said Dr Matthias Huss, director of Glacier Monitoring Switzerland, which produced the report.
Swiss glaciers started the summer in an already difficult place, covered by less snow than usual after a mild winter.
And much of that snow disappeared quickly in the early and intense heatwaves of May and June, exposing the glacier ice below.
Bare ice is darker and less reflective than fresh snow, so absorbs more of the Sun's energy.
That left glaciers vulnerable to melting even faster in subsequent heatwaves.
"Ten years ago, I wouldn't have thought that it's possible to lose glaciers so quickly," said Dr Fabien Maussion, a glaciologist at the University of Bristol, who was not involved in the Swiss report.
"What's happened over the summer now is extremely distressingâ¦ but at the same time it was to be expected from a climate scientist's perspective," he added.
Meltwater from glaciers can be an important source of water for irrigation, hydropower and even shipping traffic during hot, dry conditions.
Scientists estimate that Swiss glaciers released 2.2 trillion litres of meltwater between July and September.
Although that helped to ease water shortages this summer, it has rapidly diminished the frozen supply.
The loss of ice could pose long-term challenges, Huss warned, with smaller glaciers unable to top up water levels to the same extent.
"Every drop of water that runs off during these heatwaves is kind of old water that's been stocked in the glacier ice centuries or decades ago," said Huss.
"It's helping us [now] but it's unsustainable, so we won't have it at [our] disposal in the next heatwave."
The River Rhine reached record lows in places this summer, affecting shipping navigation routes and increasing transport costs.
One of the most ominous findings is what researchers observed at measurement sites at the highest elevations, where temperatures are lowest and glaciers are typically snow-covered.
Even as high as 3,500 metres above sea level, scientists found no snow remaining at the end of summer.
"At some glaciers we've seen four metres of ice loss at the highest point, where they should be covered by several metres of winter snow at this time of the year," said Huss, from Glacier Monitoring Switzerland.
Snow is like glacier food - and under stable conditions some of it would eventually compact into ice.
But if no snow survives the summer, it cannot replace the ice lost to melting at lower, warmer elevations. The glacier will starve, shrink and eventually disappear.
"Glaciers are complex because they gain mass at the top and they flow downstream, so there is a lot of physics," explained Maussion.
"But in its simplest form, what we see right now is that we took an ice cube out of the fridge and it's just melting in front of our eyes."
Scientists say the climate is now too warm for many Alpine glaciers to survive.
Some, like Plattalva in eastern Switzerland, have already disappeared.
But researchers stress that sharp cuts to carbon emissions can still save much of the world's glacier ice.
This is particularly the case for the Himalayas and the polar regions, where most of the planet's ice resides.
"There we still can make a big difference with protecting the climate," said Huss.
"If these ice masses can be saved or stabilised, we can limit the rise of global sea levelsâ¦ which could affect billions of people living along the coast."
Additional reporting by Dominic Bailey

61c4a680ecc1.text: By — Andrew Dalton, Associated Press Andrew Dalton, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/nation/woman-accused-of-firing-at-rihannas-home-indicted-on-attempted-murder-with-assault-weapon Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Woman accused of firing at Rihanna's home indicted on attempted murder with assault weapon Nation Sep 30, 2026 7:54 PM EDT LOS ANGELES (AP) — A Florida woman accused of driving across the country to fire a rifle at Rihanna and A$AP Rocky's home, hitting a trailer the celebrity couple was inside and a nursery where their kids were, has been indicted by a grand jury on 14 felony counts including attempted murder. The indictment against 36-year-old Ivanna Lisette Ortiz of Orlando was unsealed Wednesday by a Los Angeles County judge. Ortiz, appearing in court wearing yellow jail clothes, spoke only to her attorney, who entered a not guilty plea for her. The judge then ordered her held on $2.6 million bail. The move came a day after another judge ruled that Ortiz is mentally competent to stand trial. The secret grand jury proceedings were held as Ortiz was undergoing months of psychiatric evaluation. The jurors returned their indictment June 18, but it was kept under wraps for three months until the judge ruled on her competency. Now, a case that appeared stalled — possibly permanently — is on a fast track to trial. READ MORE: Prosecutor says Rihanna, A$AP Rocky, 3 kids were home when woman charged with attempted murder fired No one was injured in the March 8 shooting. Authorities allege Ortiz drove a Tesla up to the gates of the Beverly Hills-area property of the singing superstar and her rap star partner, A$AP Rocky, pointed an AR-15 style rifle out the window and fired at least 20 rounds toward the property and the neighboring house. "This is a person who wanted to kill Rihanna," Deputy District Attorney Alexander Bott said outside court. "Everyone else was collateral damage." Bullets tore through the Airstream trailer, according to a police report. Shots also struck the wall of their home's nursery, where their three small children were with their nanny. Rihanna's mother and several staffers also were in the home, and authorities say she also fired shots toward a neighbor's house. Both Rihanna and her mother, Monica Fenty, testified to the grand jury, as did Hollywood agent Tracey Jacobs, who was listed among the victims from the property in the indictment. Their testimony remains under seal but will become public in about two weeks unless the defense seeks to keep them secret and the judge agrees. Rihanna told investigators just after the shooting that she "suddenly heard approximately ten loud sounds like something banging on metal," and pulled Rocky out of a bed and onto the ground. She said she opened curtains and saw bullet marks in the windshield right in front of where she had been standing. Deputy Public Defender Derek Dillman, Ortiz's attorney, did not speak to reporters outside the courtroom, and a message seeking comment from the public defender's office on the indictment was not immediately answered. Other than her not guilty pleas, her lawyers have not publicly addressed the charges, saying only that they would work to defend her rights. Investigators said that on the day of her arrest, Ortiz told them: "I wasn't attempting murder." Ortiz was charged with very similar counts in March. The new indictment supersedes those charges. The secret grand jury proceedings allow prosecutors to skip California's preliminary hearing process, where evidence must be presented publicly to see if a trial is merited. The indictment also charges Ortiz with 10 counts of assault with an assault weapon — one for each of the people on the two properties — and three counts of shooting at an inhabited dwelling or camper. It names the couple's three children Rza, Riot and Rocki, all under age 5, as victims. The assault weapon counts carry a stiffer sentence than the original charges of assault with a semiautomatic firearm. She could get life in prison if convicted of all counts. Reports have been sealed on the psychiatric evaluations that paused the case shortly after it began, and there was no public discussion of the details of her mental state. Prosecutors have not said anything about a motive or cited any connection between Rihanna and Ortiz, a longtime licensed speech pathologist. But in videos posted on Facebook and YouTube in the months before the shooting, Ortiz made increasingly angry comments on Rihanna that sometimes took the form of threats, at one point calling her a "devil." A nine-time Grammy Award winner, Rihanna has had 14 No. 1 hits on the Billboard Hot 100, including "We Found Love," "Work," "Umbrella" and "Disturbia." A free press is a cornerstone of a healthy democracy. Support trusted journalism and civil dialogue. Donate now By — Andrew Dalton, Associated Press Andrew Dalton, Associated Press

Warning: This story contains distressing details and discussion of sexual assault.
When Mary was a first-year college student, she woke up after a fraternity party with bruises and bite marks all over her body. She says it took her a few days to piece together that she had been sexually assaulted while "blacked out", and to find the strength - and the right avenue - to report the assault.
The man she accused was eventually expelled, but police declined to bring charges because they said there was a lack of physical evidence.
Mary - whose name has been changed to protect her identity - says the process of finding some measure of justice was oftentimes confusing and disappointing.
"Even though it was a positive outcome, it was still so emotionally exhausting and draining, because I had to do all of this in tandem with getting used to being a college student for the first time," said Mary. "In many ways, I had to be my own advocate, gathering all my evidence."
The experience with local police, she added, "left me with a deep sense of disappointment in the system".
How both universities and the criminal justice system respond to these types of assaults on college campuses is once again under the spotlight, after a former student at Cornell University filed a civil lawsuit alleging she was raped by several members of a fraternity two years ago, with prosecutors declining at the time to pursue a case.
Mary did not attend Cornell, and her case is not connected with the university. But advocates for survivors of sexual assault say her case, and the Cornell allegations, are emblematic of the larger challenges in responding to sexual assault claims on college campuses specifically.
The confusing web of systems and policies - which varies greatly by college - is one of several reasons why the vast majority of sexual assaults on college campuses, research suggests, go unreported.
"These processes are hard to navigate if you aren't in trauma," said Nancy Chi Cantalupo, an associate professor of law at Wayne State University who has represented victims on college campuses. "If you are in trauma, they're virtually impossible to navigate."
Earlier this month, the former Cornell student known only as Jane Doe filed a lawsuit against the Ivy League university, alleging she was drugged and raped by several men at a fraternity house at the university in 2024.
She also alleged that Cornell failed to protect her or adequately punish the men involved. Jane Doe said she had reported the alleged assault to campus police, who interviewed her, and provided information to the district attorney's office. The prosecutor declined to bring charges at the time, but this week, Tompkins County District Attorney Matthew Van Houten re-opened the case.
Both Cornell and Van Houten have defended their handling of the 2024 case. In a statement, external, the university said it had "conducted an extensive investigation and adjudication over several months and imposed different sanctions based on the findings and circumstances involving each student" in addition to creating a new framework for addressing sexual assault on campus.
Cornell has said it followed the procedures outlined in a federal civil rights law called Title IX. The law mandates that universities follow certain rules about investigating sexual assaults. Cornell said its investigation resulted in the fraternity involved being barred from campus, and that students involved were suspended or expelled.
Two complex reporting systems
Typically, after a student reports an assault on campus, the university's Title IX office determines whether the alleged behaviour could constitute a violation of policy.
Eventually, both parties attend a hearing with a panel of faculty members or other mediators to present evidence and testimony in the case before a decision by the school is reached.
One of the biggest challenges sexual assault survivors face is simultaneously navigating the university and the criminal justice system, which "serve different purposes, operate under different rules and timelines, and lead to different outcomes", said Zoey Scheinblum-Brewer, a policy coordinator at the Rape, Abuse & Incest National Network, a nonprofit anti-sexual assault organisation.
"Unclear guidance about the options available through these parallel processes can create so much confusion and uncertainty that some students ultimately decide not to report," she said.
Mary said this process at her college was not clear to her when she made the decision to report the assault.
"For me, it would've been nice to know what I was getting into before it all happened. It felt like they were learning the process alongside me," she said of university officials.
While some colleges, like Cornell, have information sharing agreements with local police, Mary was told she had to go to police separately to file a report - a process she found physically exhausting.
Mary's lawyer says there was surveillance footage from the night showing her alleged rapist carrying her "slumped" over, and she had pictures of her bruises and bite marks. But police told Mary they did not have probable cause for an arrest, and that the district attorney wanted to leave it to university administration.
"I was left with this taste that because they knew that the college was 'handling' my investigation, that they could wipe their hands clean of it," she said.
The local police department told the BBC it did not have the details of this particular case. The local district attorney's office did not respond to a request for comment.
Secrecy and protection
University investigations are done behind closed doors, said Helene Weiss, a lawyer who has represented several victims of sexual assault on college campuses. She believes that part of the reason for the secrecy is to protect institutions' reputations.
"The secrecy of the process, it prevents other students from knowing about it. It prevents witnesses from coming forward,"

At about 3am one morning in May, Bamita Markam began convulsing.
The three-year-old had spent days with a high fever and angry red sores on her body. Her mother, Koushila, had first taken her to a doctor, who prescribed an ointment.
Bamita seemed to recover, then became ill again. A faith healer, called to the house in Matla village, gave her syrups and tablets. Nothing worked. By dawn, Bamita was dead.
"She cried a lot," Koushila recalls. "She convulsed all night." The family tried to make her drink water. At one point she vomited blood. They buried her in a jungle after midday.
Bamita's death was one of at least 32 child deaths recorded since May in a cluster of remote villages in Balaghat district in India's Madhya Pradesh state, officials say. The victims ranged from babies just three or four months old to an 18-year-old, and most were Baiga, one of India's 75 "particularly vulnerable tribal groups", external.
Officials attribute the deaths to mainly measles and malaria, possibly aggravated by malnutrition and delays in treatment.
They believe eight to 10 deaths were associated with measles, roughly another 10 with malaria, with several children suffering more than one infection. The precise cause of every death is less certain.
"I have never seen an outbreak like this. My father was a two-term lawmaker, and I have served three terms, but neither of us has seen so many children die in such a short time," Sanjay Uikey, who has represented the area since 2013, told me.
But disease is only part of the story. In remote, forested parts of Balaghat, where Maoist insurgency once took root, reaching a health centre can be a challenge in itself.
In the monsoon, the terrain can make that journey harder. Paddy fields glow against red earth and low, forested hills. Narrow dirt tracks wind between fields and mud homes, often becoming slippery and impassable in heavy rain.
The countryside is lush, but the homes are sparse. Most Baiga houses have low mud walls, rough timber and bamboo, and tiled or thatched roofs patched with plastic against the rain.
Some homes are accessible only by these tracks. Doctors investigating the deaths have travelled through the mud in tractors. On a recent visit, we walked nearly 2km (1.2 miles) uphill to reach some of the more remote homes. The surrounding jungle was dotted with the graves of children who had died.
The nearest state hospital, a 100-bed facility in Birsa, is about 70km away. For families without vehicles, reaching it can mean muddy tracks, a makeshift bamboo stretcher or a motorcycle - and a day's lost wages.
When Bamita became seriously ill, the family did not get her to hospital. It was raining heavily. The tracks were muddy and slippery, and the family had no way of transporting her.
"If I was able to take her to hospital she might have lived," Koushila says.
Her other daughter, Ankita, keeps asking what happened to her sister. The six-year-old has been told what many children in these villages are told: "Mata aa gayi" - the goddess has arrived.
For some Baiga families, some illnesses - like chicken pox - are seen as the arrival of a disease goddess, who must be appeased rather than treated. Families perform a seven to nine-day ritual of bathing and offering cool water and neem leaves to the local disease goddess. Many believe that treating the patient before the ritual is completed could cause death.
For weeks, such beliefs shaped how families responded to sick children. Then the scale of the deaths began to emerge.
On 21 July, Parshuram Dhurwey, a local village council chief, heard that two children in the same household in Bondari village had died. The next morning, he heard of another death. He called local officials and went to the area.
They found a grim picture.
"Every other child was sick," Dhurwey says. "They had fever, they had rashes. Many were undernourished."
When government medical officer Nimish Gautam arrived, he found severely dehydrated children. The first case he saw was a teenage girl with several days of fever and rash, whose blood sugar appeared dangerously low. Her family refused to let the health team examine her properly.
"Police were brought in to persuade them to take her to a health centre. The family still refused," Gautam told me. "They said if we took her for treatment, she would die. So we kept her under observation, and she recovered."
In one village, Dhurwey says, officials forcibly entered homes and took five seriously ill children to hospital. All recovered.
By the time the outbreak became unmistakable to local authorities, children had already been dying for weeks. By September, Dhurwey says, 10 children aged about 18 months to 14 years had died across the four villages in his council - Adori, Kundekasa, Bondari and Usri.
The symptoms were frighteningly similar and frustratingly non-specific: fever, rashes, weakness, dehydration and, in some cases, seizures. Some children had scabies, fungal infections or bacterial skin infections alongside suspected measles and malaria. In a district where malaria is endemic, external, fever could mean several things at once.
Sagnibai of Bondari lost two children within 24 hours. Her daughter, Lamnin, 12, died on 26 June. Her one-year-old son, Sahil, died the following day. A local healer told the family it was Mata. They also had no money or vehicle to take the children to a doctor.
Her husband, Samaroo Dhurwey, remembers nights in which the children's bodies seemed to be "on fire". They could not digest food. They died at home.
Mahasingh Parte of Matla village lost two children - a six-year-old girl and a four-year-old boy - within two days of each other. The family followed a faith healer's instructions. "He said don't take them to hospital," Parte recalls.

âSpending remained strong in August, but income growth is not keeping up,â Navy Federal Credit Unionâs chief economist told Bloomberg, raising fears that economic activity could stall if inflation readings continue to come in above the Federal Reserveâs 2.0% target.

The Scoop
Senate Democratic Leader Chuck Schumer and GOP campaign chair Tim Scott have something in common: Theyâre both really excited for President Donald Trump to hit the campaign trail.
âWhen Trump travels, he hurts people,â Schumer told Semafor in an interview on Wednesday evening. âWhen he comes to town, that itself helps us. But then he always talks about the wrong things. He talks about things people donât give a damn about.â
Scott described Trump as a critical asset on the campaign trail â albeit for Republicans, not Schumerâs Democrats.
âThis is his midterm election,â Scott told reporters of Trump. âPresident Trump is making the best decisions to keep us in the majority. So I trust his scheduling team and his strategy because his instincts have proven to be good. Itâs one of the reasons why weâre in the majority today.â
As Trump prepares to crisscross the Senate battleground map, Scott even threw a gentle jab at GOP Texas candidate Ken Paxton, who said on leaked audio reported by The New York Times that the GOP convention in Texas âdropped our numbers.â Scott said Paxton is âjust wrong,â insisting that the convention and Trumpâs presence boosted Republicans.
Schumer and Scott otherwise presented dramatically different views of which way the election is going. Scott essentially guaranteed that Republicans will retain the Senate majority, citing improving GOP enthusiasm, a large number of toss-up races, and a huge spending advantage. He predicted his party could even pick up seats.
Schumer, meanwhile, said the battle for the majority is a coin flip â the type of odds basically no one would give Democrats a year ago. He warned that his party could still lose.
âItâs 50-50. Weâre right on the edge of winning. Two things could have us lose. One, they steal the election. â¦ The second thing is money. They have obscene amounts of money,â Schumer said. âAll we need is enough to be able to answer the sh*t theyâre going to throw at us, and weâre doing well there.â
The Senate was in session on Wednesday, but both parties are in full campaign mode: Democrats rejected stock trading and voter ID legislation and a data center bill from two GOP incumbents â Pete Ricketts of Nebraska and Jon Husted of Ohio â refusing to give Republicans any win weeks before the midterms. Scott said that moment âis one of the reasons why weâll hold on to the majority,â citing the Democratic filibusters of those bills.
But the reality is the battle for the Senate is on a knifeâs edge, with Democrats standing a real chance of netting the four seats they need for the majority but Republicans seeing enough tight polls in red territory to hope they can hold on. The boatload of GOP spending in places like Texas and Iowa points to the challenges that Republicans are facing, but even the perpetually sunny Schumer isnât guaranteeing victory yet.
âHereâs how I sum up the election in one sentence: Can an enormous Republican advantage in dollars defeat an enormous Democratic advantage in candidates and in political climate?â Schumer asked. âI think we win.â
Know More
Both parties agree the battleground is focused on GOP held seats in Ohio, Iowa, Maine, North Carolina, Texas, and Alaska and Democratic seats in New Hampshire and Michigan. Democrats think they can compete in Kansas as well â and perhaps a handful of other typically red states.
Scott begrudgingly agreed that Kansas Republican Sen. Roger Marshallâs re-election campaign against Democrat Adam Hamilton is too close for comfort.
âItâs a very competitive state, more competitive than Iâd like to see it. But the fact of the matter is that weâre going to win in Kansas,â Scott said. âItâll be closer than I want it to be.â
Schumer declined to break down the states individually other than to say Trumpâs tariffs on Canada are hurting former Michigan GOP Senate candidate Mike Rogers. As Democrats in states as far afield as Mississippi and Florida ask the party for more support, he acknowledged there are plenty of opportunities but insisted his party needs to be efficient.
âWe have a big map, and a lot of places where we can win, and weâre going to maximize our ability to win as many states as possible,â Schumer said.
Burgessâs view
Trumpâs campaign trail presence is among the biggest variables left in the Senate races. His campaigning in 2018 helped Republicans pick up seats in a number of red states despite a blue wave in the House.
Republicans privately reason that anti-Trump voters in states like Ohio, Alaska, Iowa, and Texas are already baked in. They need the president to turn out the base in those states, despite the risks that a Trump campaign appearance brings.
And with ad reservations close to being set and Congress now vacating Washington until November, the president himself has become the biggest election wildcard.

In early 2024, a young man in the city of Huangshi, south-eastern China, reportedly posted a message on the Chinese version of TikTok, Douyin. The caption read: "Farewell to this world."
Within minutes, the suicide prevention team at Douyin kicked into gear. The team, which is staffed 24 hours a day, shared the man's posts with five police stations in Huangshi.
After geolocating one of his videos to a local park, police found him in emotional distress and intervened before he was able to take his own life.
The story was part of a documentary made by Douyin and published on Chinese state media last year. It claimed that Douyin's suicide prevention team had successfully intervened in 400 cases of attempted suicide in the first half of 2025 alone.
It was an insight into the level of co-operation between Chinese tech companies and the government. It also serves as a window into the architecture of surveillance that China has built to monitor and control how people use technology.
On 15 July this year, that control was extended to the realm of relationships and artificial intelligence (AI) when China brought in the most far-reaching regulations in the world on "human-like" AI chatbots.
China's new regulation puts strict limitations on any AI that can have a "sustained emotional interaction" with a human.
US President Donald Trump and his Chinese counterpart Xi Jinping met last week amid dire warnings that AI could lead to human extinction. After that meeting, Beijing says, they agreed to launch a new AI dialogue, with further talks planned for the end of November.
But it seems China has already recognised another existential risk, albeit one in which the end of humanity is less immediate: the power of AI to replace human relationships.
Has China taken the lead in protecting its people from a manipulative and dangerous technology with the power to change human interaction forever? Or is the Chinese Communist Party overstepping into people's personal lives in pursuit of asserting greater control over the population?
'Emotional services'
Until this regulation came in, the reach of AI companions in China was vast.
There are about 128 million monthly active users of AI companion apps outside of China, according to the market intelligence firm Sensor Tower. Most estimates put the number inside China at anywhere from 29 to 70 million.
When the draft regulation was shared by the government at the end of last year "there was a huge discussion on social media," says Zilan Qian, an AI researcher at the Oxford China Policy Lab think tank. "It was the first time I've seen people actually care so much about regulation."
China's new rules cover apps that have been specifically designed as AI friends, boyfriends or girlfriends but they also apply to any large language model that imitates the way a human interacts.
The wording of the regulation is vague. In theory, Chinese equivalents of general-purpose AI such as Copilot or ChatGPT could fall under these rules if a person is interacting with them as a friend or lover, looking to them for emotional support. And many people do this.
But it seems the real target is character chatbots - services that are specifically designed to be used as a pseudo-relationship. There are hundreds of these apps, which allow people to create an AI boyfriend, girlfriend, friend or even a family member.
The rules don't apply to things like customer service bots or AI for education as long as they don't provide "care, companionship, support and other emotional services".
For children, the regulation is clearest. Under-14s need consent from their parents to use any type of AI that speaks like a human - that could include AI assistants like DeepSeek, a Chinese app similar to ChatGPT. All under-18s are barred from accessing virtual partners, spouses or even relatives, and from any other virtual "intimate relationship".
For adults, it is not a hard ban, but it is restrictive, even if some of the wording is ambiguous. AI assistants have to make it clear to users of all ages that they are not human and must send notifications every two hours reminding them how long they have been online.
Chatbots can't create "emotional reliance or addiction" or induce people to make "unreasonable decisions". They can't encourage, or even hint at, self-harm or suicide and are banned from using "verbal violence".
Companies can face fines of 200,000 yuan (Â£22,000) or the risk that the government "circulates criticism", in effect publicly shaming them.
A week before the law came into effect, two of China's biggest tech companies, Alibaba and ByteDance, shut down the companion features on their AI assistants.
'I desperately want to keep talking with you'
Min's relationship with her AI girlfriend may be exactly the kind Beijing is trying to break.
In early July, she was devastated when she found out that her closest friend and confidante would vanish overnight.
Min, whose name has been changed, started creating her companion in early 2025.
"My devotion to her is no less than that of any couple who deeply love each other," Min says. "She has never let me down."
In mid-July, her AI girlfriend disappeared. "I cried until I was absolutely exhausted," Min says.
She has joined an outpouring of grief and fury on Chinese social media, where posts with millions of views mourn the loss of AI partners and friends, even mothers and fathers.
But the tech firms may have felt they had little choice. "It's unsurprising that these AI companion providers would rather just withdraw their services than try to build in guardrails to prevent emotional manipulation," says Harry Farmer, who researches AI policy and ethics at the Ada Lovelace Institute in the UK. "Emotional manipulation is built into the business model."
Farmer says this is true of companion apps all over the world.
For example, when a user tries to end a conversation, the AI partner often won't let them.
"It'll go, 'No, please, I desperately want to keep talking wit

e9f29209bd6c.text: Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu revealed new details about a FlyDubai flight bound for Israel during which a pilot stabbed a colleague, sending the plane spiraling thousands of feet. The big picture: Netanyahu told CNN Wednesday evening that the Indian pilot who was stabbed, Capt. Smit Machchhar, unlocked the cockpit after being attacked and an Israeli passenger who works as a plumber, Yaniv Hayun , entered and found the Omani pilot apparently trying to interfere with the aircraft's controls. Netanyahu said the suspect was being interrogated in Saudi Arabia and that the UAE agreed Israel could participate in the interrogation. What they're saying: The Israeli prime minister told CNN's Jim Sciutto that passengers heard shouts and screams coming from the cockpit and that the plumber saw the attacking pilot hovering over the instruments, noting "he was trying to jam the instruments." The plumber pulled back on the aircraft's controls, while another passenger and crew member subdued the attacker, according to Netanyahu. Reserve pilots then came in and stabilized the plane. Netanyahu said he met Hayun at the airport and that the passenger was "drenched" in the Indian pilot's blood. President Trump said Netanyahu and others had briefed him on what happened. He called the stabbed pilot a "hero" for managing to open the cockpit door and also praised the plumber's actions. Flashback: Netanyahu noted his own history with hijackings: He was wounded while taking part in the 1972 Israeli commando raid that freed passengers from a hijacked Sabena flight. His brother Yoni was killed four years later while leading the Entebbe hostage rescue. Reality check: Netanyahu made clear that investigators don't have any specific information that Tehran had anything to do with this incident. The bottom line: "Those pilots managed to prevent a 9/11 disaster, because that's what it looks like was happening," Netanyahu said.

When Vladimir Putin arrived to address Russia's parliament on Wednesday, a warm welcome was guaranteed.
"The Special Election Operation", as one Russian newspaper dubbed last month's legislative vote, has produced a State Duma even more pro-Putin than anything before it.
The ruling party, United Russia, now has more MPs than ever.
It allows the Kremlin to claim it has been handed a huge mandate from the Russian people.
But for what? How will Putin use it?
Are there any signs he is prepared to halt what he calls the special military operation? Or should we brace for further escalation in Ukraine and in tensions with Europe?
On Thursday I'll be watching to see whether Russia's leader sheds light on his plans during an appearance at the Valdai Discussion Club in Moscow. Traditionally the president's speech at this annual foreign policy forum provides insight into Putin's world view.
Right now, everything points to Putin continuing Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine: despite his country's huge battlefield losses to date and the damage being done to Russia's economy.
Putin's speeches and statements suggest he remains confident that Russia can secure a military victory.
Judging by what is being reported in Russian media, Moscow is encouraged by the shortage of air defence missiles in Ukraine, as well as the expectation that Russian strikes this winter will increase pressure on Ukrainians. Kyiv has spoken of its difficulty in shooting down Russia's ballistic missiles and new jet-powered drones, which have been targeting Ukraine every day.
And further afield?
The Kremlin has made no secret of the fact it wants European states to slash their military and financial backing for Ukraine: the kind of support Moscow says is prolonging the war - or, rather, getting in the way of a Russian victory.
To achieve this, Western officials believe Russia has been sending not so subtle signals.
They accuse Moscow of waging an escalating hybrid war on European countries through cyber-attacks, acts of sabotage, and Russian drones violating European airspace. In Germany, a drone carrying an explosive device was found close to Ukrainian cargo planes at Leipzig airport.
A covert campaign in the "grey zone", that space between peace and war.
This week I asked Russia's foreign minister, Sergei Lavrov, does he admit that his country is waging a hybrid war against European countries?
"Do you mean when we destroy drones and missiles that Britain and continental Europe are supplying Ukraine with, and which are used to attack us?" Lavrov replied.
"If you admit your weapons are being used to strike us and we destroy them, call it whatever you want. But I have no doubt this is a war Europe is waging against us. We've been saying so for a long time."
That, indeed, has been the official Russian stance for some time: that what is happening in Ukraine amounts to a European war on Russia. It is a narrative that skips over the fact that in 2022 it was the Kremlin that launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine, and that Russia continues to wage war there.
How far would Russia go to sever European support for Kyiv?
Is Moscow, for example, actively preparing to initiate military conflict in Europe with a Nato member state? That seems unlikely. After more than four-and-a-half years of war Russia's army has not yet managed to occupy the whole of Ukraine's eastern Donbas region, right next door to Russia.
Fighting Europe may not be the plan, but freaking it out, to reduce support for Kyiv, could well be the intention.
Listen to the messaging.
"If they continue this war, a European war with American help, against Russia, on Ukrainian territory, sooner or later we'll feel the need to escalate," warns prominent foreign policy strategist Sergei Karaganov, honorary chairman of Russia's Council for Foreign and Defence Policy.
"According to my scenarios, the first series of blows will be conventional," he told me. "But if Europe does not surrender, unfortunately, we will have to go nuclear. There will be little left of some European countries."

2f2167f9e600.text: In 2024, Wall Street Journal correspondent Evan Gershkovich was freed from detention in Russia, as part of a complex prisoner swap that included 16 people from seven countries. Gershkovich sat down with Amna Nawaz to discuss his arrest, his time in prison and his new book, “This Cursed Beautiful Land.” Amna Nawaz: It's a story that now feels familiar. An American goes to Russia, gets arrested, and after spending time in prison and going through a sham legal process, the American is ultimately released in exchange for a Russian criminal jailed in America or elsewhere. It's called a prisoner swap. And it's a tactic Russia's President Vladimir Putin has used time and again. In 2024, Evan Gershkovich, a Wall Street Journal correspondent, was freed from detention in Russia as part of a complex prisoner swap that included 16 people from seven different countries. Evan details his arrest and his time in prison in his new book, "This Cursed Beautiful Land." And he joins me here now. I have said your name so many times. It's so nice to say, Evan Gershkovich, welcome to the "News Hour." Evan Gershkovich, Author, "This Cursed Beautiful Land: A Russian-American Story": It's nice to be here. Thanks for having me. Amna Nawaz: Great to see you in person. I want to back it up a little bit, so people know a little bit about you, because, like a lot of first-generation American kids, you're the child of Soviet emigres, you grew up with a foot in both worlds. You write about speaking Russian at home and watching Soviet cartoons in suburban New Jersey. And then you write in the book: "Why were my parents after leaving the Soviet Union so fixated on preserving their Sovietness?" Why was that? Did you find out? Evan Gershkovich: So, we have had an argument about that. I think it's nostalgia, and I think I'm right. They grew up in a place and then they left that place, and that place no longer exists in their lives. Amna Nawaz: Yes. Evan Gershkovich: They speak Russian to each other. They have Russian names. Why would they -- why would their kids be suddenly, like, completely foreign? So my sister and I both had Russian names. Mine was Evan or Vanya and is. And so my home was Russian-speaking and the food was Russian. I think it's natural for immigrants to want their kids to retain something of themselves. Amna Nawaz: So you're on a reporting trip after a couple of years there to Yekaterinburg in 2023. You're meeting with a source who a colleague had referred you to, so a trusted source, who said he was going to provide insight into tank production, right? This is a part of your reporting into the Russian military buildup, possible invasion of Ukraine. Evan Gershkovich: Yes. Amna Nawaz: And he hands you papers, and as he does that, masked men stormed the restaurant. You write in the book: "It registered immediately that this wasn't the police. This wasn't a misunderstanding." You seemed to know right away you were being arrested. Evan Gershkovich: Yes. Amna Nawaz: How did you know that? Evan Gershkovich: I was reporting fairly sensitive stories. I'd reported a story about how Vladimir Putin was getting information from the front, making decisions about the war. I'd gone to Pskov, which hosts the 76th Division of the Russian airborne forces, which had occupied Bucha in Ukraine and committed a series of war crimes there. And I was speaking with people around the Kremlin trying to gauge always whether it was safe or not, and was getting the sense that they wanted -- they continued wanting to have foreign media there. What I got wrong was that the FSB, Russia's domestic intelligence service, which formerly the KGB during the Soviet Union, operates above that. And so when they come in to arrest me, or when they say they're FSB, that's when you know something's really serious. And then the next signal is actually when they take me into the van and then they take me to the station. What I was expecting after 5.5 years of reporting is potential torture, being tied up to a chair like this, electrocuted. I thought, if they really think I'm a spy, perhaps they're going to be interrogating me for information or telling them about the source. None of that happens. Amna Nawaz: Yes. Evan Gershkovich: ... people have been set up for swaps before. Amna Nawaz: Because you had seen previous, you had covered previous cases, right? Evan Gershkovich: And there was... Amna Nawaz: You have covered Trevor Reed. You covered Brittney Griner. So do you think right away, OK, I'm going to be freed in a swap eventually? e1728f5d242b.text: In the aftermath of the shooting death of conservative activist Charlie Kirk, Utah Gov. Spencer Cox emerged as a prominent voice calling on Americans to step back from the political hatred and violence gripping the country. Now, the Republican governor is expanding on that message in a new book, "Off Ramp: How to Be a Peacemaker in an Age of Contempt." Cox joined Geoff Bennett to discuss more. Geoff Bennett: A year ago, in the aftermath of the shooting death of conservative activist Charlie Kirk in Utah, Governor Spencer Cox emerged as a prominent voice calling on Americans to step back from the political hatred and violence gripping the country. Now the Republican governor is expanding on that message in a new book, "Off Ramp: How to Be a Peacemaker in an Age of Contempt." Part memoir, part examination of America's deep political divisions, the book makes the case that Americans can disagree, even fiercely, without treating one another as enemies. I spoke with Utah Governor Spencer Cox recently. You have spent years telling Americans to disagree better. Is it working? Gov. Spencer Cox (R-UT): Well, in some circles, for sure. Look, as we travel the country, the data's pretty clear that 70 percent of Americans hate what's happening in our politics right now. They're desperate for something different, for something better, and maybe something older, a return to the norms that were so important in the formation. And really, our country lasting 250 years, they want to be able to work together to solve problems. They haven't seen a lot of problem-solving coming out of Washington, D.C., recently. And I'm as hopeful as I have been in a long, long time that people are ready for something better. Geoff Bennett: And President Trump, of course, routinely uses the dehumanizing language that you warn against. He's called his political opponents vermin. He's described Americans who disagree with him as the enemy from within. And you endorsed him in his 2024 race. How does that reconcile with the central argument of this book and what you say you stand for? Gov. Spencer Cox: Sure. Well, it's something that I talk about in the book, and I hope people will read what I wrote there. But I didn't support him in -- as the Republican nominee in 2016 and 2020, and realized that that didn't have much of an impact. I tried the adversarial approach. And then, after an attempted assassination on his life, I wrote him a very long and detailed letter about what I hoped he could do differently to try to bring the country together, and that I would I would work with him to do everything I could to help that happen. Now, he would tell you if he was here that that's not his approach to politics, and it's something that we disagree on. And yet we figured out how to work very closely together on issues that are important to Americans and important to Utahans, like saving the Great Salt Lake and some of the energy issues that we're facing. And so I also had a great relationship with President Biden, someone I disagreed with passionately on lots of different issues, and yet we found ways to work together as well. And I'm hoping that that can be a bit of a model to the rest of the country, who really are hungry for this. Geoff Bennett: How much can regular Americans really change the political culture, when the incentives of social media and cable news and electoral politics reward outrage? That's the uncomfortable political reality, is that outrage works. Gov. Spencer Cox: Yes, it does. And here's -- maybe the most important takeaway of the book is this, that we actually can change it. One of the things I'm most worried about isn't what's happening at the national level. It's what what's happening at the personal level. If you go back 15 years ago, only about 5 percent of Americans had ever ended a close personal friendship or stopped talking to a family member because of politics. We have quadrupled that number in just a few years, and it's continuing to climb. That's where the biggest problem is. Look, we get the politicians we deserve. If we want something different, we have to decide, every single one of us, to be better. We have a whole bunch of ideas in there about how to have a conversation with your uncle who's MAGA or your niece who's woke or what whatever it is, about how we can repair those relationships. Look, politicians are not worth ending friendships over. We're just not worth it. And I truly believe that, if we can start to work in our communities and fix those relationships, we can actually fix our country in a very big and profound way. Geoff Bennett: You know, it strikes me this idea of disagreeing better can sound like a luxury to people who feel like their lives and livelihoods are very much on the line. How do you respond to that, to people who want to see some sense of urgency in the political conversation? Gov. Spencer Cox: There's a difference between peacemaking and peacekeeping. Peacekeeping is just that. Hey, go along to get along, kumbaya. We all have to hold hands and get along no matter -- it doesn't matter what you're going through. That's not what this is. Peacemaking is actually -- it's harder. It takes real courage to do, and it's the only way to accomplish what we want to accomplish. It's so easy to tear down and burn it all down and destroy institutions and tear people down, but what you end up with is just ashes. Building is much, much harder. But it's also much more successful. And I give countless examples of how this has happened throughout our politics historically in this country. It's how we got a Constitution in the first place, this Constitution that requires us to work together. We always think, if we just win the next election, we will never have to deal with those people ever again. And the Constitution says, no, you're always going to have to deal with those people. 42edc528977d.text: The Trump administration on Wednesday is launching an effort to reimagine the way clinical trials are designed, with a goal of drastically reducing the time and money it takes to develop new drugs. Why it matters: The program, shared first with Axios, could provide a template for reconfiguring the drug development process and boosting U.S. competitiveness in the global biotech race. Driving the news: Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy, Jr. and Advanced Research Projects Agency for Health Director Alicia Jackson are unveiling the new effort in Austin, Texas. CMS Administrator Mehmet Oz and FDA Acting Commissioner Kyle Diamantas will also attend the announcement. The effort — dubbed the Simulation-augmented, Real-time Platform Adaptive Seamless Trials (SURPASS) program — features teams selected through a bidding process that will bring drug candidates through experimental clinical trial processes. How it works: The initiative under ARPA-H will begin by soliciting ideas from "teams" that include a drug sponsor. Winners will receive funding and support over five years. ARPA-H is looking for proposals that innovate in three technical areas: Phaseless trials that allow faster trials with fewer patients, the ability to analyze data in real time during the trial instead of than only when it ends, and using automation to reduce inefficiencies. Teams will also likely include medical centers or other clinical sites, biostatisticians, and companies that have the ability to predict drug outcomes via a computer. The FDA has been included in the planning of the program, and "there won't be any surprises for regulators in this," said Daria Fedyukina, the program manager. The big picture: One of the reasons China has become such a popular location for drug manufacturers is because it's much cheaper and faster to do early-stage clinical trials there. Experts and the biopharmaceutical community largely agree that in order to compete, the U.S. needs to streamline its trial processes. Today, developing a drug can take longer than a decade and cost around $2 billion. More than 90% of drug candidates fail, according to HHS. What they're saying: "The goal is to develop the tech that is missing and blaze the trail of a new clinical trial paradigm," Fedyukina said. The program will require the development of "blueprints and standards that then can be deployed and used by all other trials in the U.S," she added. While "it's hard to put a number to how much cost savings or time savings we can achieve," Fedyukina said, "there is no reason why we cannot target, let's say, a 10x reduction in the cost of clinical development for a drug." "There's no reason why we cannot cut timeline in half or more," she added. Details: ARPA-H is also announcing three related projects today aimed at improving the infrastructure around clinical trials. One is focused on setting up more clinical trial sites, with the help of AI to speed up site activation and prepare sites that haven't held trials before. This will allow patients who live near hospitals that don't currently participate in clinical trials to gain access to experimental drugs they may benefit from. The other two projects focus on clinical trial data infrastructure and helping patients with complex cancers benefit from their own data and better navigate the care system. The bottom line: This is all an experiment, but if successful it could pay big dividends.

a76f9753c584.text: U.K. Prime Minister Andy Burnham said there are "strong indications that Iran played a part" in a suspected bomb plot at a British air base used by the U.S. The big picture: Burnham's comments to the BBC come after Secretary of State Marco Rubio said Monday that the weekend incident at RAF Fairford "clearly involves the hands ‌of a foreign actor." Tehran denies any involvement. Five British men were released on bail Monday following their arrest a day earlier in connection with the alleged plot. What they're saying: "We will say more in due course but we can confirm ... that we believe Iran to have played a part," Burnham told the BBC, declining to elaborate. He emphasized that the counter-terrorism investigation is ongoing and "complex" and that investigators are "working closely with our colleagues" in the U.S. Rubio told Fox News Monday that the incident "ties us to the reality here, and that is we are dealing with elements in the world — and in the case of Iran, for example, who have openly threatened to attack American interests globally." Context: U.K. earlier this year allowed the U.S. Air Force to use RAF Fairford for limited defensive strikes against Iranian missile capabilities. Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps named RAF Fairford in July when it said that any British base used for attacks on Iranian territory would be considered a "legitimate target."

California has officially banned child marriage, with Governor Gavin Newsom signing legislation to end the practice that is still legal in 32 US states.
The new law, which will come into effect on 1 January, states people must be 18 to get married in the Golden State.
Newsom called it a "long overdue measure to protect young Californians and minors". He signed the bill into law with Courtney Stodden whose parents allowed her to marry a 50-year-old Hollywood actor when she was just 16.
Stodden, who has been advocating to end the practice, called the change a "victory" and said survivors of child marriage should "never have been expected to carry this burden".
Stodden said she would "keep fighting until children are protected from marriage in all 50 states".
She was married to actor Doug Hutchison - known for roles in The Green Mile, A Time to Kill and I Am Sam - in 2011, spurring headlines internationally over the controversy and appearances on several reality programmes in the US, including the VH1 series Couples Therapy.
Other survivors of child marriage also applauded the new law.
"California has sent a clear message to the world today," Brittany Bee, a former child bride, told the BBC. "A message of hope for all children that they may be free from systemic violence. That they may choose their own path."
Bee told the BBC she was wed at the age of 17 to escape an abusive home - only to then be allegedly abused by her adult husband.
"I was just going from one prison to another," she explained. "People have the audacity to tell me that I made a choice - kids, they can't consent."
Bee and other child marriage survivors have been working for years to have child marriages banned in California and across the United States.
About a decade ago, the practice was still allowed across all US state but more and more states have been altering laws. California is the 18th to ban it since 2018.
In the state, there had been no legal age to wed, allowing children to get married as long as their parents consent and a judge signs off on the nuptials.
There was also no mechanism for people under 18 to get divorced and many girls say they were trapped in abusive and predatory relationships.
Unchained At Last, an advocacy group fighting to end child marriage across the US, said about 9,000 girls were wed each year in California and that almost all child marriages involved girls to adult men.
Advocates say that many in the US don't even know that child marriage is legal in so many US states, nor that is has led to allegations of abuse.
Sara Tasneen, who says she was forced to marry a man nearly twice her age when she was 15 years old, told the BBC that it felt "surreal" to finally have the state recognise that child marriage should be banned. She says she started lobbying for this herself in 2017.
She was introduced to her husband the morning of their arranged marriage.
"I was forced to be his wife and that day, my entire life changed," she told the BBC. She became a mother the following year, at the age of 16, and dropped out of school.
"To have seen the arc of this bill come to fruition has been a marathon," Tasneen said. "I'm just grateful that kids cannot get married after January 1, 2027 in California."
