A pilot has been arrested after he stabbed the other pilot on a flight from Dubai to Tel Aviv and "apparently tried to crash the plane", Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has said.
Passengers and crew overpowered the attacker and retook control of the Flydubai aircraft, landing it safely at an airport in Tabuk, northwestern Saudi Arabia, with more than 170 people on board.
The passengers, who were almost all Israeli, arrived later on Wednesday in Tel Aviv on a repatriation flight.
The stabbed pilot, named as Indian national Captain Smit Machchhar, has been taken to hospital but is reported to be in a stable condition. Netanyahu and India's leader Narendra Modi praised him as a "hero".
"Despite being stabbed and seriously injured, he fought back, resisted, opened the cockpit door, and enabled passengers and crew to overpower the attacker â preventing a catastrophic mid-air disaster," Netanyahu wrote on X.
"He saved the lives of 174 people, including Israeli citizens and other nationals."
The Indian embassy in Saudi Arabia said Machchhar was in a stable condition in hospital.
Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi praised the pilot's actions, writing on X: "In the face of the gravest danger and despite being seriously injured, he showed immense courage and an unwavering resolve to protect the lives of others.
"India is proud of Captain Machchhar."
No motive for the incident has been given and the pilot was under investigation in Saudi Arabia, Netanyahu told Fox News on Wednesday night, before he was expected to be taken back to the United Arab Emirates (UAE), where the flight took off from.
Israel was "likely" to contribute to the investigation, the prime minister added.
US President Donald Trump said he had spoken with Netanyahu following the incident, saying it seemed as though the attacker was "perhaps a terrorist" or there were other reasons behind the attack.
Israeli Defence Minister Israel Katz has also called it an "attempted jihadist terror attack", without giving any details.
Flydubai's flight FZ1073 took off from Dubai International Airport in the UAE at 03:05 GMT (07:05 local time), en route to Ben-Gurion Airport in Israel.
Around two and a half hours into its journey, data from flight tracking website Flightrader24 reported a rapid descent over Saudi Arabia, dropping more than 17,000 feet (over 5,000m) in less than two minutes.
Minutes later, the plane signalled an emergency code - squawk 7700 - before switching it to a squawk 7500 code reporting a hijacking.
Around 20 minutes after these codes were signalled, the plane looped back into Saudi Arabia, where it later started its manual descent for landing.
Less than an hour later, the plane returned to squawk 7700.
Shortly after the incident, the Israeli and Saudi Arabian air forces dispatched fighter jets, while Netanyahu held urgent consultations.
Initial media reports suggested a fight had broken out between the aircraft's two pilots, causing the rapid descent and landing.
However, in the hours after the plane touched down in Tabuk, eyewitness accounts and a statement by Netanyahu confirmed one of the pilots had stabbed the other and, according to the Israeli prime minister, "apparently tried to crash" the aircraft.
He said an Israeli passenger told him "the plane went into a spin and began to descend" before the passenger and a crew member entered the cockpit and overpowered the "pilot who had carried out the stabbing".
Two on-duty crew travelling on the flight were then able to land the plane safely, Flydubai said.
In an address on Wednesday evening, Netanyahu called the situation "a very serious security incident" and said Israeli security forces were "maintaining close contact with the relevant authorities to ensure the continued safety of the passengers".
Unlike Israel's defence minister, Netanyahu did not give a motive for the incident.
"I salute these heroes who demonstrated extraordinary resourcefulness and courage," he added. "They saved many lives and prevented a major disaster."
Flydubai said in a statement that "an altercation occurred in the flight deck" and the flight was "successfully secured by on-duty Flydubai crew travelling on the flight, who diverted and landed the aircraft safely at Tabuk airport".
An airline spokesperson added: "Our immediate priority is to ensure the ongoing safety, health, and wellbeing of all passengers and crew members involved in this incident and support the official investigation."
The passengers who had been on board flight FZ1073 arrived in Tel Aviv at around 18:40 local time (15:40 GMT). They were greeted at the airport by crowds of onlookers playing music, singing, dancing and waving Israeli flags.
A number of people were "very emotional and crying as they came off the plane," a paramedic from Israel's ambulance service told the BBC.
One passenger, Yaniv Hayun, met Netanyahu and told him how he and others on the flight had restrained the attacker.
"The pilot who was stabbed was simply very close to the door, so it was hard for us to open it," Hayun said in a video posted on social media by the prime minister's office, but before the stabbed pilot - now identified as Machchhar - collapsed, he was able to open the door.
Yaniv said he put the attacker, who was trying to disable the plane, in a chokehold before other passengers helped pin him down.
He added that he "pulled the controls" of the plane and after it levelled out, another pilot took over control.
Zvika Meness, another passenger, told Israeli public broadcaster Kan News that he and other passengers tied the attacker up "with his own zip ties and with the multimedia headphones".
He said: "There are children and families here who have been through a very severe, highly traumatic event."

a40df220edfd.text: Exhausted GOP senators are preparing to fly home mostly empty-handed after staying in D.C. longer than expected. Why it matters: The midterm outlook is getting bleaker by the day, and Republicans have a monster to-do list for the lame-duck session that could be a last chance to capitalize on their trifecta. Between the lines: Republicans decided against breaking for an early recess last week. The biggest thing to show for it: A historic — and bipartisan — college sports package that doesn't do much for those defending their seats in November. It faces long odds in the House. 😖 Otherwise it was a week of pain: Failed votes: A vote addressing Americans' concerns about data centers driving up energy costs failed today, as did another to curb congressional stock trades and enforce voter IDs. A line of attack that backfired: A major hearing with Jack Smith was overshadowed by a failed attempt by Sen. Eric Schmitt (R-Mo.) to link the special counsel and Atlanta prosecutor Fani Willis. The Trump issue: Republicans have been tiptoeing around whether Trump's unpopularity will hurt the party in November, only for Texas nominee Ken Paxton to be caught blaming Trump's midterm convention for hurting his polling. NRSC Chair Tim Scott (R-S.C.) said Paxton's analysis was "just wrong" and called the convention "a boost in the right direction." 🤕 Zoom out: Some of the GOP senators are returning to fresh campaign headaches. Sen. Susan Collins (R-Maine) lost a week of in-state campaigning and didn't even get a vote on one of her key priorities: a bipartisan bill to lower insulin costs. Sen. Pete Ricketts (R-Neb.) is the target of a new ad campaign hitting him over his pardon of a man who pleaded guilty to first-degree sexual assault. Sen. Roger Marshall (R-Kan.) has been batting down accusations that he went after mothers of new babies over unpaid medical bills. His lawyers sent a cease-and-desist letter to his opponent — Rev. Adam Hamilton — on Monday. The GOP has a cash advantage , but the campaign apparatus now has to spend heavily in states Trump handily won in 2024 — Ohio, Iowa, Alaska, Texas, Kansas, Nebraska and Florida. ‼️ The other side: Former Rep. Mary Peltola (D-Alaska) was also hit with a damaging report from the New York Times about her personal behavior and office culture (some of which she denied). She is challenging GOP Sen. Dan Sullivan. What to watch: The Senate will return in November staring down a list of must-pass items. Fund the government Pass the National Defense Authorization Act Reinstate FISA Section 702, the warrantless wiretap authority Pass the farm bill 💰 The bottom line: That's just what they must get done. There's also a growing list of maybe-to-dos, like: Take a whack at a bipartisan permitting reform bill that finally came together hours before the Senate took off for home. Pass some form of AI guardrails. Raise the debt ceiling, potentially through reconciliation.

Plummeting Israel flight like 'rollercoaster', says passenger
A passenger on board Flight FZ1073, which fell 17,000ft (5,200m) in less than two minutes when a pilot apparently stabbed his co-pilot, told the BBC about his experience.
The aircraft had been flying to Israel when the incident took place, which Almog Itali described as feeling like a "rollercoaster".

Watch: What we know after Christa Pike survived two lethal injections
Tennessee death row inmate Christa Pike has been taken to hospital after her heart was still beating following two lethal injections during her execution, her lawyer says.
Her legal team filed an emergency motion to halt the convicted murderer's execution as it was happening, saying: "Ms Pike has lost consciousness and still has a heartbeat and is audibly snoring."
One of her attorneys told the BBC that Pike, 50, was "being provided life-saving measures" in hospital after two syringes of pentobarbital had been administered on Wednesday.
Pike was sentenced to death in 1996 for the murder of 19-year-old Colleen Slemmer.

A Michael Jordan jersey from his 'Last Dance' season has sold for $12.3m (Â£9.3m), a record for a piece of Jordan memorabilia.
The jersey was worn in game three of the 1998 NBA Finals in his last season with the Chicago Bulls.
Jordan helped the Bulls win the series 4-2 for his sixth and final NBA Championship. He was named Finals' Most Valuable Player in all six.
The previous record for a piece of Jordan memorabilia was $10.1m (Â£7.6m) for his jersey from game one of the 1998 Finals.
The jersey was put up for sale by entrepreneur Ryan Gough and sold at Joopiter, Pharrell Williams' digital auction house, which gave it an estimated price of $10-15m (Â£7.5-Â£11.3m).
Jordan's 1997 Ferrari 550 Maranello was sold for $2.7m (Â£2m), four times the auction record for that model.
"Few objects in the history of sport embody greatness as completely as Michael Jordan's game three jersey from the 1998 NBA Finals," Joopiter said in the auction posting.
"Worn during the Last Dance... it marks the culmination of an era that transformed basketball into a global cultural phenomenon.
"Today it stands among the most important game-worn sports artifacts ever to come to market."
The record price for a piece of game-worn sports memorabilia is the jersey worn by baseball legend Babe Ruth when he "called the shot" during the 1932 World Series, which was sold for $24.1m (Â£18.2m) in 2024.

Prominent Zimbabwean businessman Wicknell Chivayo and his wife have been killed in a helicopter crash that left six people dead, his family have confirmed.
The helicopter came down in the Marondera rural area, about 70km (43 miles) east of the capital, Harare, on Wednesday evening. Police said all six people on board died.
Family spokesperson Herbert Chivayo confirmed the deaths of the businessman and his wife Lucy Muteke to state broadcaster ZBC, saying the family was devastated by the tragedy.
Chivayo was known for his lavish lifestyle, close ties to some African presidents and lucrative government contracts that had repeatedly attracted scrutiny.
He had denied allegations of wrongdoing linked to his business dealings.
Police spokesperson Commissioner Paul Nyathi said the aircraft crashed at about 17:00 local time (15:00 GMT) and had six occupants, but authorities did not immediately identify all those on board. Two of the six were pilots, according to government officials.
ZBC reported that the group was travelling from Gandami in Chikomba, where Chivayo and his wife were building a rural home, when the helicopter crashed at Kudenga Farm about 40 minutes after take-off.
"We are at a loss for words after the tragic news," the family spokesperson, told the ZBC.
The cause of the crash was not immediately known, and police said investigations were under way. Emergency services were sent to the scene on Wednesday evening.
Earlier, government spokesman Nick Mangwana confirmed the crash, saying the helicopter was carrying "a prominent businessman, three other passengers and two pilots".
"Current information indicates that there were no survivors in this crash," Mangwana posted on X.
Chivayo was the managing director of Intratrek Zimbabwe and had built a high public profile through government contracts, philanthropy and displays of wealth on social media.
Among his best-known business ventures was a $172m (Â£128m) solar power project in Gwanda awarded to Intratrek by the state-owned Zimbabwe Power Company. The project became the subject of years of legal disputes.
He also came under scrutiny over the procurement of materials for Zimbabwe's disputed 2023 elections. Zimbabwe's anti-corruption commission investigated allegations surrounding contracts awarded to South African company Ren-Form but closed the inquiry in 2025, saying it had found no evidence linking Chivayo or the Zimbabwe Electoral Commission to wrongdoing.
Widely known as "Sir Wicknell", Chivayo frequently used the title publicly and on social media, although he was never given a British knighthood.
He was also known for giving away luxury cars and large sums of money to musicians, religious leaders and other public figures, often publicising the gifts on social media.
His connections extended beyond Zimbabwe.
Kenya's President William Ruto, who had previously appeared in public with Chivayo, paid tribute to him as a "dear friend" and sent condolences to the families of those killed.
"I will remember him for his friendship, his energy and his deep conviction in the possibilities of our continent," Ruto added.
Kenyan opposition figures had questioned Chivayo's repeated access to Ruto and State House.
He frequently publicised his access to African leaders, posting photographs of meetings with presidents including Zambia's Hakainde Hichilema, South Africa's Cyril Ramaphosa and Tanzania's Samia Suluhu Hassan, as well as Eswatini's King Mswati III.

0a5e1073e5cb.text: Immigration — the issue that helped propel Donald Trump to the presidency and rally his supporters over the past decade — has become an afterthought for voters. Why it matters: It's another ominous sign for Trump and the GOP heading toward November. What was once a rallying cry for the party is losing salience with voters across the spectrum — and harsh crackdowns have even made it a liability among some Republicans. "On net, Republicans win out as the more trusted party on only two topics, and it's border/immigration [and] crime and safety," said Avery James of Echelon Insights, a Republican polling firm. "But the problem if you're a campaign strategist is quite simple: crime and immigration are just not the top issues for voters." The big picture: Just two years ago, immigration was a top concern for voters nationwide, especially self-identified Republicans. After President Biden dropped his reelection bid, the GOP spent half its advertising budget on immigration-related ads, per an AdImpact analysis . "If you ask [about] immigration as an overall issue that people care about, it went from like a top three issue two years ago to way down the list now, in single digits," said Erik Iverson, a GOP pollster working with the Republican Senate campaign arm. Between the lines: Pollsters say concern about immigration peaked during Biden's tenure, when illegal border crossings and asylum seekers at the Southern border surged. But weeks into Trump's term, crossings dropped dramatically after he deployed the U.S. military at the border, instituted a ban on asylum claims and paused refugee admissions. "You become a victim of your own success," Iverson said. Zoom in: Cost of living ranks as the top issue for voters, far outpacing immigration. That's especially bad news for Republicans trying to turn out voters in competitive statewide races. More than half of Texas Republicans and one-quarter of independents said border security and immigration was Texas's most important problem about one year ago, according University of Texas poll . Its latest survey, conducted in August, shows that figure cut in half. In Michigan, only 14% of all voters said it was their top issue in a survey for AARP co-conducted by Trump pollster Fabrizio Ward. A September poll of Ohio voters shows a higher share concerned about immigration, 25%, when asked to name their top three issues. But it was dwarfed by a combined 70% who were most concerned about the economy and inflation. "That issue just dropped with Republicans because they weren't seeing it every day. They weren't feeling threatened by it every day," said Brent Buchanan, of Cygnal, a Republican polling firm. The intrigue: Tying immigration to the economy and cost of living still resonates with low-propensity Trump voters, according to polling Iverson recently shared with Senate Republicans. And Buchanan said that border security can still be used effectively to draw a contrast between candidates in specific races. But it's unlikely to drive turnout among what he called "soft Republicans." By the numbers: Voters are starting to sour on Trump's handling of immigration. His disapproval rating on immigration jumped to 58% in a late August survey from Ipsos, up from 38% when Trump took office last year. Stunning stat: A September New York Times/Siena poll showed Democrats are more trusted on immigration than Republicans by 51 to 45%. Most other polling, however, still shows Republicans ahead on the issue. "Everyone likes enforcement until it hits close to home or they get the wrong person. It's not necessarily the policies. It's the tactics that are turning people off. There has to be a middle ground," a former White House official said. The other side: "Americans are less concerned about immigration because President Trump stopped the invasion of our country and delivered the most secure border in American history," White House spokeswoman Lauren Bis said in a statement. "Thanks to President Trump's strong immigration enforcement policies, approximately three million illegals have left the United States and zero illegals have been released at the border in sixteen months." What they're saying: The polling trends are giving Democrats a new opening, especially in areas with sizable Hispanic populations. Republicans are "trying so hard to distance themselves from Trump on the overall immigration issue because they know it is toxic with Latino voters right now," said Stephanie Valencia, founder of the Latino-focused polling firm Equis. "Democrats should be giving Trump credit for the control and the maintenance of the U.S.-Mexico border," she said. But "at the end of the day, people are asking for a lot more than that."

Healthcare Is Scary. Channel Your Fears Into a Haiku.
Something wicked this way comes, and it’s 5-7-5.
Our annual Halloween haiku contest is back, and we’re once again summoning readers to turn the horrors of healthcare into three tiny lines of poetry. Surprise us with a verse about medical bills, insurance, hospitals, health policy, or whatever else keeps you up at night.
Whether you’re inspired by a botched surgery, a ghastly charge, or insurance-induced existential dread, we want to read about it.
Our newsroom’s panel of judges will choose their favorites, which we’ll share on our social channels. Winning haikus will be announced on Friday, Oct. 30.
Rules:
- Submit your haiku to https://kffhealthnews.org/contact-haiku/, along with the link to the related KFF Health News article.
- “Like” KFF Health News on Facebook, and follow @KFFHealthNews on X, @kffhealthnews.org on Bluesky, and @kffhealthnews on Instagram.

🎃 Follow the format of a haiku (a three-line poem with 17 syllables, written in a 5/7/5-syllable count).

The top three haikus will rise again with a custom comic illustration drawn by staff illustrator Oona Zenda. Hospitals Have a Little-Known Tool To Prevent Medical Debt. Here’s How It Works.
If you have medical debt, there’s a good chance you owe money to a hospital.
One way patients can avoid medical debt is through hospital financial assistance, also known as charity care. Most of the nation’s hospitals offer free or discounted medical care to patients with very high medical debt or low incomes.
Getting financial assistance, however, can be challenging. Many patients don’t know that hospitals offer financial help, surveys show, and complex application forms leave others stymied.
Hospitals often demand that applicants turn over bank statements, pay stubs, tax returns, divorce filings, or other materials, and submit their applications in person, by mail, or by fax.
“They don’t make it easy,” said Neale Mahoney, a Stanford University economist who studies medical debt.
Such hurdles leave many patients with unpaid bills they should never have had to pay in the first place. In a single year, hospitals and health systems billed patients for at least $2 billion that they likely didn’t owe, one analysis found.
As healthcare costs climb and more people lose their coverage, states and hospitals are testing an emerging approach to fix this problem: automatically screening patients to see if they qualify for assistance and proactively wiping out debt when they do. This is known as “presumptive eligibility.”
Under this approach, patients may have the cost of their care wiped out before they see any bills — but not always. Hospitals differ on when, how, and for whom they use auto-enrollment, potentially impinging on patients’ finances.
Here’s what you need to know about how auto-enrollment works.
What is hospital financial assistance?
In many states, hospitals set their own criteria for whom they provide financial aid. Eligibility is typically based on income for the patient’s entire household. The closer patients are to poverty, the less they have to pay. Patients with middle incomes and insurance are sometimes eligible for discounts, especially if their bills would gobble up a big chunk of what they earn.
At least 11 states require hospitals to wipe out bills for low-income patients, though income cutoffs vary. Georgia, for example, mandates free care for anyone with income slightly above the federal threshold for poverty. In several states — including Oregon, North Carolina, and Maryland — patients can earn double that amount and still get free care.
But in most states, many patients must complete applications to receive assistance.
Several states in recent years have launched investigations and passed legislation designed to make it easier for people to get help. Research into medical debt, however, suggests gaps persist.
How many hospitals use auto-enrollment?
Nearly all nonprofit hospitals say they screen and automatically reduce bills for certain patients.
Under the Affordable Care Act, nonprofit hospitals must make reasonable efforts to find people who are eligible for help before they take patients to court, sell their debt to collection agencies, or ding their credit over bills. Presumptive eligibility is one way hospitals can comply with the regulation, which took effect in 2016.
In the first year under the new rules, about 70% of tax-exempt hospitals nationwide said they screened patients and proactively reduced bills, according to an analysis of federal data for Tradeoffs by the independent research institute RTI International. As of 2022, that figure was nearly 90%.
The federal law doesn’t apply to for-profit and public hospitals, which don’t have to report the actions they take before going after patients for unpaid bills.
In six states, policymakers require hospitals to use presumptive eligibility and skip applications for certain patients. Those states are California, Delaware, Illinois, Maryland, North Carolina, and Oregon.
Who is eligible to be automatically enrolled in financial assistance?
In most states, hospitals decide which patients can skip the application.
Common groups automatically screened include people who are homeless, deceased, or already enrolled in state or federal programs to help low-income households with housing, food, or prescriptions. Other hospitals have more unique criteria, like Christus Health, which will write off bills for anyone in a religious order who took a vow of poverty.
Eligibility criteria are often buried in official policies and hard to find or decipher. Some hospitals share little to no public information about whom they will proactively screen. Thirteen hospitals owned by Ascension, one of the nation’s largest Catholic health systems, state only that they may screen patients “with a sufficient unpaid balance.”
Across the half-dozen states with presumptive eligibility mandates, eligibility rules vary. Maryland, for example, requires hospitals to proactively wipe out bills only for patients who already get government help for food or utilities but are ineligible for Medicaid. In Illinois, lawmakers created less-stringent requirements for rural hospitals compared with urban facilities.
In Oregon, starting in 2024, hospitals had to screen anyone who owed more than $500 and every patient on Medicaid or who is uninsured. In 2025, roughly 80% of Oregon patients who got financial help with bills never filled out an application, based on data shared publicly by the first 26 hospitals to do so. The state’s legislature this year raised the screening threshold to include patients who owe at least $1,500 for a single visit.
Without an application, how do hospitals figure out who gets help?
Hospitals have several ways to find patients eligible for financial assistance.
Typically, hospitals turn to public records, any information patients have previously volunteered, or tools from consumer credit companies to estimate whether patients qualify to have bills reduced.

For Europe’s fishing industry, it turns out size does matter.
Of 60,000 European-flagged fishing boats, just 638 are responsible for most of the harm, according to a new report by French non-profit BLOOM. The largest in the fleet, at 108 feet or longer, pose the greatest threat to food security, cost taxpayers the most and cause unparalleled environmental harms.
As the European Union decides how to spend its almost $8 billion fisheries budget for 2028-2034, environmentalists are calling for the dismantling of these “mega-industrial” ships.
“They’re one percent of the fleet, and they threaten 99 percent of fishers,” said Claire Nouvian, founder and director of BLOOM. “They’re a zombie industry in the sense they’re actually creating death, creating misery, creating pillage and creating injustice.”
These floating factories, capable of catching and processing hundreds of tons of fish each trip, account for 55 percent of the fish caught by European vessels. And they do so with disproportionately more ecologically impactful gear.
Indeed, 84 percent of these vessels used “towed” gear, such as bottom trawling nets or demersal seines that ensnare marine life indiscriminately, resulting in high volumes of unwanted bycatch.
“Bottom trawlers are linked to seabed abrasion, destruction of bottom habitats and the disruption of the food web,” said Léna Fréjaville, BLOOM’s head of fisheries and the report’s lead author. “There is a link between the size, the extraction capacity and the gear used,” added Fréjaville, highlighting that below 108 feet only about 17 percent of boats use this type of gear, with the vast majority of smaller vessels instead using lower-impact, passive equipment.
“Trawling has wiped out habitats for animals to feed and sleep and reproduce, and now you’ve got gravel and rubble at the bottom of the ocean,” said Nouvian, who has termed the activities of these mega-ships as “counter-fishing” because of their longer-term ecological damage.
The ships also operate outside E.U. waters, harvesting marine life, on average, 2,600 miles from their home port. With European coasts unable to sate their voracious appetite, the E.U. pays over $100 million annually for fishing rights in other nations’ coastal waters.
Often, they’re no longer fishing to feed humans: “They’re catching anything that moves to transform into money and feed,” said Nouvian, pointing to the ever-growing fishmeal and fish oil industry that depends on “absolutely pillaging [African] waters.”
Industry players have historically pushed back on these claims. The Pelagic Freezer Trawler Association—which represents eight fishing companies and at least 18 vessels ranging from 180 to 470 feet—maintains the larger vessel size is environmentally advantageous.
“The size of our freezer trawlers makes them enormously efficient and therefore sustainable for fishing. Big is therefore not always bad,” the association argues on their website. “Not the size of the vessel, but scientifically derived quotas determine how much freezer trawlers can fish,” the association added, noting that 70 percent of a ship’s capacity is usually reserved for sorting, processing and storage.
These sizable steel ships however, are also accused of squeezing small-scale fishing.
In France, artisanal fishing generates ten times more jobs than mega-trawlers when you compare them pound for pound of fish caught. Yet, over the last two decades, 80 percent of European fisheries funding has gone to industrial fleets while small-scale coastal fishers have received just one percent of the budget.
“You see the despair in ports,” said Nouvian. “Small-scale fishers are desperate. They’re really hopeless and want these boats out of their waters.”
There are now calls for the European Parliament to spend $3 billion to dismantle these boats by 2035 and refit them for other purposes, such as goods transportation. With just 2.7 percent of fisheries subsidies allocated to ocean protection since 1994, BLOOM is calling for an equal split of the remaining budget between conservation and small-scale fisheries.
Establishing a “maximum tolerable length” of 108 feet would alleviate the pressure currently placed on stocks and allow for a more equitable redistribution of quotas to coastal fishers, according to Nouvian: “Transitioning away from mega-industrial counter-fisheries towards small-scale can revitalize the ocean’s health, repopulate the ocean and increase the fish catch in the long run.”
About This Story
Perhaps you noticed: This story, like all the news we publish, is free to read. That’s because Inside Climate News is a 501c3 nonprofit organization. We do not charge a subscription fee, lock our news behind a paywall, or clutter our website with ads. We make our news on climate and the environment freely available to you and anyone who wants it.
That’s not all. We also share our news for free with scores of other media organizations around the country. Many of them can’t afford to do environmental journalism of their own. Two of us launched ICN in 2007. Six years later we earned a Pulitzer Prize for National Reporting, and now we run the oldest and largest dedicated climate newsroom in the nation. - Published
Nasa scientists are studying rocks in the Scottish Highlands to help them understand if there was once life on Mars.
The US space agency announced last year that its Perseverance rover had found potential biosignatures, markings on rocks possibly made by ancient microbes.
This summer, scientists took samples from a geological feature called the Stoer Formation, external around Clachtoll, in Assynt, in the north-west Highlands.
Nasa said the area's rocks formed in environments comparable to ancient Martian lakes and rivers, but could also hold evidence of microbial life from 1.2 billion years ago.
Clachtoll is a small crofting community on the Sutherland coast about 100 miles north of Inverness, and is a popular destination along the North Coast 500 tourist route.
Nasa's Goddard Instrument Field Team, which specialises in studying Earth's extreme environments, led the research expedition.
Experts from the universities of Glasgow and Cambridge were among those involved.
They took rock samples from cliffs for further analysis.
Nasa said: "Though Mars is dry today, the Martian landscape, like our own planet's, is shaped by an ancient history of flowing water.
"Both worlds have layered areas of mudstones and siltstones rich in clay minerals.
"Learning how signs of ancient life show up in Earth rocks like these Scottish cliffs can help us understand the story of habitability and the potential for biosignatures to be preserved and detected on Mars."
It is not the first time Scotland's ancient geology has been used by scientists to help them understand how life could have existed on Mars.
Last year, technology which will be used in the search for evidence of Martian life was tested by a University of St Andrews team at Lower Diabaig, in Torridon.
The rocks in the area are billions of years old and similar to those found on the Red Planet.
Eight years ago, a Nasa Mars rover, Curiosity, explored a part of the planet named after Torridon.
Martian geological areas and features have been named by Nasa after places on Earth.
Several of the names were taken from Scotland and, as well as Torridon, there is a Siccar Point, Muck, Wick, Sandwick and Holyrood on Mars.
Nasa chose the name Torridon due to the Torridonian Supergroup, a geological formation in the north-west Highlands that contains some of the oldest evidence of life of any rocks in the UK.
In 2012, Glenelg held a celebration in honour of a location on Mars being named after the small Highland community.

PLYMOUTH, N.C.—Fall had just arrived when a nor’easter began stewing in the Atlantic Ocean, its gale-force winds carrying the pungent smell of chlorine westward, away from downtown. Against the backdrop of dingy stratus clouds, the Domtar pulp mill loomed.
The plant occupies 2,400 acres at the confluence of Welch Creek and the Roanoke River, where logs are turned into absorbent materials used in diapers and other paper hygiene products. But those goods come at an environmental cost.
For 50 years, Domtar’s predecessor, Weyerhaeuser, discharged toxic dioxins, furans and mercury—byproducts of the bleaching process—into the Roanoke River. Scientists have found dioxins in river sediment, wood duck eggs and fish.
Federal and state regulators have now reached a tentative agreement with Domtar to restore and protect natural areas in the Roanoke River watershed. A federal court has issued a proposed consent decree and restoration plan to correct the damage that Weyerhaeuser caused.
Although Domtar isn’t responsible for the original damage, the company assumed liability for the cleanup after buying the property from Weyerhaeuser in 2007.
Fish can absorb dioxin through their gills. The contaminant accumulates in the fatty tissues of larger, predatory fish that rank higher on the aquatic food chain. Large fish eat smaller, bottom-feeding species that have consumed even tinier, contaminated organisms.
Since 1990, dioxin levels in and near the river have declined, but state health officials still recommend limiting consumption of car and catfish caught there to no more than one meal per month.
Even at very low levels, dioxin can cause reproductive and developmental problems, damage the immune system and cause cancer, according to the World Health Organization. The U.S. Environmental Protection Agency has set limits for dioxin in drinking water and requires facilities to report their releases as part of their pollution permits.
In addition to the toxic dioxin discharges, state records show Weyerhaeuser withdrew water from the river as part of the manufacturing process. Those withdrawals killed larval fish by inhaling them into cooling tanks, reducing the total number of striped bass, river herring and white perch by 100,000 each day, state and federal records show.
The Nature Conservancy in North Carolina owns and protects about 2,000 acres near Domtar. The group is reviewing the draft restoration plan and plans to submit comments, said Julie DeMeester, Freshwater and Coastal Plains director.
The Roanoke River boasts the largest intact systems of bottomland forests on the Atlantic Coast, as well as diverse populations of diadromous fish—species that travel between fresh water and salt water.
The river’s last 137 miles, which include the segment that passes Domtar, are exceptional habitat, DeMeester said, which prompted the Nature Conservancy to begin protecting the lands in 1982.
“There are many imperiled fish that use this river,” DeMeester said. “It’s truly one of the wildest remaining rivers,” with floodplains as much as five miles wide in the lower basin.
How to comment on the proposed restoration plan
The agreement between Domtar and state and federal regulators would require the paper company to fund the restoration of more than 1,000 acres of sensitive habitat along the Roanoke River.
- A proposed conservation deed restriction protecting 760 acres of Warren Neck forested wetlands. The tract provides fish nursery habitat important to the river’s health.
- Roughly $1.75 million to reconnect floodplains, protect wetlands and install water crossings and culverts to help fish passage. The project will reconnect three miles of historic stream channels to their natural flow and improve more than 600 acres of habitat.
The public can comment on the proposal through Oct. 16.
By mail: Howard Schnabolk
National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration
2234 South Hobson Avenue Charleston, SC 29405 
By phone: 854-429-2252
By email: [email protected]
“Residents of Plymouth and downstream communities deserve a healthy and clean Roanoke River,” said North Carolina Secretary of the Environment Reid Wilson. “This settlement ensures protection of fish and wildlife habitat, abundant recreational opportunities and strengthened resilience to flooding.”
Domtar did not respond to a request for comment, but issued this statement to WCTI, a television station in New Bern: “We are aware of the consent decree that has been filed and reserve further comment until the public comment period is concluded and the decree is ordered.”
The Roanoke is often overshadowed by its more well-known river peers, the Neuse and the Cape Fear, but it is equally important. The Roanoke begins in the Blue Ridge Mountains of Virginia and squiggles for 410 miles before it empties near Plymouth into the Albemarle Sound, among the largest estuaries in North Carolina.
This story is funded by readers like you.
Our nonprofit newsroom provides award-winning climate coverage free of charge and advertising. We rely on donations from readers like you to keep going. Please donate now to support our work.
Donate Now
More than 200 bird species live or breed in the Roanoke River floodplain, among them yellow-throated vireos, American redstarts and cerulean warblers. The river supports one of the most diverse fish communities in North Carolina, including striped bass, alewife and Atlantic sturgeon, which is on the endangered species list.
“It’s a lifeblood for North Carolina,” said Larry Baldwin of the North Carolina Environmental Advocacy Corps, a new nonprofit group.
The Importance of the Roanoke
Pulp and paper mills, as well as the chemical and metals industries, routinely discharged dioxin into waterways until the late 1980s, when the EPA National Dioxin study found the contaminant in fish and sediment. Those findings prompted the federal and some state governments to more closely regulate dioxin releases.
Dioxin releases have fluctuated over the last decade.

As the US hosts G20 trade ministers in Wisconsin, Canada is taking the opportunity to strengthen its ties to other countries.
US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer reiterated on Wednesday that he is in âfairly frequent contactâ with Canadian negotiators like Canada-US Trade Minister Dominic LeBlanc, adding that Washingtonâs âdoor is always openâ amid the countriesâ spiraling trade war.

Democrats are feeling newly optimistic about Texas, even in deep-red seats.
Polls shared with Semafor show Democratic candidates running surprisingly competitively in the 9th and the 10th Congressional Districts.
In the 10th, Democrat Caitlin Rourk is polling at 41% to Republican Chris Goberâs 48%, with Trumpâs favorability underwater at 50% unfavorable and 47% favorable.
Democratic Senate nominee James Talarico is also statistically tied with Republican Ken Paxton in the district, which Trump won by 22 points in 2024.
And in the 9th District (also handily carried by Trump), Democrat Leticia Gutierrez is trailing Republican Alex Mealer by six points, with Trumpâs favorability negative and the Senate race statistically tied.
Still, both Democratic candidates trail the Republicans in fundraising and are looking for more resources. Gober, the former lawyer of Elon Muskâs America PAC, might be able to call for substantial backup.
âWe have been doing the path-breaking foundational work and are ready to go exponential in the final stretch. Now, we just need the investment to go execute and win this race,â Rourk said in a statement.
The polling, shared by Democratic campaigns, could nevertheless be a warning sign for Paxton and Republican Gov. Greg Abbott.

President Donald Trumpâs decision to kick off a month of midterm campaign travel with rallies in red states like Oklahoma and Alabama has confounded some Republicans, but those involved in the plans argue thereâs a strategy behind them.
Both rally sites â Durant, Oklahoma, and Mobile, Alabama â âhit multiple states and media marketsâ because of their proximity to neighboring states, a Republican official familiar with the strategy said.
Trump officials hope to turn out low-propensity voters, particularly in close races that Republicans need to win to keep control of Congress.
The Republican official also emphasized that Trump will travel to actual battleground states like Florida, Texas, Ohio, Iowa, and Michigan.
Not everyone in Trumpâs orbit is convinced.
âI donât really buy it, but itâs a well-thought-out explanation,â one person close to the White House told Semafor. âI think they want big rallies.â

The News
Senate Republicans are departing Washington to defend their majority â and many are carrying with them real fear that the party didnât do enough to address constituentsâ economic concerns ahead of the impending election.
Despite passing a huge tax cut law last year, Republicans are fretting they have not demonstrated to voters that they are tackling high gas prices, stubborn inflation, and sky-high interest rates that threaten their House and Senate majorities come November.
âIf youâre not worried, youâre living in a cave,â Sen. Jim Justice, R-W.Va., told Semafor. âThereâs no question that thereâs people out there that are hurting.â
Justice said West Virginians love President Donald Trump but people in the Mountain State âreally probably feel like Congress deserves what they get â a 14 percent approval rate.â And if thatâs the case in a conservative state like West Virginia, it explains why Republicans are praying Trump can help turn out his voters to support the congressional GOP in the midterms.
âIf youâre sitting home without a job and you canât make ends meet â¦ at some point in time, what do you decide? You decide, âWell, I canât stand to vote for those Democrats because they got us all in this mess. But Iâm just not going to vote,ââ Justice said. âIf you lose your base, youâre in trouble, and then youâre going to have a bad outcome.â
The unease with the economy â and votersâ perception of it â is widespread across the Republican Party. Some House members desperately want the body to return to Washington to address fuel prices. And many GOP senators think the party made a mistake by not staying and working on cost-of-living issues deeper into the fall.
Battleground campaigns are largely being fought on cost-of-living and economic issues â the same challenges that cost Democrats the 2024 election just two years ago.
âIf we had done enough, our constituents wouldnât be continuing to raise it, and it wouldnât be the No. 1 thing that everyoneâs campaign is talking about,â Sen. Lisa Murkowski, R-Alaska, told Semafor.
Her colleague, Sen. Dan Sullivan, R-Alaska, is in the fight of his political life, as are Republican Sens. Susan Collins of Maine and Jon Husted of Ohio and GOP candidates in open seats in Iowa, North Carolina, and Texas. Democrats are also targeting Sens. Roger Marshall of Kansas, Darline Graham of South Carolina, and Cindy Hyde-Smith of Mississippi â all of whom are red state incumbents.
Republican leadership tried to address concerns about utility costs with a data center bill from Husted, but Democrats blocked it because its requirements were voluntary. And Sen. Rand Paul, R-Ky., prevented Marshallâs medical price transparency bill from getting a vote.
âEnding Joe Bidenâs inflation crisis has been a Day One priority for President Trump,â White House spokesperson Olivia Wales told Semafor, pointing to the tax bill as well as progress on private-sector jobs, manufacturing investments, and beef, drug, and insurance prices. He âremains laser-focused on delivering even more economic relief for American families,â she added.
But both Marshall and Husted told Semafor that they wanted Republicans to do more. Husted said voters ârightly always want us to do all we can to make their lives more affordable and thatâs exactly what we should do.â
Sen. John Kennedy, R-La., said that he wanted the Senate to stay longer, âbut there are a lot of folks that are in tight campaigns and want to go back home and campaign, and I understand that.â And while there is broad recognition of the economic challenges facing the country, there isnât exactly agreement on what to do about them.
âEveryoneâs looking for the magic bullet. Thereâs no one magic bullet here. I mean, yes, the war in Iran is not helping at all. And in my view, thatâs the first piece. But there is so much more to this,â Murkowski said.
Republicans are increasingly calling for an end to the war, a break with Trump that underscores the conflictâs unpopularity. Sen. John Cornyn, R-Texas, who was defeated in his primary by Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton, said the ânational mood is not great for us.â Paxton is struggling to defeat his Democratic opponent James Talarico in a state that rarely votes for Democrats.
âForeign wars donât typically motivate people to want to go vote. And kitchen table issues do,â Cornyn said. âAnd I certainly think the president hasnât been focused on that and has kind of deprecated the suggestion that we spent more time and effort to focus on it. So, thatâs not going to help.â
Know More
Trump signed Republicansâ signature legislation last summer, which preserved many tax cuts and enacted some new ones on things like overtime pay, tipped wages, and car interest.
âJust think what we did to put money in the pockets of working men and women,â said Senate Finance Committee Chair Chuck Grassley of Iowa, home of another tough race.
Nonetheless, Grassley is leaning on Trump to help lower fuel prices, the most visible sign of high prices.
Consumer confidence in September sank to its lowest level since 2014, The Conference Board said Tuesday, as higher oil and gas prices eclipsed more positive economic indicators.
The AI buildout, higher tariffs, and the Iran war together âhad the effect of raising the prices that consumers and businesses face,â Federal Reserve Gov. Michael Barr told the Detroit Economic Club Tuesday. âWhile the effects of tariffs may have diminished, high energy prices are still with us â and there is considerable uncertainty about when the conflict driving them may be resolved.â
The House left town two weeks before the Senate after passing bills like the data center legislation, giving lawmakers more time to campaign in their districts.

A South Korean court has handed a suspended one-year prison sentence to K-pop singer Song Min-ho after he was convicted of violating the country's military service law.
The 33-year-old member of the boy band Winner was found to have been absent multiple times at a community centre in Seoul, where he had worked as a social worker from 2023 to 2024.
All able-bodied men in South Korea have to serve at least 18 months in the military. But some are alternatively assigned as social service personnel for health reasons.
The prison sentence handed on Thursday is suspended for two years. That means he can avoid incarceration if he does not commit any crime during that two-year probationary period.
The court heard that Song, who is also known by his stage name Mino, had recorded 102 unauthorised absences during his 21-month stint as a social service agent.
Military service is a duty to be performed "faithfully", and social service agents are "no exception", the court said.
But the court also noted that Song had admitted to the charges and shown remorse.
Authorities launched an investigation into Song shortly after he was discharged in 2024, when local media reported that he was frequently absent from his social service duties and took excessive sick leave.
Song's supervisor at the social service centre was also given a suspended jail sentence for helping him dodge his duties, including falsifying records to make it look like Song had reported to work.
The conscription of South Korea's entertainers has long been a topic of national public debate.
Gangnam Style singer Psy famously had to enlist twice, once in 2003 and another time in 2007, after a Seoul court ruled that he had neglected his duties by continuing his showbiz activities during his first national service stint.
Steve Yoo, one of the country's biggest pop stars in the 1990s and early 2000s, was embroiled in a national scandal after he was found to have evaded military service in 2002. South Korean authorities banned him from the country after he renounced his citizenship and became a US national shortly before he was due to serve in the military.
Going on hiatus to serve in the military is often a threat for budding careers in South Korea's fast-moving entertainment industry. But the evasion of military service also comes with intense public scrutiny and legal repercussions.
Ahead of the ruling on Thursday, Song told reporters that he regretted his actions and was "sorry toward the people who gave me so much love", Seoul Economic Daily reported.
But he did not answer a question about whether he would re-enlist to serve the mandatory duty.

Japan has raised fees for foreigners seeking permanent residency in the country by 20 times to 200,000 yen ($1,270; Â£955).
Those seeking permanent residency must now also meet new income, pension and Japanese-language requirements.
Long lines formed outside immigration offices earlier this week as applicants sought to beat the fee hikes, with Tokyo's main immigration bureau reporting wait times of over seven hours.
The fee increases are part of a series of changes to Japan's immigration policy under Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi, which aim to manage its rapidly growing foreign population.
In July, Japan implemented a five-fold increase in visa fees for all foreigners â its first visa fee hike in 50 years. Authorities said this was meant to "reflect inflation and exchange rate fluctuations".
Although immigration remains politically sensitive and restrictive in Japan, the nation's ageing population is increasingly relying on foreign workers to plug a labour shortage.
Japan's foreign resident population surpassed 4.12 million at the end of 2025, marking a record 9.5% increase from the previous year. This however has led to growing anxieties over immigration and social change.
Takaichi has made managing immigration one of her key priorities since she took office in October last year.
In an X post days before the residency permit hikes set in, Takaichi wrote that her government recognises that "some members of the public may feel a sense of concern or unfairness" as Japan's foreign resident population grows.
"To address these concerns, [the government] is working to ensure that its policies toward foreign nationals are orderly, and that both Japanese citizens and foreign residents can live safely and securely," she wrote.
Before the hikes, it would cost non-permanent residents in Japan 6,000 yen each time they applied to change their residency status or extend their period of stay.
From 1 October, the fee varies according to the duration of stay sought â from 10,000 yen for three months or less, to 75,000 yen for five years or more.
Applicants who face financial hardship or are designated as refugees would be granted discounts.
Aspiring permanent residents must now also earn a stable income at or above the Japanese average. Latest data released in July puts average household income at 5.75 million yen as of 2024.
Micaiah Stevens, who has been living and working in Tokyo for 10 years, was not able to compile the necessary documentation to submit his application for permanent residency before the price hike.
The 37-year-old still plans to apply, but questions the new measures aimed at foreign residents.
"My immediate reaction was that foreigners were being treated a bit too conveniently. We're being asked to make more than the average Japanese person, pay a significantly higher fee, just to be able to work in Japan and provide taxes," he tells the BBC.
"There's already a significant language and cultural barrier that prevents some talent from coming over. This just doesn't strike me as a plan that was thought out to the long term."
From April next year, permanent residency applicants will face even tighter requirements, including basic Japanese language proficiency. This has led to a surge in enrollments at Japanese language schools as well as people signing up to take the Japanese-Language Proficiency Test, local media reported.
Applicants' expected pension benefits must also be equivalent to that of someone who has enrolled into the employee pension system for 30 years, although the value of one's financial assets can be considered if their expected pension benefits fall short.

da5f95001844.text: President Trump and the AI industry have co-signed one of the biggest economic and technological wagers of all time. If it goes right: A new age of abundance — explosive productivity, staggering wealth and a generational leap in American power. If it goes wrong: A catastrophic bust that destroys capital, jobs and, in the words of several involved, threatens widespread human harm . Why it matters: Neither Trump nor the AI titans have plausible deniability. Their fortunes have become so tightly bound that success will be shared — and failure impossible to disown. The big picture: Trump and Big AI have fused their futures around four enormous bets. 1. The economic bet: That trillions poured into chips, data centers and power will create a productivity engine powerful enough to fuel a new Industrial Revolution. AI infrastructure spending is projected to reach $10.3 trillion by 2032, but the payoff remains unproven : one analysis found hyperscalers have spent nearly $1 trillion more on AI since 2024 than AI has generated in revenue. The promise sold by Trump and his tech allies is a new era of growth and abundance. The peril is a historic misallocation of capital on a scale few industries have ever seen. 2. The regulation bet: That Washington can clear the runway for an AI takeoff while leaving the companies largely responsible for policing themselves. The new White House accord signed by Trump and the AI giants enshrines voluntary safeguards, company-led testing and third-party reviews instead of new federal mandates. The promise is American dominance over China. The peril is that self-regulation fails, forcing Washington to intervene only after damage has already been inflicted. 3. The safety bet: That AI can grow vastly more powerful without becoming vastly harder to control. Many of the most dire safety warnings come from AI researchers themselves. Anthropic's own IPO prospectus contemplates scenarios in which advanced AI kills humanity. The promise is almost limitless: superintelligent systems that help cure diseases and accelerate scientific discovery . The peril is self-improving AI that evolves faster than its creators can comprehend or contain. 4. The political bet: That Trump and Big AI can become inseparable without making each other even more toxic. Trump has staked his legacy on winning the AI race — dismissing fears about data centers costing Republicans in the midterms — while the industry has staked billions on the policy environment he's creating. The promise is that Trump and Big AI become partners in the defining technological transformation of the century. The peril is that every AI failure, disruption or backlash becomes a liability they share. The bottom line: Trump and the AI industry are asking the country for a leap of faith at a uniquely fragile moment for both. Americans are deeply dissatisfied with both the economy and Trump's presidency , with his approval rating plunging to record lows ahead of a potentially disastrous midterm season. The AI industry faces an even more basic credibility problem: A new Quinnipiac poll found 74% of Americans lack trust in AI executives, while only 34% believe AI will do more good than harm in their daily lives.

3bc96ec27c59.text: The great AI rebranding is on, led by President Trump and tech titans like Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, who are embracing an alternative term: "Superintelligence," or SI. Why it matters: Leaders in D.C. and Silicon Valley are worried the public backlash against AI and data centers will hamper the development of this staggeringly powerful and existentially dangerous technology. The new label is part of a broader effort to shift the narrative. Driving the news: Flanked by the most powerful figures in tech on Tuesday, Trump officially declared "superintelligence" the preferred terminology of the executive branch. He'd previously solicited alternative terms for AI on Truth Social. "Now we're calling it, again, super. We can say the word super, because the other word is a fake word," Trump said after Tuesday's White House summit. Leaders from Google, Anthropic, Meta, OpenAI, xAI and Nvidia all signed the "White House Accord on Super Intelligence." Huang has recently extended the label to physical infrastructure, referring to data centers as "superintelligence factories." Opposition to the huge, energy-guzzling facilities is dimming the prospects for fast-growing AI firms and some congressional candidates. Between the lines: A rose by any other name would smell as sweet, and AI by any other name will likely seem as scary. Communities are building bipartisan coalitions against data centers, younger workers are anxious about their career prospects, and AI insiders continue to warn about catastrophic risks, notes Axios Communicators author Simon Hernandez-Arthur. Calling it "super intelligence" attempts to evoke the technology's promise without immediately bringing to mind all that negative baggage. What they're saying: Some of the tech executives who appeared with Trump continued to use "AI" in their remarks, but xAI CEO Elon Musk caught himself and pivoted to "SI." Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg has long used the "superintelligenc" branding. Huang, CEO of the world's most valuable company, appears to be leading the charge. He used the term superintelligence twice in a post about the accord and repeatedly invoked it in a panel discussion at the White House. When he slipped once and said "AI," Huang corrected himself: "I am going to get good at this." AI company representatives declined to comment about the name change on the record. Some said their companies were generally supportive of the rebrand and plan to use "SI" when meeting with the president and working with the federal government. Others said they didn't expect it to catch fire outside of those contexts. One source compared it to Trump's renaming of the Gulf of Mexico as the Gulf of America, which many (though not all) oil executives adopted in their external comms and internal communications. By the numbers : "SI" has yet to catch on with the public. A YouGov poll conducted this week found that 53% of respondents considered "artificial intelligence" the better term for the tech, vs. 9% who preferred "super intelligence." What to watch: Trump said on Tuesday that "artificial" intelligence made the technology sound like a hoax: "The name is now superintelligence. That's not a hoax, in fact it's the exact opposite." Polls suggest most Americans agree with him that AI is anything but a hoax. That's why they're so worried.

Member of the Senedd from all parties have urged Welsh ministers to work with the UK government to make sure polluters pay for cleaning up contaminated land.
A motion introduced by Plaid Cymru MS Niamh Salkeld, backed across party lines, also calls for a UK fund to investigate and remediate sites where costs cannot be recovered, and for a framework to test affected land.
The calls come after a BBC documentary by Michael Sheen examined claims toxic waste poisoned people at 14 sites in Wales and England.
A Welsh government minister promised a plan to "progressively restore post-industrial land" and protect communities from "potential risks".
Earlier this month, Sheen went to Westminster to urge MPs to support a testing programme.
Buried with Michael Sheen
What is the truth lying beneath our feet? Michael Sheen uncovers claims of conspiracy, complicity and denial over alleged toxic 'forever chemical' contamination in south Wales.
In the Senedd on Thursday, one member after another recounted in detail the history of sites in their area that they were worried about.
Salkeld, who represents the constituency of Blaenau Gwent Caerffili Rhymni, said her motion was about "making sure that the legacy of our industrial past is managed properly and fairly".
"It's about having a clearer national picture of contaminated land," she said.
"It's about prioritising the sites where the risks are greatest.
"It's about giving local authorities the support that they need, and it's about making sure that where possible, those responsible for pollution contribute to the cost of putting it right.
"The communities living alongside these sites did not create this contamination, so they should not be left with carrying the uncertainty, the potential risks, all the costs."
A number of speakers highlighted the results of a Freedom of Information inquiry by the environmental campaign group Friends of the Earth, external, indicating there were potentially over 45,000 contaminated land sites in Wales, with only 82 sites being designated as contaminated.
Reform MS Andrew Griffin said communities across Wales living near sites that are potentially unsafe "deserve answers".
"They deserve a system capable of establishing the facts, and where action is needed, they deserve to know that the money and the determination are there to see it through.
"As their representatives, the least we can do is to make sure their questions are heard and keep asking them until they get a proper answer."
Welsh Labour leader Ken Skates highlighted a combined pledge of more than Â£240m from the previous Welsh government, led by his party, and Labour ministers at Westminster for coal tip remediation.
He said this demonstrated "that all levels of government need to act fast and need to act together in partnership" to tackle this pollution.
"Councils, citizens and communities cannot afford the cost of remediation, nor can they afford to wait any longer for action."
He called on Plaid Cymru ministers to "stand up for the people of Wales by taking urgent action where it can now".
Conservative Janet Finch-Saunders said local communities "should be able to understand where these sites are located, what risks have been identified, what action is being taken, and whether that action is satisfactory".
"Regular inspections and up-to-date public registers would help," she said.
"We must ensure that lessons are learned from previous incidents where contamination occurs, the response should be timely, coordinated, and proportionate, with clear responsibility for investigating the source.
"This is not simply about dealing with contamination after it has occurred. It is about prevention, enforcement, and accountability."
Rural Resilience and Sustainability Minister Llyr Gruffydd promised the Welsh government was "absolutely committed to developing a Wales-wide strategy to progressively restore post-industrial land and to protect communities from those potential risks that come with that legacy".
He said he had heard the "calls for action", pledging he would "ensure that former industrial land is made safe".
"I will protect public health and deliver long-overdue environmental justice for the communities that have been most affected by this," he added.
The motion was passed with no objections.

Explosions were heard overnight in Ethiopia's capital, some in the area of the military headquarters in the west and another in the south of the city, residents and diplomatic sources say.
The blasts came hours after drone flights were banned over Addis Ababa and a week after fighting erupted in the north between the army and a newly launched alliance of armed groups including forces from the Tigray region.
A source linked to the opposition fighters told the Reuters news agency they were behind what they said were drone strikes.
"It was very loud. It was strong enough to set off car alarms," a resident in a southern area of the city, near the base of the secret service, told BBC Amharic.
He estimated that he heard the explosion in the Gotera neighbourhood some time around 00:30 local time (21:30 GMT).
Another resident told the BBC that he and his friends were playing games when they heard an explosion.
He lives in the western suburb of Torhayloch, a neighbourhood close to the military headquarters.
There were no official reports confirming the cause of the explosions, the exact locations affected or whether there were any casualties or damage.
The office of Ethiopia's Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed, the defence ministry as well as the federal and Addis Ababa police have not responded to BBC requests for comment.

Asiaâs most populous countries are grappling with a graduate employment crisis, with huge numbers of young people entering job markets that lack roles to absorb them. In Indonesia, job creation has largely stalled in high-skilled sectors; India has seen college graduate numbers far outpace new, available jobs; and Chinaâs record number of university leavers has driven youth unemployment up to 18.9%.

- Published
US convicted murderer Christa Pike is in hospital and being given "life-saving measures" after Tennessee authorities failed in their attempt to execute her by lethal injection.
The case of Pike, whose attempted execution had already been the subject of a high-profile legal battle, has raised a number of questions.
These include what went went wrong, what happens next, and - for opponents of the death penalty - fresh concerns around the suffering of an inmate when an execution does not go to plan.
What happened?
Pike, 50, was sentenced to death in 1996 for the murder of 19-year-old Colleen Slemmer, an attack that was perpetrated alongside her then-boyfriend Tadaryl Shipp.
She was scheduled to be put to death on Wednesday evening, local time. The injections were allowed by the US Supreme Court at the eleventh hour after the legal battle.
Pike was given two syringes of the drug pentobarbital, though her legal team said these failed to stop her heartbeat and that she could still be heard snoring.
The Tennessee Department of Correction defended the method it used, and said "the protocol does not allow for additional procedures beyond what was carried out this evening".
The state protocol does not clearly specify what should happen if an inmate remains alive after a second dose, according to the AP news agency.
Authorities have yet to provide their explanation of why the dosage given to Pike proved to be non-fatal, although medical experts have provided theories of their own.
Dr Joel Zivot, a professor at the Emory University School of Medicine who told the BBC he had been retained by Pike's legal team as a medical expert, said she probably never achieved a sufficient blood level of pentobarbital to cause apnoea and cardiovascular failure.
What happens next?
The state correction department added that Pike had been taken to an off-site medical facility.
One of her lawyers said she was "being provided life-saving measures" in hospital.
Her health status is unclear as of Thursday morning.
In his emailed comments to the BBC, Zivot said: "It's very possible that as a consequence of the delay of the beginning of resuscitation she will have a brain injury."
A third-party review has been ordered by the state governor, Bill Lee, who also says the year's last remaining execution will not go ahead as planned.
May Martinez, the mother of Colleen Slemmer who had pushed for Pike's execution to take place, told NBC News the events had been "a mess".
Opponents of the death penalty have similarly been quick to react.
Maya Foa, the chief executive of international legal organisation Reprieve, said: "We cannot know exactly what went wrong, because so much happened behind a curtain â lethal injection relies on secrecy at every stage, to hide the violence of the state taking a human life."
Authorities are yet to say whether they will try again to execute Pike. There is a historical precedent of authorities making a second attempt to execute those on death row.
What is the drug pentobarbital?
Pentobarbital is a potent sedative that slows down the body, including the nervous system. Doctors sometimes use it as a treatment for certain conditions, but in high doses it can also be used as a lethal injection to cause death.
Its use in lethal injections came under renewed scrutiny last year after a US federal government review - which took place under the presidency of Joe Biden - raised concerns about the drug's potential for "unnecessary pain and suffering".
His government banned its use in federal executions but that did not bind individual states such as Tennessee, which can choose their own methods.
In recent years, states have found some drugs needed for lethal injections harder to come by, because pharmaceutical companies have opposed the use of their products for such purposes.
The Tennessee Department of Correction has not specifically addressed an allegation from Pike's legal team that the pentobarbital it used was "degraded". Drugs may degrade for a number of reasons, including if it has aged beyond its use-by date and its potency has decreased.
The department issued a broader defence of its method, writing in a statement: "The lethal injection chemical in the protocol has consistently been effective."
Has this happened before?
The attempted execution of Pike was not the first in Tennessee in 2026 that did not go to plan.
The execution of Tony Carruthers, who was convicted of kidnapping and murdering three people in 1994, was postponed in May after staff were unable to find a vein to administer a lethal injection. He was given a one-year reprieve by Governor Bill Lee.
More widely across the US, the issue of botched executions continues to cause alarm.
In 2022, more than a third of executions in the US were botched or highly problematic, according to the Death Penalty Information Center (DPI) - an organisation that provides statistics and research on the death penalty but does not take a stance on it morally.
The DPI says lethal injection has the highÂest rate of botched exeÂcuÂtions.
An incident in Oklahoma in 2014 gained particular notoriety. The execution of Clayton Lockett was postponed after 20 minutes because the lethal injection of three drugs failed to work properly when one of his veins ruptured, and he went on to write and shake uncontrollably.
In the US, 27 of the 50 states have the death penalty under state law. The federal government can also carry out executions after President Donald Trump, a supporter of capital punishment, ended a moratorium last year, However, it is yet to actually carry out any executions since then.

The Iran war has been a proving ground for ADNOCâs massive bet on artificial intelligence. AI firm AIQ, which counts the Abu Dhabi oil giant as its largest customer and shareholder, has gone from a nice-to-have before the conflict to a source of crucial real-time insight into drilling, production, and facilities management, AIQ CEO Dennis Jol told Semafor. Six months of war and AI fever have added urgency to the rollout of Genesis, an operating system AIQ is pitching to energy companies. It runs large-scale agentic AI across upstream and downstream operations without relying on any single AI model provider like Anthropic or OpenAI.
AIQ is testing its tools in energy patches, including Kuwait, India, Malaysia, and Vietnam. A pilot in Egypt predicted a pump failure 45 days in advance, according to the firmâs chief technology officer. AIQ has made its first hire in the UK, is weighing other locations such as Houston, and has identified 100 potential acquisition targets as it seeks growth, Jol said.

04ff6a702d60.text:
The Scoop
Texas state politics could delay the final investment decision on one of the USâ largest new data center projects.
Project Kilby, a joint venture between Chevron and the newly formed energy project developer Joulent, is set to use nearly 3 gigawatts of âbehind-the-meterâ gas turbines â that is, unconnected to the state grid â to power a massive Microsoft data center in West Texas. Preliminary earthmoving work is already underway at the site while the developers finalize construction contracts and await final state permits.
But the final investment decision, originally expected by the end of this year, could be pushed to 2027 following a moratorium on new data center permits imposed last month by Gov. Greg Abbott, according to Daniel Droog, Chevronâs vice president for power solutions. In general across the AI infrastructure industry, which has been growing rapidly in Texas, âthe permitting and regulatory side has caused some slowdown or potential delay in the system,â Droog said in an interview. Still, Kilby is on track to produce its first electrons by 2028, he said. The project also has some new management: Two former executives from the LNG exporter Cheniere were tapped by Joulent for C-level leadership roles, Semafor can exclusively report.
Know More
Project Kilby has a number of advantages over other nascent hyperscaler data center projects that should give it staying power through the current political backlash. For one, the project will generate all its own power, and therefore not raise electricity costs for other consumers on the local grid. Joulent was formed from the investment firm Engine No. 1, which bought up a number of gas turbines several years ago before the supply chain crunch really kicked in, meaning the project is already equipped with its most essential hardware. It sits on top of the Permian oil and gas basin, where gas has been so abundant that itâs practically treated as a waste product; part of Chevronâs motivation for pursuing the project is to create a new anchor customer for its own gas. And itâs located in a rural area where NIMBYs and land use conflicts arenât much of a concern. âFor getting that equation right, the Permian is very advantageous,â Droog said.
Michael Wortley, Joulentâs new CFO, said that the finalization of the projectâs construction contracts is âa couple weeks, if not days, away.â As for state permits, he said he was confident that the project ticks off the various prerequisites Abbott has outlined: âIf youâre part of the solution rather than the problem, ultimately youâll get your permits.â
Timâs view
The most draconian restrictions on data center development, including the moratoria imposed by New York and Texas, are likely a temporary phenomenon that will ease once the November elections have passed and more basic ground rules take shape. Still, the direction of travel for this industry is from a Wild West of essentially unbridled development to a more regulated status quo. That means investors will need to practice patience, despite the market signals screaming at them to build AI infrastructure as quickly as possible.
I donât see any signs that Project Kilby is fundamentally in jeopardy: A 20-year offtake deal with Microsoft is about as bankable as a power project can get. But as is often the case in the US, politics remain a bigger roadblock than capital, hardware, or workforce. If even a project with as much momentum behind it as Kilby sees a possible slowdown ahead, other data center developers should temper their expectations for pacing accordingly.
Notable
- Federal legislation to shield consumers from higher power costs related to data centers was blocked by Senate Democrats on Wednesday, who said the legislation was âtoothlessâ and did not address energy affordability concerns.

Saudi Arabia expects wider budget deficits for several years as it ramps up spending to support growth in the face of regional conflict. Higher oil prices have largely offset lower export volumes, lifting revenue above prewar estimates, but spending is set to rise faster.
Next yearâs preliminary budget shows the kingdom is willing to keep borrowing to bolster its defenses and build trade routes that bypass the Strait of Hormuz. That raises the prospect of government debt breaching its 40%-of-GDP ceiling before the decade is out if growth doesnât pick up.
The Finance Ministry now sees the governmentâs budget deficit at 4.9% of GDP this year, up from the 3.3% it predicted late last year.
