Zambian President Hakainde Hichilema used his first trip abroad since his re-election last month to tell Gulf investors to fully comply with the countryâs local procurement rules, he said.
Zambia is Africaâs second-largest producer of copper, whose prices have soared as demand rises for metals used in electric vehicles and power grids. Hichilemaâs stance matches that of regional rivals who are trying to use the scramble for critical minerals to drive economic development.
Regulations introduced a year ago require mines to source a higher share of core goods and services locally. During his trip, Hichilema met Ali Rashed Alrashdi, CEO of an Abu Dhabi-based owner of Mopani mine, one of Zambiaâs oldest copper mines. In a Facebook post, he urged Mopani to raise output as Zambia pushes to more than triple copper output to 3 million tonnes by 2030. Critics say the drive to buy local goods can inflate costs where domestic suppliers lack capacity, opening the door to middlemen who resell imports.
During the visit, Zambia signed six non-binding agreements worth $2.14 billion with UAE investors, covering healthcare, renewable energy, logistics, and technology.

dfe8ea3ded2c.text: The Supreme Court on Monday will hear arguments in a case that could determine the fate of state-court lawsuits nationwide seeking climate damages from oil giants. Why it matters: Billions and billions of dollars are at stake for the oil industry in dozens of cases brought by state and local governments. Governments face mounting costs from climate change that litigants link directly to the companies' products. The big picture: SCOTUS is considering whether federal law blocks damage claims under state laws for the effects of interstate and global emissions. State of play: It's specifically about litigation against Exxon and Suncor that the city and county of Boulder filed in 2018. But dozens of state-court cases are active in California, Connecticut, New York, Massachusetts and beyond. The cases aren't identical. But overall they accuse oil giants of concealing risks or making deceptive statements, and seek damages for climate-related costs. Here are a few big themes and dynamics ahead of Monday morning: This is a blockbuster. The decision will be the culmination of an intense, years-long battle (unless it's not, but more on that in a moment). There's a high level of organizing, lobbying and advocacy among industry and climate advocates alike around these state cases. Industry and allied groups say the wave of cases threatens oil companies' very ability to operate. It's a sign that both sides see litigation as a critical battleground on climate. Take a spin through the case docket and you'll see what I mean. A kicked can is possible. SCOTUS might not decide the question of federal preemption. That's because it's also considering whether it even has jurisdiction right now. The question turns on whether a Colorado Supreme Court decision to let Boulder's case proceed in state court can be reviewed at this stage. Trump policies are a new(ish) wrinkle. U.S. and industry briefs argue that addressing an interstate and global topic with these state claims is preempted by federal law and the Constitution. But watch whether the White House attempt to repeal key Clean Air Act authority over greenhouse gases is used as a cudgel against federal preemption claims. This won't be the main argument — instead, the litigants against oil companies contend these cases are well within the bounds of traditional, longstanding state powers. But it could surface. There's an important absence on the bench. Justice Samuel Alito this week recused himself from the case. "Justice Alito's recusal is likely bad news to the petitioners as he is among the more preemption-friendly justices on the Court," writes environmental law scholar Jonathan Adler. There could be ripple effects. A ruling in favor of the oil companies could also jeopardize separate state climate policies. New York and Vermont have "climate superfund" laws that assess damages against fossil fuel companies to help fund climate adaptation. They're both tied up in court. Several states are considering some version of these laws. Sign up here for Axios' Future of Energy newsletter.

ccba07dc1e57.text: President Trump is expected to tap Jay Clayton , his director of national intelligence, for a new role as the White House's artificial intelligence — or in Trump's words, " super intelligence " — czar. Why it matters: Clayton, who Trump previously told Axios would be a good idea for AI czar, is expected to take on the second title, sources told Axios. Calls for government intervention into AI's rapid development are growing, but the president has repeatedly said he favors a light regulatory touch and has called fears about the tech's threat to humanity a hoax . Trump had been warming to the idea of tapping Clayton, who as DNI has shown that he sees the security threats AI poses as serious. Driving the news: Trump could make the announcement as soon as Friday, sources familiar confirmed to Axios. A White House official said in a statement to Axios that "[a]ny personnel announcement will be announced directly by the President. Any reporting until then is baseless speculation." Catch up quick: Asked by Axios earlier this week who he wants to be AI czar, Trump said: "I have somebody in mind." Clayton is "a good man. He's right here. That's a good idea," Trump added when prompted. Zoom out: Trump announced last month that he'd create an "AI Force" and would soon name a new AI czar, but offered few details on what the Force would do. Since then, he's huddled with several titans of the AI industry — some of whom have been key voices in advocating for a slowdown of the tech . Flashback: Clayton was elevated to be Trump's principle intelligence adviser atop the 18-agency intelligence community earlier this year after his prior DNI, Tulsi Gabbard, resigned in May. Previously the U.S. Attorney for the Southern District of New York, Clayton's qualifications received bipartisan blessings. After sidestepping questions over who won the 2020 election during his confirmation, Clayton was confirmed on party lines, without Democratic support. Go deeper: Trump's call for "AI Force" sets off weekend scramble

Riot police have clashed with protesters as thousands of students demonstrating over education standards disrupted more than 560 schools in France on Friday.
Fires have burned in the streets as high school pupils and others objected to a lack of teachers, overcrowded classrooms and run-down buildings.
The protests began last week in Paris and have spread across the country, with cities including Montpellier, Nantes and Marseille affected.
French justice minister Gerald Darmanin said things had "gone from high-school student demonstrations to a public order disturbance".
On Friday, a 17-year-old was arrested on suspicion of attempted homicide after protests in Belfort, north-eastern France, where a police officer was targeted.
At least 65 staff members have been injured in the unrest, the education ministry said.
In the Paris suburb of Pantin police charged at protesters and made arrests after projectiles where thrown at officers.
Meanwhile, in Strasbourg tear gas was deployed as police feared conditions would become more hostile, according to the Reuters news agency.
Rubbish bins have also been set on fire in Rennes and Paris.
"As far as we're concerned, we've won - our school is closed this morning," Lola, a 16-year-old protester, told the AFP news agency on Friday.
She said police actions had made things worse.
"It makes us even angrier - the police have no right to hit us or use tear gas on us," she added.
In Marseille, fireworks were thrown at police and teachers were also inadvertently splashed with petrol at a school there, officials said.
"Significant damage" had been done to school facilities, the education ministry said.
Nelson Mandela high school in Nantes had suffered more than â¬2m (Â£1.7m) damage, according to the regional government.
The blockades and protests started last week before spreading to hundreds of schools across the country.
Students say school hours are too long, classrooms too hot and too many members of staff are off work.
It comes at a crucial time for French President Emmanuel Macron, six months before next year's presidential election.
Budget cuts planned, which will impact on education funding, have infuriated the young protesters.
French Education Minister Ãdouard Geffray claimed on Friday that the movement had been hijacked by non-students.
He told French broadcaster BFMTV teachers had said "the people in front of me were not my students".
Parents have also been worried that their children have become caught up in a wave of violence and unrest.
At the Claude Monet school in southern Paris, 53-year-old Anya was looking for her son.
"We banned him from coming. I hope he isn't here, but he did leave the house, so," she told AFP.
"We're afraid the situation might escalate."
Darmanin, the justice minister, said prosecutors had been asked to hold parents liable for damage caused by their children and "pay for repairs".
He said since the start of the movement, about 2,000 people - most of who were children - had been taken into custody.
Many French unions have given their support to the protesting students.
Education union SNEP-FSU, public services union SNUEP-FSU and Solidaires have all called for members to support them.
Solidaires Trade Union Federation said in a statement: "Let's not let them fire on our children.
"Secondary school pupils have the freedom of assembly, association and demonstration."

334def10a106.text: By — Collin Binkley, Associated Press Collin Binkley, Associated Press By — John Leicester, Associated Press John Leicester, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/world/g7-nations-agree-to-release-100-million-barrels-of-oil-including-diesel Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter G7 nations agree to release 100 million barrels of oil, including diesel World Oct 2, 2026 12:16 PM EDT WASHINGTON (AP) — The Group of Seven industrial nations said on Friday that they plan to release 100 million barrels of oil in the coming weeks, starting with "substantial" amounts of diesel after the fuel recently hit record high prices in the United States, where President Donald Trump said the diesel release would happen "immediately." Trump and his Republican Party face pressure to address surging prices ahead of the Nov. 3 midterm elections, and Trump announced the action Friday on social media. The president's approval ratings on the economy hit a new low according to an AP-NORC poll as the Iran war and his trade battles have increased U.S. prices for oil and other goods. WATCH: How the diesel price spike is rippling through nearly every part of the economy Gas prices in the U.S. and abroad have soared during the eight-month-long war, a cost Trump has repeatedly said is worth it for making sure Iran does not obtain nuclear weapons. The national average for a gallon of diesel in the U.S. was $6.37 on Friday, according to AAA, after hitting a record $6.52 on Sept. 22. Educate your inbox Subscribe to Here’s the Deal, our politics newsletter for analysis you won’t find anywhere else. Enter your email address Subscribe Form error message goes here. Thank you. Please check your inbox to confirm. France holds the rotating presidency of the G7 group and made the announcement in a statement released after videoconference talks that Macron presided over. The International Energy Agency will coordinate the effort to combat soaring fuel prices. "We will implement our commitments with a coordinated release through the IEA of 100 million barrels (MB) to begin immediately over 4 months, including a front-loaded substantial diesel release within the first 20 days by G7 members and partners," the statement said. Some Republicans in the U.S. had called for Trump to ban U.S. exports of diesel to try to bring domestic prices down. New York Governor Kathy Hochul has said the woman at the centre of the Cornell University rape case was "failed" at "every turn".
The woman, known as Jane Doe in legal documents, alleges she was drugged and raped by several men at a fraternity house in 2024.
The case was investigated at the time but no charges were laid. It recently reopened after the woman filed a civil lawsuit last month that thrust the allegations into the national spotlight.
At a news conference on Friday, Hochul said she was "deeply disturbed" by how the investigation was handled. She has now appointed New York Attorney General Letitia James to lead it.
This appointment was made after Hochul said she "lost faith" in the local prosecutor's ability to oversee the investigation.
Expressing outrage that local prosecutors did not interview the accuser themselves, Hochul on Friday said Doe was "failed by people and institutions with an obligation to protect her".
She has also vowed to close a "loophole" that prevents prosecutors from pursuing rape charges in cases when the victim has voluntarily consumed drugs or alcohol.
"If someone is too intoxicated to consent it should not matter if they chose to use drugs or alcohol," said Hochul, adding: "Voluntary intoxication is not a licence for gang rape."
James appeared alongside Hochul at Friday's news conference, pledging to "lead a process guided by the facts and the law".
She said her office would interview witnesses and pursue prosecutions if warranted.
District Attorney Matthew Van Houten, who previously led the investigation, has defended his office's previous decision not to file charges in the case, arguing they were not given enough evidence to meet the legal threshold.
Van Houten said much of the information released in recent weeks about the case was not passed to his office.
Cornell has said it provided evidence to the district attorney's office from its own investigation, including a Snapchat group chat in which fraternity members discussed a "free" sexual encounter with Doe on the night of the alleged assault.

51e6a41bf25f.text:
A toad’s winter refuge could be a biohazard.
Some young Yosemite toads emerge from their first winter underground infected with the deadly chytrid fungus Batrachochytrium dendrobatidis, or Bd, researchers report September 23 in Functional Ecology. Although the fungus typically spreads through water, the finding points to an unexpectedly risky period as toads wait out harsh winters in burrows beneath feet of snow.
Bd has hit amphibian populations hard. The fungus attacks amphibians’ skin, preventing electrolytes and fluids from entering the body, and often leads to heart failure. Infections, which can kill the frogs, are responsible for declines in at least 500 species and 90 possible extinctions, according to a 2019 estimate.
The disease is one reason why Yosemite toads (Anaxyrus canorus) are listed as threatened under the U.S. Endangered Species Act. The toads live in California’s Sierra Nevada mountains, where the toads spend most of their time on dry land. Mature adults breed in shallow pools of water. But high-elevation living also means they spend roughly half the year underground during brumation, a hibernation-like state for reptiles and amphibians.
How a water-loving fungus sticks around even after toads spend a long, cold winter underground is a mystery, says David Daversa, an ecologist at UCLA. “It’s a waterborne pathogen; how does that happen?”
To find out, Daversa and colleagues trekked to Yosemite National Park. The team captured Yosemite toads of all ages — including the youngest toads both before they went into their burrows and after they emerged — and swabbed their skin to test for Bd.
Surprisingly, the fungus was more prevalent in juvenile toads after their first winter than in adults breeding in the water. An average of roughly 23 percent of juveniles tested positive for Bd before their first brumation. In the spring, more than 90 percent of those young toads emerged from their burrows with sometimes severe infections. Less than half of breeding adults tested positive.
Daversa says it’s unclear why the fungus thrives underground. It’s possible that young toads burrow with undetectable infections that grow over time, or that the fungus spreads when many toads burrow together.
Also unknown is whether other brumating amphibians face similar risks during the winter. Still, the findings have already had some practical implications. A reintroduction program with the San Francisco Zoo and U.S. National Park Service that aims to boost Yosemite toad populations now focuses on releasing mature toads that are past those first Bd-vulnerable years.
By thinking beyond the water, Daversa says, perhaps conservationists “could nip chytrid in the bud in these early life stages when it seems to proliferate most.”

d07c12be1fe2.text: By — Fabiola Sanchez, Associated Press Fabiola Sanchez, Associated Press By — Jonathan Castellón, Associated Press Jonathan Castellón, Associated Press By — Sarah Raza, Associated Press Sarah Raza, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/nation/live-map-track-the-path-of-hurricane-rachel Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter LIVE MAP: Track the path of Hurricane Rachel Nation Oct 2, 2026 11:55 AM EDT MEXICO CITY (AP) — Hurricane Rachel has been upgraded to a Category 3 storm off Mexico's Pacific coast as northern Mexico and parts of the U.S. Southwest were reeling from flooding and damage from the remnants of Hurricane Polo earlier this week. Track the path of Hurricane Rachel below. The storm, located about 235 miles (380 kilometers) south off the southern tip of Baja California, was continuing west-northwest at 3 mph (6 kph) and expected to strengthen Friday before weakening this weekend, according to the National Hurricane Center. READ MORE: Tropical Pacific moisture drenches central U.S. as another Pacific hurricane forms The maximum sustained winds were 120 miles per hour (193 kph) as of Thursday evening. Rachel's swells are expected to generate life-threatening surf and rip-current conditions off Mexico's coast, the NHC warned. Mexican authorities said Thursday they remain on alert because of forecasts of very heavy rain in the states of Baja California Sur, Sinaloa, and Jalisco, and the possibility of landslides, rising river levels, overflowing rivers and flooding in low-lying areas. On Wednesday night, the U.S. Embassy in Mexico warned U.S. citizens in Cabos San Lucas, a popular vacation destination for Americans, of beach and port closures and deadly rip currents. The Pacific has seen an unusually busy hurricane season, which experts have attributed to El Niño, which has fueled crippling droughts in Mexico and Central America and floods in other parts of the region. In the Pacific, it has resulted in warmer waters and wind patterns that act as fodder for hurricanes. Tropical Storm Nolo continued its northwest approach away from Hawaii on Thursday, though the National Weather Service said it could strengthen into a hurricane by the weekend. Northern Mexico still reeling from Polo Parts of northern Mexico were still reeling from floods and wider destruction left by Polo. Hundreds of people remained displaced or had their homes destroyed, and at least 13 municipalities remained flooded Thursday night, according to local authorities. Lucía Vegas, who lives in the small town of Bacabachi in the border state of Sonora, said it was a miracle she survived severe flooding as it swept through her community. She, her husband and three children were left homeless. READ MORE: Hurricane Polo makes landfall in Baja California, toppling trees and flooding coastal communities Vegas said she and her family managed to survive thanks to their dog. In the middle of the night, as the floodwaters were rising, the dog woke her by shaking water off herself, giving the family enough time to climb a ladder onto the roof of their home just minutes before it was completely flooded. "Right now, we have been left with nothing," the 39-year-old woman said through tears. Storm remnants drench central U.S. Areas in Texas, Nebraska, Missouri and Iowa were still under flood watch Thursday afternoon as storm remnants continued to batter the region, flooding streets and neighborhoods and setting off water rescues. Wednesday was the wettest day on record for Lincoln, Nebraska, which received 6.1 inches of rainfall, according to the University of Nebraska-Lincoln Climate Office. In Omaha, which received 4.7 inches of rain Wednesday, the fire department said it responded to 80 water rescues over a three-hour period ending early Thursday. Some floodwaters reached depths of 8 feet. Schools remained open. But many buses never made it out of flooded parking lots, prompting officials to ask parents to transport their students to school. San Antonio, Texas, was under a flash-flood warning through Thursday evening, and the city urged residents to avoid unnecessary travel. More than 19,000 residents across the state were without power Thursday afternoon, according to PowerOutage.us. Videos posted on social media showed floodwaters in Texas creating waves along Interstate 35 in Denton. In Chicago, a wastewater treatment and stormwater management utility urged residents to conserve water use to prevent flooding and stormwater backup. "We encourage everyone to conserve water when possible to create more capacity in our systems," utility President Kari K. Steele said in a statement Wednesday. In Kansas, Gov. Laura Kelly issued an emergency proclamation on Wednesday ahead of the storms that allows state resources to assist first responders in hard-hit communities. Raza reported from Sioux Falls, South Dakota, and Castellón reported from Bacabachi, Mexico. Associated Press writer John Raby in Cross Lanes, West Virginia, contributed to this report. - Published
Intensified Russian drone and missile strikes are "tearing Kyiv apart", the mayor of Ukraine's capital has warned.
Vitaliy Klitschko said the city was now in a "very dramatic situation" as Moscow was battering its "critical infrastructure, logistics, housing" and other key facilities.
He was speaking after Kyiv's defence council held a crisis meeting, following new Russian strikes on a key bridge that caused traffic chaos. The city's data centres have also been recently hit, resulting in internet outages.
President Vladimir Putin earlier said Russia was acting in response to Ukraine's strikes on Russian energy facilities, despite the fact that it was Moscow that had first launched such attacks.
"We're talking about survival," Klitschko said at Friday's defence council meeting with Kyiv's top military, security, emergencies and police officials.
Russia's aim was to "sow panic", he said, stressing that the capital would "prevail - but only through the joint efforts of those who love it and care for it".
The mayor was speaking just hours after Kyiv's key Pivdennyi (Southern) bridge was hit in an overnight Russian drone attack. On Friday evening it was struck again - the fourth time in two days.
The bridge is one of the main transport arteries across the Dnipro River dividing western and eastern parts of Kyiv.
All metro and automobile traffic is now suspended across the bridge, causing major delays across the city. Restrictions are also in place on Kyiv's two other key bridges.
Kyiv's current population is estimated to be about three million, and many residents rely heavily on the city's metro network.
One person was killed in the capital when a multi-storey residential building was hit overnight, Ukraine's state emergencies service DSNS said.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said Putin had decided in early September that "there are no rules now" when attacking Ukraine.
In a published excerpt from his interview to the Financial Times, Zelensky said: "The Russians have failed to occupy us. So now they are carrying out massive attacks and mass killings.
"They want to destroy our bridges... our data centres, the internet, mobile networks, hospitals, kindergartens, schools, universities - everything. They want people to flee their cities."
Putin insisted that Russia's attacks on Ukrainian economic targets were a direct response to Ukraine's strikes on Russia's oil refineries and its ships in the Black Sea.
"Now from every direction we're receiving calls 'let's stop'. But they started it," Putin said after his Thursday's wide-ranging speech at the Valdai foreign policy forum.
Putin admitted Kyiv had "got some results" from its refinery attacks and Russia had lost about 1% of its GDP. Ukraine maintains it began attacking Russian oil infrastructure because it helps the Kremlin finance the war.
Russia has targeted Ukrainian energy infrastructure, ramping up attacks every winter since Putin launched a full-scale invasion in 2022.
